title: ComPart: From First Principles to FCC
subtitle: Complete Series & Lecture Planning Documentation: Deliverables, Abstracts, Learning Outcomes, and Verified Reference Catalogs
scope: 15 Curriculum Series (Parts 0–14) · 123 Dedicated Lectures · 1426 Verified Primary References
description: ComPart: From First Principles to FCC is a unified graduate-level training programme spanning the full intellectual and engineering stack of experimental and phenomenological high-energy physics—from foundational mathematical physics and quantum field theory through detector instrumentation, Monte Carlo simulation, Particle Flow reconstruction, and machine learning to flagship analyses at the CERN Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee and FCC-hh).

architecture.structure: 15 Parts (Parts 0–14) and 123 enumerated Lectures (138 dedicated unit planning pages in this document). Note: the summary header in the original draft outline listed 107 lectures; this complete specification covers all 123 enumerated lectures across Parts 0–14 without omission.
architecture.dependencySpine: 1 → 2 → 3 → 5 → 7 → 8 → 9 → 11 → 13, bookended by Part 0 (Orientation) and Part 14 (Research Practice). Parts 4, 6, and 10 run in parallel; Part 12 branches from Parts 3 and 9.
architecture.fourTrackDesign: Dedicated navigation paths for Analyst, Detector, Simulation, and Software specialists, sharing a common mathematical, statistical, and Key4hep/EDM4hep core.
architecture.twoStageLabs: Every lecture pairs a transparent Stage 1 Python/NumPy/PyTorch first-principles prototype with a Stage 2 production HEP workflow (ROOT, Geant4, DD4hep, ACTS, PandoraPFA, FastJet, Key4hep, FCCAnalyses, pyhf, hls4ml).
architecture.referenceRigor: Every Part and every Lecture includes ≥ 10 verified primary references (textbooks, arXiv preprints, peer-reviewed DOIs, CERN Yellow Reports, and official documentation) with clickable links.

parts.abstract: Part 0 situates the entire ComPart: From First Principles to FCC curriculum inside the operational reality of modern collider physics. Rather than treating theoretical formalisms, detector instrumentation, Monte Carlo simulation, and data analysis as disconnected silos, this orientation maps the end-to-end chain from fundamental length and energy scales through the CERN accelerator complex and general-purpose hermetic detectors to the 91 km Future Circular Collider (FCC) integrated programme. It establishes standardized study workflows, reproducible software environments, and four role-specific learning tracks—Analyst, Detector, Simulation, and Software—so learners can navigate the graduate spine systematically while building production-grade HEP literacy from day one.

deliverables.lectureNote: A 35-page orientation monograph defining ComPart’s natural-unit conventions (ℏ = c = 1, GeV–fm–barn conversions), collider coordinate systems (x, y, z, r, ϕ, θ, η), luminosity and cross-section scaling relations, the CERN injector chain from Linac4 to LHC/FCC, and the four-track dependency graph.
deliverables.lab: Reproducible containerized/Conda environment setup bridging local Python notebooks ( numpy , scipy , vector , pdg API) with CERN open-source infrastructure ( ROOT , Key4hep , FCCAnalyses , CERN Open Data ).
deliverables.problemSet: Dimensional-analysis and scale-conversion drills, an end-to-end luminosity/event-yield calculation for LHC vs. FCC-ee (Z-pole, W W , ZH, tt̄), and a verified software-stack smoke test executing a minimal pdg query and FCCAnalyses /Scikit-HEP script. Exit criterion: reproducible environment verification and ≥ 85% accuracy on unit/scale diagnostics.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine pairing CERN official accelerator/experiment documentation, the 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics, and the 2025 FCC Feasibility Study Report; advanced/optional progression into the 2019 FCC Conceptual Design Reports (CDR Vols. 1–3), ATLAS/CMS JINST detector papers, and HSF/Key4hep software architecture papers.

lectures.abstract: This lecture constructs a quantitative map of experimental high-energy physics, linking the de Broglie resolution relation λ = ℏ/p across ten orders of magnitude from atomic physics to the 100 TeV frontier. Students examine the staged CERN accelerator complex—Linac4, PS Booster, PS, SPS, and the 27 km LHC—before transitioning to the 91 km FCC integrated programme: FCC-ee as a high-luminosity electroweak, Higgs, and top-quark factory √ operating at s = 91, 160, 240, and 365 GeV, followed by FCC-hh. The lecture concludes with an end-to-end anatomical walkthrough of a collider experiment, tracing a single bunch crossing from parton collision through onion-layer detection, trigger selection, reconstruction, and final cross-section measurement.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete scale-conversion table (GeV, fm, ps, pb −1 + − 4 2 4 R ), synchrotron radiation power scaling P γ ∝ E /(ρ m ) contrasting e e vs. pp machines, collider luminosity formula L and event yield N = σ L dt, and an annotated end-to-end signal flow diagram for ATLAS/CMS and FCC-ee concepts (CLD/IDEA).
deliverables.lab: Python notebook querying the 2024 pdg REST/Python API to plot Standard Model particle masses, widths, and lifetimes across scales, paired with an interactive CERN Open Data event-display inspection ( opendata.cern.ch ).
deliverables.problemSet: Five quantitative exercises: (1) natural-unit conversions of ℏc and cross-section barns; (2) computing synchrotron energy loss per turn at LEP, LHC, and FCC-ee (Z vs. tt̄); (3) estimating expected Z, ZH, and tt̄ yields from FCC-ee Feasibility Study integrated luminosities; (4) comparing lepton vs. hadron collider initial-state kinematics; (5) identifying particle signatures (e ± , γ, µ ± , π ± , jet, E T miss ) in a real CMS Open Data event. Exit criterion: all five problems verified within 2% numerical tolerance.

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes the pedagogical methodology and technical operating system for ComPart. Graduate-level mastery in experimental and computa- tional HEP requires closing the loop between pen-and-paper derivations, clean numerical prototypes, and community-maintained production frameworks. We define the ComPart three-pass study cycle (analytic derivation, Python first-principles verification, and production HEP tool execution) and map four structured specialization tracks: Analyst (kinematics, statistics, ROOT / RDataFrame , Scikit-HEP , FCCAnalyses ), Detector (electromagnetism, drift/signal physics, Garfield++ , DD4hep ), Simulation (Monte Carlo integration, particle transport, Geant4 , EDM4hep ), and Software (numerical linear algebra, C++/Python interoperability, ACTS , Key4hep ). Learners construct a personalized curriculum plan and validate their local-to-CVMFS/container toolchain.

deliverables.lectureNote: ComPart Study Playbook detailing the four track dependency matrices, required vs. optional lecture depth per track, standards for scientific note-taking, unit testing of physics code, and reproducibility checklists (version pinning, random-seed control, provenance).

Exit criterion: green CI build and verified execution log.

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 0 (Orientation) and standard undergraduate single-variable calculus and introductory linear algebra. parts.abstract: Part 1 builds the rigorous mathematical spine required to formulate physical laws, design detector and accelerator models, and implement stable scientific software for collider experiments. Spanning eight tightly integrated lectures, it progresses from multivariable vector calculus and numerical linear algebra through complex-plane transforms, boundary-value PDEs, Lorentz-covariant tensor algebra, variational mechanics, and Lie group representation theory, culminating in IEEE-754 floating-point analysis and high-precision numerical algorithms. Every mathematical construct is anchored directly to its HEP realization—Jacobians in phase-space integrals, SVD and Kalman covariance propagation in tracking, Laplace poles in front-end pulse shaping, Green’s functions in Shockley–Ramo signal induction, and Poincaré/SU(N ) representations in particle classification.

deliverables.lectureNote: An 8-chapter graduate mathematical-methods reference (~220 pages) with uniform notation, explicit metric signature convention (+, −, −, −) vs. (−, +, +, +) crosswalks, complete proofs of core theorems (Stokes, spectral theorem, Cauchy residue, Noether, Wigner classification), and HEP-specific worked derivations.
deliverables.lab: Eight modular Python labs ( numpy , scipy , sympy , vector ) paired with production-bridge benchmarks in Eigen (C++), FEniCSx , Garfield++ , ACTS , and vegas .
deliverables.problemSet: Eight weekly analytical + computational problem sets plus a Part 1 Synthesis Exam integrating coordinate transformations, covariance propagation, Green’s functions, Lorentz tensors, Noether currents, Lie-algebra commutators, and stiff ODE error control. Exit criterion: ≥ 80% on analytical proofs and all eight numerical test suites passing within specified tolerances.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine anchored by Arfken–Weber–Harris, Riley–Hobson–Bence, Boas, and NIST DLMF, paired with specialized graduate monographs per lecture (Axler, Trefethen & Bau, Spieler, Zangwill, Carroll, Goldstein/Arnold, Georgi/Hall, Higham/Hairer).

learningOutcomes: Execute multivariable coordinate transformations, Jacobian
determinant calculations, and Gauss/Stokes integral conversions across Cartesian, cylindrical, spherical, and collider (p T , η, ϕ) coordinates.
Formulate linear inverse problems, covariance propagation, and recursive Kalman track filtering using spectral decompositions, Cholesky factorization, and SVD.
Apply contour integration, residue calculus, and Fourier/Laplace transforms to evaluate physical integrals and analyze causal front-end detector pulse shapers.

Solve elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic PDEs via separation of variables, Green’s functions, and finite-element methods for electrostatic field cages and carrier drift-diffusion. Manipulate covariant and contravariant Lorentz tensors, metric
contractions, and invariant contractions cleanly in index notation and vectorized software ( scikit-hep/vector ).
Derive equations of motion and conserved currents from action principles using Euler–Lagrange, Hamiltonian, and Noether formalisms for particles and classical fields.
Classify spacetime and internal symmetry multiplets using Lie algebras, Casimir invariants, and irreducible representations of SO(3), SU(2), SU(3), and the Lorentz/Poincaré groups.
Diagnose conditioning, catastrophic cancellation, quadrature accuracy, and ODE stiffness in IEEE-754 arithmetic, selecting appropriate solvers for HEP simulation and fitting.

lectures.title: Multivariable & Vector Calculus — Jacobians, Curvilinear Fields, and Integral Theorems

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: single-variable calculus and Part 0 collider coordinate conventions. Downstream: required by Lectures 1.4 (PDE boundary integrals & Gauss’s law), 1.5 (coordinate differentials & metrics), 1.6 (functional derivatives), and later phase-space integration and Maxwell-equation modules.

lectures.abstract: This lecture develops multivariable and vector calculus with the precision demanded by collider kinematics and detector electrodynamics. Beginning with total differentials, directional derivatives, Taylor expansions in R n , and the inverse/implicit function theorems, we focus on change-of-variables Jacobians—explicitly deriving the transformation between Cartesian momentum (p x , p y , p z ) and collider variables (p T , η, ϕ) as well as n-body phase- space measures. We then construct orthogonal curvilinear coordinates, differential operators (∇, ∇·, ∇×, ∇ 2 ), and the generalized integral theorems of Green, Gauss (divergence), and Stokes (curl), emphasizing flux conservation, solenoidal/irrotational Helmholtz decompositions, and distribution-valued derivatives (∇ · (r̂/r 2 ) = 4πδ (3) (r)).

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of scale factors h i and differential operators in cylindrical, spherical, and toroidal coordinates; exact Jacobian derivations for d 3 p = p T dp T dϕ dp z = p 2 T cosh η dp T dη dϕ and Lorentz-invariant phase space d 3 p/(2E); complete proofs and singularity caveats of Gauss’s and Stokes’s theorems.
deliverables.lab: Python symbolic-numeric lab using sympy.vector (coordinate systems, Del() , vector_integrate ) verified against numerical quadrature in scipy.integrate for magnetic flux through non-planar solenoid/toroid surfaces and phase-space volume integrals.
deliverables.problemSet: Six problems: (1) Jacobian derivation for (p x , p y , p z ) ↔ (p T , y, ϕ) and (p T , η, ϕ); (2) verifying ∇ × (∇f ) = 0 and ∇ · (∇ × A) = 0 in general orthogonal coordinates; (3) applying Gauss’s theorem to a cylindrical drift-tube electric field with space charge; (4) applying Stokes’s theorem to an ATLAS-like toroidal magnet coil; (5) Helmholtz decomposition of a test vector field; (6) numerical validation of flux integrals in scipy.integrate.dblquad . Exit criterion: analytical derivations verified symbolically in SymPy with zero residual.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: MIT OCW 18.02SC, Griffiths Ch. 1, and Arfken–Weber–Harris Ch. 3; advanced/optional: Zangwill Ch. 1, Riley–Hobson–Bence Ch. 10–11, and Spivak’s Calculus on Manifolds for differential-form unification of Stokes’s theorem.

learningOutcomes: Compute partial derivatives, gradients, Hessians, and multivariable
Taylor expansions to linearize nonlinear physical models around operating points.
Construct and evaluate Jacobian determinants for arbitrary coordinate transformations, including collider (p T , η, ϕ) and Lorentz-invariant phase-space measures.

Express gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian operators in Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates using scale factors h i . Apply Green’s, Gauss’s divergence, and Stokes’s curl theorems to
convert between local differential conservation laws and global integral flux/circulation laws.
Handle singular vector fields and three-dimensional Dirac delta functions rigorously when applying the divergence theorem to point and line charges.
Perform symbolic vector calculus and automated flux/line integration in SymPy and cross-check numerically with SciPy .

lectures.title: Linear Algebra & Matrix Decompositions — Covariance Propagation and Kalman Track Fitting

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 1.1 (Jacobians and linearization). Downstream: directly powers Lecture 1.5 (bilinear forms & metrics), Lecture 1.7 (matrix Lie groups), Lecture 1.8 (conditioning), and downstream track/vertex fitting ( ACTS ), calorimeter calibration, and multivariate statistical unfolding.

lectures.abstract: This lecture elevates linear algebra from elementary row reduction to operator structure and numerical matrix decompositions tailored to experimental HEP. Starting from abstract vector spaces, inner products, adjoints, and the spectral theorem for Hermitian/normal operators, we develop LU, Cholesky, QR, and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) alongside Moore–Penrose pseudoinverses and least-squares regularization. The second half translates these factorizations directly into collider data analysis: multivariate error propagation V y = JV x J T , positive-definiteness preservation of covariance matrices, and the complete derivation of the discrete Kalman filter and smoother for charged-particle track and vertex reconstruction with multiple-scattering process noise.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous derivations of the spectral theorem, SVD geometry, Cholesky factorization for symmetric positive-definite (SPD) covariance matrices, generalized least squares (χ 2 minimization), and the Frühwirth Kalman filter/smoother gain-matrix and weighted-means formulations.
deliverables.lab: Python implementation ( numpy.linalg , scipy.linalg ) of a 2D/3D helical track Kalman filter with multiple Coulomb scattering and outlier χ 2 rejection, benchmarked against C++ Eigen matrix kernels and mapped to the ACTS KalmanFitter state/covariance representation. T and diagnosing rank deficiency; (2) solving an ill-conditioned calorimeter
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) proving positive semi-definiteness of JVJ unfolding problem via truncated SVD vs. naive normal equations; (3) deriving the equivalence between the gain-matrix and information-matrix Kalman update via the Woodbury identity; (4) implementing a synthetic silicon-tracker Kalman fitter and verifying pull distributions (µ ≈ 0, σ ≈ 1); (5) comparing QR vs. Cholesky accuracy on Hilbert-like design matrices. Exit criterion: Kalman pull distributions pass unit-Gaussian consistency within 3σ over 10 4 simulated tracks.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Strang (MIT 18.06), Axler Linear Algebra Done Right (4th ed. OA), Cowan Ch. 1 & 7, and Frühwirth (1987); advanced/optional: Trefethen & Bau, Horn & Johnson, Strandlie & Frühwirth (2010 RMP), and ACTS non-linear Kalman filter papers.

using the spectral theorem, rank-nullity theorem, and orthogonal projections.
Compute and interpret LU, Cholesky, QR, and Singular Value Decompositions, choosing the numerically stable factorization for SPD, overdetermined, and rank-deficient systems.

Propagate multivariate uncertainties through linear and linearized nonlinear transformations while maintaining symmetry and positive definiteness of covariance matrices. Formulate weighted least-squares estimation and diagnose collinearity
and ill-conditioning via singular-value spectra.
Derive the prediction, filtering, and smoothing equations of the linear and extended Kalman filter for charged-particle track reconstruction.

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 1.1–1.2. Downstream: feeds directly into Lecture 1.4 (transform solutions of PDEs and Green’s functions), quantum-field propagators (iϵ prescriptions, dispersion relations), and detector front-end electronics/noise optimization.

lectures.abstract: This lecture connects the analytic structure of complex functions to spectral analysis and physical detector readout. We develop holomorphic functions, the Cauchy–Riemann equations, Cauchy’s integral theorem and formula, Laurent expansions, branch cuts, and the residue theorem, including Jordan’s lemma and principal-value/Sokhotski–Plemelj contours ubiquitous in scattering amplitudes and Green’s functions. Building on analytic continuation into the complex frequency plane, we derive Fourier and Laplace transforms, convolution theorems, Parseval/Plancherel energy conservation, and Kramers–Kronig causality relations. The capstone translates pole-zero diagrams in the s-plane directly into front-end detector signal shaping—analyzing charge-sensitive preamplifiers, CR–(RC) n semi-Gaussian shapers, pole-zero cancellation, ballistic deficit, and equivalent noise charge (ENC).

deliverables.lectureNote: Unified reference covering residue evaluation of physical integrals, Fourier/Laplace transform tables with consistent physics sign conventions, causality and left-half-plane pole stability, and full s-domain derivations of CR–(RC) n impulse responses and noise weighting functions.
deliverables.lab: Python signal-processing lab using scipy.signal ( TransferFunction , impulse , bode , lfilter ) and scipy.fft to simulate realistic sili- con/gaseous sensor current pulses through a charge-sensitive preamplifier and CR–(RC) n shaper, computing peaking time, pileup tails, and ENC vs. shaping time τ s .
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) evaluating improper and branch-cut integrals via residue calculus (including a Feynman-propagator-style pole shift); (2) proving the convolution and Parseval theorems and computing aliasing in discrete FFTs; (3) deriving the time-domain output of a CR–(RC) n shaper from its s-plane transfer function; (4) designing a pole-zero cancellation network to eliminate exponential preamplifier undershoot; (5) computing optimal shaping time τ opt balancing series voltage noise (1/τ s ) and parallel current noise (τ s ) in scipy.signal . Exit criterion: analytic and scipy.signal impulse responses agree to < 10 −6 relative error.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: MIT OCW 18.04, Arfken–Weber–Harris Ch. 11 & 20, Spieler Ch. 3–4, and scipy.signal / scipy.fft guides; advanced/optional: Stein & Shakarchi Complex Analysis, Oppenheim & Willsky Signals and Systems, and Radeka’s Low-Noise Techniques in Detectors.

Apply Fourier and Laplace transforms, convolution, and Parseval’s theorem to compute transfer functions and power spectral densities. Derive the time-domain waveform and peaking time of CR–(RC) n
pulse shapers and design pole-zero cancellation for charge-sensitive preamplifiers.

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 1.1–1.3 (vector calculus, eigenfunctions, Fourier/Laplace transforms). Downstream: foundational for detector electrostatics ( Garfield++ , FEniCSx ), silicon sensor depletion and drift-diffusion, RF cavity modes, and QFT Green’s functions/propagators.

lectures.abstract: This lecture presents the theory and computational practice of differential equations governing fields, waves, and charge transport in particle detectors and accelerators. Beginning with linear ODE systems, Sturm–Liouville self-adjoint operators, and orthogonal eigenfunction expansions (Bessel, Legendre, and spherical harmonics), we classify second-order linear PDEs into elliptic (Laplace/Poisson), parabolic (diffusion/drift-diffusion), and hyperbolic (wave/Helmholtz) regimes with Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundary conditions. We construct Green’s functions via both eigenfunction expansion and image-charge methods, then apply them directly to HEP detector physics: solving Poisson’s equation for depleted silicon sensors and wire chambers, modeling longitudinal/transverse charge-cloud diffusion, and deriving the Shockley–Ramo weighting-potential theorem for induced electrode currents.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivations of Sturm–Liouville orthogonality, Green’s identities and Green’s functions for ∇ 2 , (∂ t − D∇ 2 ), and (∂ t 2 − c 2 ∇ 2 ), the analytic wire-chamber electrostatic potential, and the Shockley–Ramo theorem i(t) = −q v(t) · E w (r(t)).
deliverables.lab: Python finite-difference and FEniCSx ( dolfinx ) finite-element solver computing the 2D electric and Shockley–Ramo weighting potentials of a segmented silicon pixel/strip sensor, coupled with a Garfield++ reference comparison for drift lines and induced current waveforms.
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) solving Poisson’s equation in a reverse-biased p–n silicon junction to obtain depletion depth and full-depletion voltage; (2) computing the Green’s function for a grounded cylindrical drift tube and verifying boundary conditions; (3) solving the 1D/2D drift-diffusion equation for a Gaussian electron cloud drifting in a TPC; (4) deriving the weighting potential of a parallel-plate R vs. strip electrode via separation of variables; (5) implementing a 2D FEniCSx or sparse-matrix Poisson solver and validating charge conservation i(t) dt = q to < 0.5%. Exit criterion: FEM potential matches analytic wire/strip benchmarks within 1%.

lectures.title: Tensors, Metrics, and Manifest Lorentz Covariance

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 1.1–1.2 (multivariable transformations and inner-product spaces). Downstream: prerequisite for Lecture 1.6 (covariant field actions), Lecture 1.7 (Lorentz/Poincaré group representations), relativistic kinematics, covariant electrodynamics, and QFT.

lectures.abstract: This lecture builds fluency in tensor algebra and manifest Lorentz covariance, the native language of relativistic particle physics. Introducing dual spaces, multilinear maps, Einstein summation, and general metric tensors g µν (with explicit crosswalks between particle-physics mostly-minus η µν = diag(+1, −1, −1, −1) and relativity mostly-plus conventions), we define contravariant/covariant transformation laws, index raising/lowering, symmetric/antisymmetric decompositions, and the Levi-Civita pseudotensor ϵ µνρσ . Physical applications anchor every operation: four-momentum invariants and Mandelstam variables (s, t, u), the electromagnetic field-strength tensor F µν and its dual F̃ µν , covariant Maxwell equations, the symmetric energy-momentum tensor T µν , and vectorized four-vector operations in collider data analysis.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete index-gymnastics handbook with signature-conversion rules, proofs of Lorentz invariance of p µ p µ = m 2 , F µν F µν = 2(B 2 − E 2 ), and F µν F̃ µν = −4E · B, plus a worked derivation of e + e − → Z(→ µ + µ − )H(→ bb̄) recoil-mass kinematics at FCC-ee.
deliverables.lab: Python notebook implementing explicit Λ ν Lorentz boost/rotation matrices and metric contractions in NumPy , validated against the production µ scikit-hep/vector library ( vector.array / Awkward Array backend) and compared to ROOT::Math::LorentzVector conventions. T
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) proving Λ ηΛ = η implies det Λ = ±1 and classifying the four connected components of O(1, 3); (2) expressing Maxwell’s equations and the Lorentz force dp µ /dτ = qF µν u ν in manifestly covariant form; (3) verifying the identity s + t + u = 4 i=1 m 2 i for P 2 → 2 scattering; (4) boosting a simulated H → γγ decay √ from the Higgs rest frame to the lab frame and verifying invariance of m γγ and E · B; (5) reconstructing the FCC-ee ZH recoil mass m 2 rec = ( s − E ℓℓ ) 2 − |p ℓℓ | 2 on 10 5 vectorized events using scikit-hep/vector . Exit criterion: all Lorentz invariants conserved to < 10 −12 relative precision under arbitrary boosts.

lectures.title: Variational Methods — Euler–Lagrange Equations, Symplectic Hamiltonians, and Noether’s Theorem

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 (multivariable calculus, ODEs, and Lorentz tensors). Downstream: directly underpins Lecture 1.7 (symmetry generators), classical/quantum field theory Lagrangians, accelerator beam optics (Hamiltonian transfer maps and Liouville emittance conservation), and symplectic integrators in Lecture 1.8.

lectures.abstract: This lecture develops the variational principles that unify classical mechanics, accelerator beam dynamics, and relativistic field theory. Starting from functionals and Gâteaux/Fréchet variations on configuration spaces, we derive the Euler–Lagrange equations with holonomic constraints via Lagrange p multipliers and examine the relativistic charged-particle Lagrangian L = −mc 2 1 − v 2 /c 2 − qϕ + qv · A. Performing the Legendre transform introduces the Hamiltonian formalism, canonical momenta, Poisson brackets, canonical transformations, and Liouville’s phase-space volume theorem— the foundation of beam emittance preservation in synchrotrons. Finally, we prove Noether’s first theorem for both discrete systems and continuous classical fields, deriving conserved four-currents j µ and the canonical energy-momentum tensor from spacetime and internal U (1) symmetries.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivations of Euler–Lagrange equations for particles and fields (∂ µ ∂(∂ = 0), the Legendre transform and symplectic ϕ) ∂ϕ µ form ω = dq i ∧ dp i , Liouville’s theorem applied to accelerator transverse phase space (x, p x ), and Noether’s theorem for Klein–Gordon, Maxwell, and complex scalar fields.
deliverables.lab: Symbolic-numeric Python lab using sympy.physics.mechanics ( LagrangesMethod ) to automatically derive equations of motion for coupled oscillators and relativistic magnetic-field motion, paired with a symplectic Störmer–Verlet phase-space integrator demonstrating Liouville area conservation vs. non-symplectic drift.
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) deriving the geodesic/brachistochrone and relativistic Lorentz force equations from Hamilton’s principle; (2) p computing canonical momentum p = γmv + qA and Hamiltonian H = (p − qA) 2 c 2 + m 2 c 4 + qϕ; (3) proving invariance of Poisson brackets under canonical transformations and verifying Liouville’s theorem for a quadrupole FODO focusing cell; (4) applying Noether’s theorem to a complex scalar field L = (∂ µ ϕ ∗ )(∂ µ ϕ) − m 2 |ϕ| 2 to derive the conserved U (1) current; (5) simulating 10 4 turns of a nonlinear accelerator map in Python and measuring phase-space area and energy drift for symplectic vs. RK4 solvers. Exit criterion: symplectic integrator preserves phase-space area to machine precision and bounds energy error over 10 4 oscillations.

lectures.abstract: Symmetry dictates both the particle spectrum and the allowed interactions of the Standard Model. This lecture develops finite groups, matrix Lie groups, and Lie algebras via the exponential map and Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff relation, focusing on structure constants, Killing forms, Schur’s lemmas, Casimir operators, and weight/root-space decompositions. We apply this machinery to the two pillars of HEP symmetry: internal gauge/flavor groups—deriving the irreducible representations and Clebsch–Gordan decompositions of SO(3)/SU(2) (spin and isospin) and SU(3) (quark triplets 3, ∼ su(2) L ⊕ su(2) R finite-dimensional antiquarks 3̄, gluon octets 8, and baryon decuplets 10)—and spacetime symmetries, constructing the so(1, 3) = (j L , j R ) field representations alongside Wigner’s classification of unitary Poincaré representations by mass m and spin/helicity.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous derivations of the SU(2) → SO(3) double cover, Pauli and Gell-Mann matrix algebras (f abc , d abc ), SU(3) root/weight diagrams and Young-tableau tensor-product rules (3 ⊗ 3̄ = 8 ⊕ 1, 3 ⊗ 3 ⊗ 3 = 10 ⊕ 8 ⊕ 8 ⊕ 1), SL(2, C) Weyl spinors, and the Pauli–Lubanski pseudovector W µ .
deliverables.lab: Python symbolic-numeric lab ( SymPy + NumPy / SciPy ) computing structure constants, Casimir eigenvalues C F , C A , T F for SU(N ), matrix exponentials ( scipy.linalg.expm ) for SO(1, 3) boosts/rotations, and Clebsch–Gordan coefficients via sympy.physics.quantum , with a bridge to Lorentz-equivariant neural networks ( lgn ).
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) proving SU(2) is the universal double cover of SO(3) and deriving the Rodrigues rotation formula via exp(−iθ n̂·σ/2); (2) computing the quadratic Casimir C 2 (3) = 4/3 and C 2 (8) = 3 for SU(3) directly from Gell-Mann matrices; (3) verifying the Lorentz Lie algebra [J i , J j ] = iϵ ijk J k , [J i , K j ] = iϵ ijk K k , [K i , K j ] = −iϵ ijk J k and decomposing it into su(2) L ⊕ su(2) R ; (4) showing that ( 12 , 0) ⊕ (0, 12 ) yields the Dirac representation and ( 12 , 2 1 ) yields four-vectors; (5) computing Wigner’s little groups SO(3) (m > 0) and ISO(2) (m = 0) from W µ W µ . Exit criterion: automated Python verification of all commutation relations, Jacobi identities, and Casimir traces to < 10 −14 .

lectures.abstract: Every precision measurement at LHC or FCC ultimately passes through finite-precision floating-point hardware. This lecture establishes rigorous numerical analysis for computational physicists. We begin with the IEEE 754-2019 floating-point model (unit roundoff, subnormals, NaN/Inf propagation, catastrophic cancellation, and Kahan compensated summation) and formalize problem conditioning versus algorithmic backward stability. We then analyze numerical root finding (bisection, Brent’s method, Newton–Raphson convergence basins), deterministic and stochastic quadrature (adaptive Gauss–Kronrod QUADPACK vs. multidimensional adaptive importance/stratified Monte Carlo VEGAS+ ), and ODE integration (explicit embedded Runge–Kutta Dormand–Prince, implicit BDF/Radau methods for stiff systems, and step-size control) as deployed in particle-stepping engines.

deliverables.lectureNote: IEEE-754 binary32/binary64 bit-layout reference, backward-error analysis of summation and invariant-mass calculation m 2 = E 2 − |p| 2 in the ultra-relativistic limit (E ≫ m), convergence-order proofs for Newton/Brent and Gauss–Kronrod quadrature, and linear stability regions (|R(z)| ≤ 1) for RK4, DOPRI5, and implicit BDF solvers.
deliverables.lab: Python benchmark suite ( NumPy , scipy.integrate.quad , scipy.integrate.solve_ivp , scipy.optimize.root_scalar ) comparing naive vs. Kahan summation, demonstrating catastrophic cancellation in ultra-relativistic invariant mass (E = 50 TeV electron) and its algebraic cure, integrating a 6D Breit–Wigner-peaked phase-space integral with VEGAS+ concepts, and propagating a charged track through a non-uniform solenoid field with adaptive RK45 vs. stiff Radau.
deliverables.problemSet: Five problems: (1) constructing an input where naive float32 / float64 invariant mass E − p fails catastrophically and implementing 2 2 a cancellation-free formulation; (2) computing the condition number κ(A) and forward vs. backward error on a perturbed linear system; (3) comparing convergence rates of trapezoidal, Simpson, and Gauss–Kronrod quadrature on a sharp Breit–Wigner resonance; (4) implementing Brent’s root finder and Newton–Raphson to solve the transcendental dispersion relation of an RF waveguide; (5) benchmarking solve_ivp ( RK45 vs. Radau / BDF ) on a stiff coupled decay-chain ODE system (Bateman equations spanning 10 −12 s to 10 3 s). Exit criterion: all solvers meet 10 −10 relative accuracy with verified step-count/stability diagnostics.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Goldberg (1991), Higham Ch. 1–4, Press et al. Numerical Recipes (3rd ed.), and SciPy integrate / optimize docs; advanced/optional: Hairer–Nørsett–Wanner Solving ODEs I, Trefethen Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice, IEEE 754-2019 standard, and Lepage (2021) VEGAS Enhanced.

learningOutcomes: Explain IEEE 754-2019 floating-point representation, machine epsilon,
subnormals, rounding modes, and catastrophic cancellation in ultra-relativistic HEP calculations.
Distinguish problem conditioning (sensitivity of the mathematical map) from algorithmic forward and backward stability.
Select and apply bracketed (bisection, Brent) and derivative-based (Newton–Raphson, secant) root-finding algorithms with rigorous stopping criteria. Choose between adaptive Gauss–Kronrod quadrature
( QUADPACK / scipy.integrate.quad ) for low-dimensional smooth/peaked integrands and adaptive Monte Carlo ( VEGAS+ ) for high-dimensional collider phase space.
Analyze local truncation error, global convergence order, and linear stability regions of explicit Runge–Kutta vs. implicit stiff ODE solvers.
Implement and validate adaptive quadrature, root finding, and ODE propagation workflows in SciPy with quantified error budgets.

parts.abstract: Part 2 establishes the complete classical, relativistic, quantum, statistical, and nuclear physics spine required to transition from undergraduate physics to graduate-level collider physics and Future Circular Collider (FCC) research. Beginning with variational mechanics and continuous symmetries, the sequence progresses through covariant electrodynamics, relativistic kinematics, Hilbert-space quantum mechanics, scattering theory, kinetic transport in detector media, and nuclear binding and decay phenomenology. Every module pairs rigorous analytical derivations in explicit SI and natural units (ℏ = c = 1) with a two-stage computational workflow—first building transparent Python/SymPy/SciPy prototypes from scratch, then migrating to community HEP engines including Scikit-HEP vector and particle , QuTiP, Meep, Garfield++, and Geant4.

deliverables.lectureNote: Seven modular LaTeX-typeset monographs (Lectures 2.1–2.7) enforcing consistent metric signature (+, −, −, −), dimensional analysis bridges between SI and GeV/fm natural units, full derivations from first principles, and worked collider/detector benchmarks (Lorentz-boosted decays, synchrotron radiation at FCC-ee, partial-wave resonances, electron drift in TPC gases, and nuclear activation chains).
deliverables.lab: Seven paired computational notebooks following the Stage 1 (pure Python/NumPy/SciPy/SymPy verification against closed-form solutions) → Stage 2 (production open-source and HEP frameworks: SymPy mechanics, Meep FDTD, Scikit-HEP vector , QuTiP, Garfield++, and Geant4/NNDC workflows) progression.
deliverables.problemSet: Seven graded analytical and numerical problem sets (6–8 problems each) with automated unit-testable verification harnesses; Part 2 exit criterion requires ≥ 85% mastery across variational symmetries, relativistic four-vector invariants, scattering amplitudes, transport coefficients, and nuclear cross-section calculations.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Two-tier progression pairing accessible conceptual anchors (David Tong’s Cambridge notes, MIT OpenCourseWare, Griffiths, Feynman Lectures) as the core spine with graduate monographs and Particle Data Group (PDG) review chapters (Arnold, Landau–Lifshitz, Sakurai– Napolitano, Sauli, Blum–Riegler–Rolandi, PDG Reviews) for advanced depth.

Manipulate four-vectors, Lorentz boosts, Mandelstam invariants, rapidity/pseudorapidity, and multi-body phase space for collider kinematics.

Construct and diagonalize quantum Hamiltonians in Hilbert space, including harmonic oscillators, spin-1/2 systems, and angular momentum couplings. Compute bound-state shifts, transition rates, Born amplitudes,
partial-wave phase shifts, and Breit–Wigner resonances in non-relativistic scattering theory.
Model equilibrium ensembles, Boltzmann transport, electron drift, diffusion, and electromagnetic cascade scaling relevant to gaseous detectors and calorimeters.
Evaluate nuclear binding energies, decay chains, cross-section observables, and radiation protection quantities using evaluated nuclear data libraries.

lectures.title: Variational Mechanics, Symmetries, and Noether’s Theorems

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 1 (ODEs, multivariable calculus, linear algebra). Downstream links: Lecture 2.2 (covariant electromagnetic action and gauge invariance), Lecture 2.3 (relativistic free-particle action), Lecture 2.4 (canonical quantization and Poisson-to-commutator correspondence), and Part 5 (classical field theory, Lagrangian densities, and gauge symmetries).

dependencies.downstream: Lecture 2.2 (covariant electromagnetic action and gauge invariance), Lecture 2.3 (relativistic free-particle action), Lecture 2.4 (canonical quantization and Poisson-to-commutator correspondence), and Part 5 (classical field theory, Lagrangian densities, and gauge symmetries).

lectures.abstract: This lecture reformulates Newtonian dynamics into the coordinate-independent Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms that underpin all modern field theory and accelerator beam dynamics. Starting from generalized coordinates, holonomic constraints, and d’Alembert’s principle, we derive the Euler– Lagrange equations from Hamilton’s principle of stationary action. We then perform the Legendre transformation to phase space, introducing canonical momenta, Poisson brackets, canonical transformations, and Liouville’s theorem—directly connecting symplectic phase-space volume preservation to accelerator beam emittance. The centerpiece is a rigorous derivation of Noether’s first and second theorems, linking spacetime translations, rotations, and internal symmetries to conserved charges and local gauge constraints.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivations of Euler–Lagrange equations (including Lagrange multipliers for constraints and velocity-dependent electromag- netic potentials), Legendre transforms, Hamilton’s equations, Poisson algebra, Noether’s first theorem (with boundary terms) and second theorem (gauge identities), and symplectic integrators; SI units with scaling to dimensionless action variables; worked examples: double pendulum, charged particle in a solenoid magnetic field, and central-force Kepler/Runge–Lenz symmetry.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Build a Python/SciPy symplectic Stormer–Verlet and RK4 integrator comparing energy and angular-momentum drift for a relativistic- inspired anharmonic oscillator and charged particle in a magnetic bottle. Stage 2: Automate symbolic Euler–Lagrange derivation, conserved Noether charge verification, and numerical code generation using SymPy ( sympy.physics.mechanics ) and SciPy .
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (generalized coordinates with constraints, Noether charge for Galilean boosts and scale symmetries, Poisson- bracket invariance of canonical transformations, Liouville phase-space preservation in a quadrupole focusing channel) + 2 computational problems (symplectic vs. non-symplectic long-term orbit stability; symbolic Noether current checker). Exit criterion: exact symbolic/numerical conservation of Noether invariants to < 10 −10 relative drift over 10 4 periods.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: David Tong’s Classical Dynamics and MIT OCW 8.223. Intermediate: Goldstein’s Classical Mechanics. Ad- vanced/optional: V. I. Arnold’s Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, Emmy Noether’s 1918 paper (Tavel translation), and Gomes on Noether’s second theorem and the gauge argument.

learningOutcomes: Derive the Euler–Lagrange equations from Hamilton’s variational
principle and incorporate holonomic constraints via Lagrange multipliers.
Construct the minimal-coupling Lagrangian L = T − qϕ + qv · A and verify it reproduces the Lorentz force law.
Execute the Legendre transformation from tangent bundle (q, q̇) to cotangent phase space (q, p) and derive Hamilton’s canonical equations.
Compute Poisson brackets, verify canonical transformations, and prove phase-space volume conservation via Liouville’s theorem. State and prove Noether’s first theorem including total time-derivative
boundary terms, extracting conserved energy, momentum, and angular momentum.
Distinguish global symmetries (Noether’s first theorem) from local gauge symmetries (Noether’s second theorem) in preparation for classical and quantum field theory.
Implement structure-preserving symplectic integrators in Python and diagnose secular energy drift in non-symplectic ODE solvers.

lectures.abstract: Classical electrodynamics governs both the acceleration of relativistic beams and the electromagnetic signals induced inside every particle detector. This lecture builds systematically from Maxwell’s equations in vacuum and macroscopic media through scalar and vector potentials, Coulomb and Lorenz gauge fixing, Green’s functions, and the Poynting energy-momentum conservation laws. We derive the Liénard–Wiechert potentials of a moving point charge, the Larmor and relativistic Liénard radiation formulae, and the angular and spectral properties of synchrotron radiation critical to circular lepton colliders such as FCC-ee. Finally, we analyze electromagnetic fields in dispersive dielectrics, wave propagation, waveguides/RF cavities, and the classical foundations of Cherenkov radiation and ionization energy loss.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivations of Maxwell’s equations in SI and Heaviside–Lorentz natural units (with explicit conversion table), gauge invariance, retarded Green’s functions, Liénard–Wiechert fields, relativistic Liénard formula and synchrotron power loss P ∝ γ 4 /ρ 2 , macroscopic D/H boundary conditions, Lorentz–Drude dispersion, √ Cherenkov cone angle cos θ C = 1/(nβ), and cylindrical RF pillbox cavity modes; worked FCC-ee synchrotron energy-loss-per-turn benchmark at s = 91–365 GeV.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python/NumPy/SciPy solver for 2D electrostatic boundary-value problems (wire-chamber drift cell via finite-difference relaxation) and numerical evaluation of Liénard–Wiechert radiation patterns for β → 1. Stage 2: Electromagnetic wave propagation, cavity eigenmodes, and Cherenkov radiation simulation in Meep (FDTD) plus drift-field visualization in Garfield++ .
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (gauge transformations and Lorenz-gauge wave equation, Poynting flux in a coaxial cable, synchrotron radiation critical energy and power loss at FCC-ee vs. LEP, Cherenkov radiation threshold and Frank–Tamm spectral yield) + 2 computational problems (numerical relaxation of a proportional-chamber electric field; FDTD simulation of a dielectric slab / Cherenkov wake). Exit criterion: reproduce analytical FCC-ee synchrotron energy loss per turn within 0.1% and verify FDTD dispersion relation against theory.

Advanced/optional: Jackson Classical Electrodynamics, Landau & Lifshitz Vol. 2, and Meep/Garfield++ technical manuals.

Compute the Liénard–Wiechert potentials and fields of an arbitrarily moving relativistic charge and derive the relativistic Liénard radiation power. Quantify synchrotron radiation power, beaming angle ∼ 1/γ, and
critical frequency for relativistic leptons in circular storage rings.
Analyze wave propagation, attenuation, and dispersion in dielectrics and conductors, including Cherenkov radiation thresholds and RF cavity modes.

lectures.title: Special Relativity, Lorentz Invariants, and Collider Kinematics

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 2.1 (action principles) and Lecture 2.2 (electrodynamics). Downstream links: Lecture 2.5 (relativistic scattering kinematics), Lecture 2.7 (nuclear reaction Q-values and thresholds), Part 3 (invariant-mass line shapes and kinematic fits), Part 5 (Poincaré group, Dirac equation, and Feynman-diagram phase space), and Part 9+ (collider event reconstruction).

lectures.abstract: Special relativity is the native geometric language of high-energy physics. This lecture develops Minkowski spacetime, the Lorentz group O(1, 3) and its proper orthochronous subgroup SO + (1, 3), covariant and contravariant four-vectors, and tensor contraction using the particle-physics metric convention η µν = diag(+1, −1, −1, −1). We derive the relativistic free-particle action, four-momentum conservation, and manifestly covariant electrodynamics (F µν and its dual). Transitioning directly to collider phenomenology, we master Mandelstam variables (s, t, u), two-body and three-body decay kinematics, Dalitz plots, rapidity y, pseudorapidity η, transverse momentum p T , transverse mass m T , and Lorentz-invariant phase space (LIPS) elements needed for fixed-target, e + e − (FCC-ee), and pp (LHC/FCC-hh) collisions.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous derivations of Lorentz boost matrices and rapidity additivity, relativistic Doppler and aberration formulae, covariant Maxwell equations ∂ µ F µν = J ν , Mandelstam identity s + t + u = P 2 m i , Källén triangle function λ(a, b, c), two-body decay momenta, Dalitz plot kinematic boundaries, and W → ℓν Jacobian peak in m T ; natural units (ℏ = c = 1, GeV) throughout; worked examples: e + e − → ZH recoil mass at FCC-ee and pp → W → ℓν transverse mass edge.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy four-vector class implementing Minkowski inner products, arbitrary 3D boosts, invariant mass, Mandelstam variables, and Monte Carlo Dalitz plot boundary verification for D 0 → K − π + π 0 . Stage 2: Vectorized relativistic kinematics on simulated collider events using Scikit-HEP vector and particle (plus comparison to ROOT TLorentzVector conventions).
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (Thomas precession / non-commutativity of non-collinear boosts, threshold energy for pp → pppp̄ in fixed-target vs. collider frames, exact derivation of the ZH recoil mass formula at FCC-ee, Lorentz invariance of d 3 p/(2E) and 2-body LIPS) + 2 computational problems (boosted H → γγ opening-angle distribution; vectorized m T Jacobian-peak reconstruction with missing transverse momentum). Exit criterion: exact Lorentz invariance of p µ p µ and s + t + u to machine precision (< 10 −12 ) across arbitrary random boosts.

Intermediate: Landau & Lifshitz Vol. 2 (Ch. 1–2) and Tao Han’s Collider Phenomenology. Advanced/optional: Byckling & Kajantie Particle Kinematics and the CORE 3.2 compendium.

Formulate the relativistic point-particle action, canonical four-momentum, and covariant Lorentz force equation using F µν .
Compute center-of-mass energies, laboratory threshold energies, and boost factors between rest, center-of-mass, and laboratory frames.

Express 2 → 2 scattering kinematics in terms of Mandelstam invariants (s, t, u) and derive the Källén function for two-body decay momenta. Construct and interpret hadron-collider coordinates (p T , η, y, ϕ, ∆R),
transverse mass m T , and lepton-collider recoil mass m recoil .
Map three-body decay kinematics onto Dalitz plots and evaluate two- and three-body Lorentz-invariant phase space integrals.
Perform high-throughput vectorized four-vector operations and boosts using Scikit-HEP vector .

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 1 (linear algebra, eigenvalues/eigenvectors, complex analysis, Fourier transforms) and Lecture 2.1 (Hamiltonian formalism and Poisson brackets). Downstream links: Lecture 2.5 (angular momentum addition, perturbation theory, scattering), Lecture 2.6 (quantum statistical ensembles), Lecture 2.7 (atomic and nuclear shell models), and Part 5 (canonical quantization of free fields as coupled harmonic oscillators).

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes the axiomatic Hilbert-space formulation of quantum mechanics using Dirac bra-ket notation, preparing students directly for canonical field quantization. We present the postulates of quantum states, Hermitian observables, projective measurement, and unitary time evolution in the Schrödinger, Heisenberg, and interaction pictures. Key structural tools—spectral decomposition, generalized Robertson–Schrödinger uncertainty relations, and symmetry generators—are developed alongside two foundational exactly solvable systems: the 1D quantum harmonic oscillator solved algebraically via creation and annihilation ladder operators (a, a † ) and coherent states, and spin-1/2 two-level systems governed by the Pauli algebra, SU (2) rotations, Bloch-sphere geometry, and Stern–Gerlach/Larmor precession dynamics.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous axiomatic development of separable Hilbert spaces, Dirac delta normalization, unitary time-evolution operator U (t, t 0 ), Ehrenfest theorem, Heisenberg vs. Schrödinger pictures, algebraic diagonalization of the harmonic oscillator (explicitly foreshadowing QFT Fock space), coherent states, Pauli matrices and SU (2) → SO(3) double cover, and density matrices for mixed states; SI and ℏ = 1 units side by side; worked examples: sequential Stern–Gerlach analyzers, spin precession in a static magnetic field, and coherent-state oscillation.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python/NumPy/SciPy finite-difference and matrix-mechanics solver for 1D potentials (harmonic and anharmonic oscillators) plus explicit 2 × 2 Pauli-matrix time evolution of spin-1/2 Larmor precession and Rabi oscillations. Stage 2: Re-implement spin-1/2 Bloch-sphere dynamics, coherent-state Wigner functions, and open-system decoherence benchmarks using QuTiP .
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff identities and translation/boost generators, Robertson uncertainty bound for non-commuting observables, harmonic oscillator coherent-state minimum uncertainty and Poissonian number statistics, SU (2) spinor rotation by 2π and two-spin singlet/triplet entanglement) + 2 computational problems (numerical matrix diagonalization of the quartic anharmonic oscillator V (x) = 12 x 2 + λx 4 ; Bloch-vector trajectory and purity decay in QuTiP ). Exit criterion: numerical eigenvalues match analytical harmonic levels to < 10 −8 and verify Tr(ρ) = 1, Tr(ρ 2 ) ≤ 1 across all simulated states.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Sakurai & Napolitano Modern Quantum Mechanics (Ch. 1–2), David Tong’s Quantum Mechanics, and MIT OCW 8.04/8.05. Intermediate: Feynman Lectures Vol. III. Advanced/optional: MIT OCW 8.321 (graduate Quantum Theory I) and QuTiP documentation.

learningOutcomes: State the Dirac–von Neumann postulates of quantum mechanics and
compute expectation values, variances, and transition probabilities in bra-ket notation.
Derive the generalized Robertson uncertainty relation and identify complete sets of commuting observables (CSCOs).
Transform states and operators among the Schrödinger, Heisenberg, and interaction pictures and verify Ehrenfest’s theorem.
Solve the quantum harmonic oscillator algebraically using ladder operators a, a † , and derive the properties of coherent states.
Manipulate the Pauli spin algebra, construct SU (2) rotation operators U (n̂, θ) = exp(−iθ n̂ · σ/2), and analyze Stern–Gerlach experiments.

lectures.abstract: This lecture builds the advanced quantum machinery that connects microscopic Hamiltonians to experimentally measurable cross sections and decay widths. First, we develop the full theory of angular momentum: SU (2) representations, spherical harmonics, addition of angular momenta via Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, irreducible spherical tensor operators, and the Wigner–Eckart theorem—tools directly transferable to isospin and flavor symmetries in hadron physics. Next, we derive time-independent (non-degenerate and degenerate) and time-dependent perturbation theory, culminating in Fermi’s Golden Rule and the Dyson series. Finally, we formulate non-relativistic scattering theory via the Lippmann–Schwinger equation, Born approximation, partial-wave phase shifts, the optical theorem, and Breit–Wigner quasi-bound resonances.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivations of J ± representations, Clebsch–Gordan recursion relations, Wigner–Eckart theorem, Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation theory (fine structure and Zeeman/Stark shifts), Dyson time-ordered exponential, Fermi’s Golden Rule for decay rates and cross sections, Lippmann– Schwinger Green’s function, first Born approximation for Yukawa and Coulomb (Rutherford) potentials, partial-wave expansion, optical theorem σ tot = 4π Im f (0), and non-relativistic Breit–Wigner resonance formula; natural units (ℏ = c = 1) with explicit conversion to barns/GeV −2 ; worked k example: Yukawa-to-Rutherford limit and s-wave resonance scattering.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python/NumPy/SciPy numerical radial Schrödinger solver (Numerov method) extracting partial-wave phase shifts δ ℓ (k), differential cross section dσ/dΩ, and optical-theorem verification for a finite-range Yukawa/square-well potential with a low-energy resonance. Stage 2: Symbolic Clebsch–Gordan and Wigner 3j/6j verification with SymPy ( sympy.physics.wigner ) and automated comparison against PDG Clebsch–Gordan conventions and cross-section formulae.
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of πN isospin scattering amplitudes, degenerate perturbation theory for the n = 2 hydrogen Stark effect, first Born approximation for screened Coulomb scattering and form-factor interpretation, derivation of the optical theorem and Breit–Wigner phase-shift jump δ ℓ = π/2) + 2 computational problems (Numerov partial-wave solver identifying Ramsauer–Townsend minimum and Breit–Wigner peak; numerical verification of unitarity bound σ ℓ ≤ 4π(2ℓ + 1)/k 2 ). Exit criterion: optical theorem identity verified numerically to < 10 −4 across k and exact agreement with PDG Clebsch–Gordan tables.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Sakurai & Napolitano Modern Quantum Mechanics (Ch. 3, 5, 6), David Tong’s Topics in Quantum Mechanics, and MIT OCW 8.06. Intermediate: PDG Clebsch–Gordan Coefficients and Cross-Section Formulae. Advanced/optional: PDG High Energy Soft QCD and Diffraction (optical theorem and eikonal scattering) and MIT OCW 8.321.

Evaluate first- and second-order energy and eigenstate corrections in non-degenerate and degenerate time-independent perturbation theory.
Derive the Dyson series in the interaction picture and apply Fermi’s Golden Rule to compute transition rates and decay widths.
Formulate potential scattering via the Lippmann–Schwinger integral equation and compute differential cross sections in the Born approximation.
Perform partial-wave decompositions, extract scattering phase shifts δ ℓ (k), and verify probability conservation via the optical theorem.
Analyze scattering resonances as poles of the S-matrix in the complex momentum plane and derive the Breit–Wigner cross-section line shape.
Numerically integrate radial scattering equations and validate symbolic angular-momentum algebra using SciPy and SymPy .

lectures.abstract: High-energy particle detectors operate at the intersection of statistical mechanics, non-equilibrium kinetic theory, and stochastic transport. This lecture develops equilibrium statistical mechanics—microcanonical, canonical, and grand canonical ensembles, partition functions, thermodynamic fluctuations, and ideal Fermi–Dirac/Bose–Einstein gases—before pivoting to non-equilibrium kinetics. Starting from the BBGKY hierarchy and the Boltzmann transport equation, we derive mean free paths, Langevin drift-diffusion equations, the Einstein–Smoluchowski relation, Townsend avalanche multiplication, and electron drift in crossed E × B fields. We conclude with stochastic cascade theory (Heitler–Matthews and Rossi–Greisen electromagnetic shower scaling), directly equipping students to model gaseous tracking chambers (e.g., FCC-ee IDEA drift chamber) and calorimeters.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of Gibbs ensembles, equipartition and fluctuation-dissipation relations, quantum statistics (Fermi energy in silicon sensors, Planck/Bose distributions), Boltzmann equation and H-theorem, Fick’s law and diffusion tensor in E × B fields (Lorentz angle tan θ L = ωτ ), Townsend first ionization coefficient α and Polya/exponential avalanche gain fluctuations, and Heitler electromagnetic shower depth t max ∝ ln(E 0 /E c ); SI and eV/cm/ns detector units; worked examples: electron drift velocity and transverse diffusion in Ar/CO 2 and He/iC 4 H 10 drift chambers, and shower-maximum scaling in lead tungstate (PbWO 4 ).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python/NumPy microscopic 3D Monte Carlo simulation of electron drift, elastic/inelastic collisions, and longitudinal/transverse diffusion in a model gas under E and B fields, plus a toy Heitler–Bethe–Heitler electromagnetic shower generator. Stage 2: Production drift-velocity, Townsend-coefficient, and avalanche simulation using CERN Garfield++ (Magboltz interface) and electromagnetic cascade comparison against Geant4 physics lists.
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (canonical partition function and energy fluctuations, Fermi–Dirac carrier density in intrinsic silicon, derivation of √ the Langevin drift velocity and E × B Lorentz angle, Heitler model for t max and calorimeter sampling-fraction stochastic resolution σ E /E ∝ 1/ E) √ + 2 computational problems (2D/3D random-walk diffusion verification of σ x = 2Dt and Einstein relation; Polya gain-fluctuation histogram from a recursive avalanche simulator). Exit criterion: simulated drift velocity and diffusion constants agree with Langevin theory within 2% and reproduce √ expected 1/ E shower-resolution scaling.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: David Tong’s Statistical Physics and Lectures on Kinetic Theory, MIT OCW 8.044 and 8.333. Detector-physics spine: Fabio Sauli Gaseous Radiation Detectors and Blum–Riegler–Rolandi Particle Detection with Drift Chambers. Advanced/optional: Garfield++ User Guide, Geant4 Physics List Guide, and BBGKY/Vlasov kinetic theory review.

Apply Fermi–Dirac and Bose–Einstein statistics to degenerate electron gases in semiconductor sensors and photon gases.
Derive the Boltzmann transport equation from Liouville’s theorem and extract macroscopic continuity, drift, and diffusion equations.

Compute electron and ion drift velocities, Lorentz angles, and longitudinal/transverse diffusion coefficients in E × B detector gases. Model Townsend gas multiplication, avalanche gain statistics, and
space-charge limitations in wire and micro-pattern gaseous detectors.
Predict electromagnetic shower longitudinal profiles, critical energy E c , radiation length X 0 , and stochastic energy-resolution scaling.
Build microscopic Monte Carlo transport prototypes in Python and benchmark them against Garfield++ and Geant4 .

lectures.abstract: Experimental particle physics relies intimately on atomic and nuclear structure: nuclei serve as scattering targets, calorimeter absorbers, calibration sources, and sources of induced radioactivity at high-luminosity colliders. This lecture covers atomic energy scales (ionization potentials, X-ray fluorescence, and Bethe–Bloch mean excitation energy I), nuclear sizes and form factors, the Bethe–Weizsäcker semi-empirical mass formula, nuclear shell structure and magic numbers, and reaction Q-values. We then analyze radioactive decay kinetics (Bateman equations for coupled decay chains), α-tunneling (Gamow factor), β-decay (Fermi theory and Kurie plots), γ-multipole transitions, microscopic/macroscopic cross sections, and operational radiation-protection quantities (activity, absorbed dose, and ambient dose equivalent) essential for collider cavern and beam-dump engineering.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of nuclear charge radius R ≈ r 0 A 1/3 from electron-scattering form factors, semi-empirical mass formula (volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, pairing terms) and valley of β-stability, Gamow WKB α-decay half-life law, Fermi β-decay phase space and neutrino-mass endpoint sensitivity, Bateman differential equations for multi-step decay chains, macroscopic cross section Σ = nσ and attenuation length λ = 1/Σ, and PDG radiation-protection definitions (Bq, Gy, Sv); natural MeV/fm units paired with SI/barn experimental units; worked examples: 60 Co/ 137 Cs calorimeter calibration sources and copper beam-dump activation cooling curves.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python/NumPy/SciPy solver for the Bethe–Weizsäcker binding-energy curve (fitting coefficients to nuclear mass tables) and numerical integration of stiff Bateman decay chains using scipy.integrate.solve_ivp . Stage 2: Querying evaluated nuclear structure/decay data via NNDC NuDat 3 / TkN and scikit-hep/particle PDG nuclear IDs (± 10LZZZAAAI ), plus simulating α/β/γ absorption and activation in Geant4 . 238 U vs. 212 Po,
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (valley of stability Z min (A) from the semi-empirical mass formula, Gamow tunneling factor for secular vs. transient equilibrium in 3-nuclide Bateman chains, neutron-capture and photonuclear giant-dipole-resonance thresholds at electron accelerators) + 2 computational problems (nonlinear least-squares fit of Weizsäcker coefficients to NuDat masses; Bateman chain solver computing activity and gamma dose rate vs. cooling time for irradiated Cu). Exit criterion: binding-energy residuals < 1% for A ≥ 40 (identifying shell-closure peaks at magic numbers) and exact mass-balance conservation in Bateman solver.

Advanced/optional: PDG Neutrino Cross Section Measurements (nuclear effects), TkN /NuDat 3 documentation, and EIC nuclear-probing proceedings.

parts.abstract: Part 3 delivers the complete statistical and computational inference toolkit used in modern experimental particle physics, scaling from foundational probability axioms to full LHC/FCC profile-likelihood combinations and high-dimensional Monte Carlo integration. Across seven lectures, students master HEP-specific probability densities (Landau, Crystal Ball, Breit–Wigner), correlated uncertainty propagation and BLUE combinations, frequentist and Bayesian parameter estimation, profile-likelihood hypothesis tests (Wilks, Asimov, CL s , look-elsewhere effect), nuisance-parameter modeling and template morphing, regularized and unbinned unfolding, and variance-reduced Monte Carlo sampling. Each lecture transitions from first-principles Python/NumPy/SciPy implementations to industry-standard HEP frameworks: iminuit , zfit , hepstats , pyhf , RooFit / RooStats , CMS Combine , RooUnfold / TUnfold , emcee , PyMC , and VEGAS .

deliverables.lectureNote: Seven rigorous, self-contained LaTeX monographs (Lectures 3.1–3.7) aligned verbatim with PDG Chapters 39 (Probability), 40 (Statistics), and Monte Carlo reviews, plus LHC Statistical Combination conventions (ATLAS/CMS/HistFactory); includes full proofs (Cramér–Rao bound, Neyman–Pearson lemma, Wilks’ theorem, BLUE optimality, Barlow–Beeston profiling, SVD/Tikhonov unfolding) and worked LHC/FCC-ee case studies.
deliverables.lab: Seven two-stage Jupyter/Python labs bridging Stage 1 (from-scratch NumPy/SciPy algorithms exposing every matrix inversion, likelihood gradient, and toy ensemble) to Stage 2 (production HEP software: iminuit , zfit , pyhf , RooFit / RooStats , BLUE-py , RooUnfold , emcee / PyMC , and VEGAS ).
deliverables.problemSet: Seven analytical + computational problem sets with reproducible random-seed validation suites; Part 3 exit criterion requires constructing an end-to-end multi-channel binned profile-likelihood model with correlated shape/rate systematics, computing asymptotic and toy-calibrated p 0 and CL s limits, and unfolding a smeared differential spectrum with validated coverage.

Intermediate: Kyle Cranmer’s Practical Statistics for the LHC, Robert Cousins’ Lectures on Statistics in Theory, and Roger Barlow’s Statistics. Advanced/optional: landmark arXiv/CERN papers (Cowan–Cranmer–Gross–Vitells, Read, Gross–Vitells, HistFactory, pyhf, CMS Combine, TUnfold, OmniFold, Lepage VEGAS).

distributions (Poisson, Gaussian, Landau, Crystal Ball, relativistic Breit–Wigner, and Voigtian).
Propagate correlated uncertainties analytically and via Monte Carlo, and combine correlated measurements using the BLUE method and joint likelihoods.
Construct binned, unbinned, and extended maximum-likelihood estimators, least-squares fits, and Bayesian posteriors, diagnosing bias, variance, and Cramér–Rao efficiency.

Formulate frequentist hypothesis tests for discovery (q 0 ) and exclusion (q̃ µ , CL s , Feldman–Cousins), applying Wilks’ theorem, Asimov datasets, and look-elsewhere trial factors. Parameterize rate, shape-morphing, and finite-MC (Barlow–Beeston)
systematic uncertainties as constrained nuisance parameters in HistFactory/ pyhf /Combine models.
Solve ill-posed detector-response inverse problems via Tikhonov/SVD, iterative Bayesian (D’Agostini), and unbinned ML (OmniFold) unfolding with validated covariance matrices.
Design and benchmark inverse-transform, accept-reject, importance-sampling ( VEGAS ), and MCMC ( emcee / PyMC ) algorithms for phase-space integration and Bayesian inference.

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes measure-theoretic probability in an applied physics register—Kolmogorov axioms, conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem, characteristic functions, cumulants, and the Central Limit Theorem (including its breakdown for heavy-tailed distributions). Beyond the standard discrete and continuous workhorses (Binomial, Multinomial, Poisson, Exponential, Uniform, Gaussian, χ 2 , Gamma/Beta), we provide a dedicated derivation and physical interpretation of the distributions unique to experimental HEP: the skewed Landau (and Vavilov) straggling distribution for thin-absorber ionization energy loss, the Crystal Ball (and double-sided Crystal Ball) PDF for radiative energy-loss tails in electromagnetic calorimeters, and the non-relativistic and relativistic Breit–Wigner resonance line shapes convolved with Gaussian detector resolution (Voigtian).

deliverables.lectureNote: Kolmogorov axioms, variable transformations via Jacobians (vs. discrete substitutions), moment-generating and characteristic functions, cumulants (skewness γ 1 , excess kurtosis γ 2 ), exact derivation of the Poisson limit of the Binomial, Landau integral representation and why its mean and variance diverge (motivating truncated-mean dE/dx estimators), piecewise C 1 -smooth Crystal Ball normalization, relativistic Breit–Wigner with s-dependent width, and Voigtian convolution; worked examples: silicon-tracker dE/dx Landau–Gaussian convolution and Z → e + e − Crystal Ball + Breit–Wigner line shape.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy/SciPy implementation of normalized Crystal Ball, relativistic Breit–Wigner, and numerical FFT convolution of Breit–Wigner ⊗ Gaussian (Voigtian) and Landau ⊗ Gaussian, verifying CDF quantiles and skewness/kurtosis. Stage 2: Building composite signal-plus-background PDFs ( RooBreitWigner , RooCBShape , RooLandau , RooFFTConvPdf ) in zfit and RooFit .
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (Jacobian transformation of p T vs. 1/p T track curvature errors, cumulant-generating proof of additivity of independent Poisson and χ 2 variables, C 1 continuity and analytical normalization of the Crystal Ball function, divergence of first/second moments of Cauchy/Breit–Wigner and Landau PDFs) + 2 computational problems (demonstrating CLT failure for Cauchy/Landau sample means vs. stability of truncated means; numerical Voigtian vs. Breit–Wigner FWHM comparison). Exit criterion: numerical PDF integrals equal 1.000000 ± 10 −6 and zfit / SciPy evaluations agree to < 10 −7 .

Advanced/optional: SLAC/DESY Crystal Ball thesis citations (Oreglia, Gaiser, Skwarnicki), Landau/Vavilov energy-straggling review, and zfit / RooFit PDF documentation.

lectures.title: Error Propagation, Covariance Algebra, and Measurement Combinations

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 3.1 (multivariate PDFs, expectation, variance) and Part 1 (linear algebra, Jacobians, positive-definite matrices). Downstream links: Lecture 3.3 (generalized least squares and Fisher information matrix), Lecture 3.5 (systematic correlation matrices), Lecture 3.6 (unfolded bin-to-bin covariance matrices), and Part 11 (LHC/FCC world-average combinations such as m W and m t ).

lectures.abstract: Real collider measurements are rarely scalar, independent, or linear. This lecture formalizes multivariate uncertainty quantification via covariance and correlation matrices, first-order Jacobian error propagation (V y = JV x J T ), and diagnostic tests for when linear propagation fails (high curvature, physical boundaries, or skewed error distributions), motivating Monte Carlo propagation (JCGM GUM Supplement 1/2). We then derive the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) for combining multiple correlated measurements of one or several physical quantities (Lyons–Gibaut–Clifford and Valassi), analyzing subtle pathologies including negative BLUE weights, Peelle’s Pertinent Puzzle (relative vs. absolute uncertainties), and why likelihood-level combinations supersede naive confidence-interval intersections.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous derivations of multivariate Gaussian covariance geometry (error ellipses and principal axes), linear error propagation V y = JV x J T and its second-order Hessian bias term, exact derivation of single- and multi-observable BLUE weights via Lagrange multipliers, χ 2 compatibility tests, Peelle’s Pertinent Puzzle and iterative relative-error BLUE, and comparison of GUM linear vs. GUM-S1 Monte Carlo propagation; worked examples: combining correlated W -boson mass measurements across Tevatron/LHC/LEP and propagating correlated track (p T , η, ϕ) errors to invariant mass m µµ .
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy implementation of Jacobian error propagation (using finite differences and symbolic Jacobians), Monte Carlo nonlinear error propagation, and a full multi-observable BLUE solver returning weights, combined covariance, uncertainty breakdown by source, and compatibility p-value. Stage 2: Cross-checking Stage 1 against BLUE-py / ROOT BLUE (Nisius) and iminuit covariance extraction on a realistic multi-experiment m W combination table.
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (error propagation for ratios/differences with correlation ρ = ±1, proving BLUE minimizes variance among all linear unbiased estimators, analytical threshold ρ > σ 1 /σ 2 for negative BLUE weights in a 2-measurement combination, demonstrating Peelle’s Pertinent Puzzle for multiplicative scale errors) + 2 computational problems (linear vs. Monte Carlo propagation for a nonlinear Breit–Wigner peak near a boundary; reproducing a multi-experiment combination with varying correlation assumptions ρ ∈ [−1, 1]). Exit criterion: BLUE weights sum to unity, χ 2 matches generalized least squares to < 10 −10 , and negative-weight sensitivity scan is correctly interpreted.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: PDG Probability (Sec. 39.3) & Statistics (Sec. 40), Cowan’s CERN lectures, and JCGM GUM-6:2020 / JCGM 102:2011. Intermediate: Lyons–Gibaut–Clifford (1988) and Valassi (2003). Advanced/optional: Nisius (2020) ROOT BLUE , the 2024 World m W Combination paper, and Fowlie et al. (2022) on combining likelihoods vs. intervals.

learningOutcomes: Construct and validate positive-semidefinite covariance and correlation
matrices from multi-source statistical and systematic error budgets.
Propagate uncertainties through nonlinear vector functions via first-order Jacobian linearization V y = JV x J T and identify regimes requiring Monte Carlo propagation.
Derive and implement the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) for single and multiple correlated physical observables.
Diagnose and interpret negative BLUE weights, anti-correlated measurement gains, and estimator-compatibility χ 2 p-values.
Identify Peelle’s Pertinent Puzzle in multiplicative/relative uncertainties and contrast iterative BLUE with full likelihood combination.
Explain why intersecting individual confidence intervals fails compared to combining full likelihoods or covariance matrices.
Validate custom Python BLUE implementations against BLUE-py , ROOT BLUE , and iminuit covariance routines.

lectures.title: Parameter Estimation — Maximum Likelihood, Least Squares, and Bayesian Inference

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 3.1 (probability densities) and Lecture 3.2 (covariance matrices and error propagation). Downstream links: Lecture 3.4 (likelihood-ratio test statistics), Lecture 3.5 (profiling vs. marginalizing nuisance parameters), Lecture 3.6 (regularized unfolding as penalized MLE/MAP), and Lecture 3.7 (MCMC posterior sampling).

lectures.abstract: Parameter estimation transforms raw detector events into precision measurements of Standard Model parameters. This lecture develops point and interval estimation from both frequentist and Bayesian foundations. In the frequentist framework, we derive the properties of estimators—consistency, bias, variance, sufficiency, and the Cramér–Rao–Frechet minimum-variance bound via the Fisher information matrix—before covering unbinned, binned, and extended Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), Baker–Cousins Poisson χ 2 , and weighted/generalized Least Squares (LS). In the Bayesian framework, we formulate posterior inference via Bayes’ theorem, prior sensitivity (flat, conjugate, and invariant Jeffreys priors), credible intervals (highest posterior density vs. central), and marginalization, contrasting frequentist vs. Bayesian behavior in small-sample and bounded-parameter regimes.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full proofs of the Cramér–Rao inequality, asymptotic normality and efficiency of MLE, extended maximum likelihood (Barlow), Baker–Cousins likelihood-ratio χ 2 for Poisson histograms, MINUIT/MIGRAD/HESSE/MINOS algorithms for asymmetric ∆(−2 ln L) = 1 intervals, p and Bayesian posterior updating with Jeffreys prior p(θ) ∝ det I(θ); worked examples: exponential lifetime MLE (τ̂ = t̄) vs. binned χ 2 bias, and simultaneous yield + mass + width extended unbinned fit to a simulated H → γγ peak.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/SciPy custom unbinned and extended negative log-likelihood (NLL) minimizer using scipy.optimize.minimize (BFGS), computing numerical Hessian covariances and profile-likelihood ∆(2NLL) = 1 contours, plus a grid-based Bayesian posterior integrator for a Poisson rate with flat vs. Jeffreys priors. Stage 2: Production frequentist fits with iminuit ( MIGRAD / HESSE / MINOS ) and zfit / RooFit , alongside Bayesian MCMC inference in emcee and PyMC .
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (Cramér–Rao bound and efficiency check for exponential and Poisson MLEs, proving Gauss–Markov equivalence of Gaussian MLE and linear LS, Neyman vs. Pearson χ 2 bias in low-count Poisson histograms, deriving the Jeffreys prior for Poisson rate µ and Binomial probability p) + 2 computational problems (toy-MC pull study verifying unbiasedness and unit pull width for extended unbinned MLE vs. binned LS; comparing MINOS frequentist intervals against Bayesian HPD credible intervals for small N ). Exit criterion: toy-MC pull mean |µ pull | < 0.05 and width σ pull = 1.00 ± 0.05 across 2,000 pseudo-experiments.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: PDG Statistics (Sec. 40.2), Cowan’s Statistical Data Analysis (Ch. 5–7), and Cowan’s Santiago 2024 lectures. Intermediate: Cousins’ Lectures on Statistics in Theory (arXiv:1807.05996) and iminuit documentation. Advanced/optional: Verkerke & Kirkby ( RooFit ), zfit , NIST Bayesian vs. GUM regression study, and PyMC / emcee probabilistic programming docs.

Fisher information matrix and the Cramér–Rao lower bound.
Formulate and maximize unbinned, binned, and extended likelihood functions, interpreting ∆(−2 ln L) = 1 contours and MINOS asymmetric errors. 2
Diagnose biases in Neyman/Pearson χ fits to low-count histograms and apply the Baker–Cousins Poisson likelihood ratio.

Contrast frequentist confidence intervals and Bayesian credible intervals, explaining the Likelihood Principle and prior-choice sensitivity. Derive invariant Jeffreys priors for one-dimensional exponential-family
distributions and compute HPD vs. central credible intervals.
Execute pull studies with pseudo-experiments to validate estimator unbiasedness and uncertainty calibration.
Perform production parameter estimation using iminuit , zfit / RooFit , emcee , and PyMC .

lectures.title: Hypothesis Testing, Profile Likelihood, CL s , and the Look-Elsewhere Effect

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 3.1 (distributions) and Lecture 3.3 (maximum likelihood estimation and Fisher information). Downstream links: Lecture 3.5 (incorporating systematic nuisance parameters into q 0 and q̃ µ ), Part 11 (Higgs discovery significance, BSM resonance searches, and FCC-hh/FCC-ee exclusion projections).
