lectures.abstract: Claiming a 5σ discovery or setting a 95% confidence-level exclusion limit at the LHC and future colliders demands airtight frequentist hypothesis testing. This lecture begins with the Neyman–Pearson lemma, Type-I/Type-II errors (α, β), statistical power, and p-value interpretation (explicitly dismantling common p-value fallacies). We derive Wilks’ and Wald’s theorems for the profile likelihood ratio λ(µ) and present the complete LHC asymptotic formalism of Cowan, Cranmer, Gross, and Vitells (q 0 , q µ , q̃ µ , and the Asimov dataset for median expected significance and ±1σ, ±2σ Brazil bands). We then contrast unified Feldman–Cousins confidence belts with the modified frequentist CL s = p s+b /(1 − p b ) prescription (Junk, Read) and derive the Gross–Vitells upcrossing method for quantifying the Look-Elsewhere Effect (LEE) trial factor in mass scans.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous proofs of the Neyman–Pearson lemma and Wilks’ theorem; explicit boundary-corrected half-χ 2 distributions for q 0 and √ q̃ µ ; derivation of the Cowan–Cranmer–Gross–Vitells asymptotic discovery significance Z 0 = q 0 and Asimov expected significance Z A = p 2[(s + b) ln(1 + s/b) − s]; construction of Feldman–Cousins likelihood-ratio ordering belts vs. CL s protection against downward background fluctuations; Gross–Vitells Euler-characteristic / upcrossing bound p global ≤ p local + ⟨N (c 0 )⟩e −(c−c 0 )/2 ; worked example: Higgs-like diphoton bump hunt over an exponential background.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy/SciPy bump-hunt engine computing local q 0 (m) and q̃ µ (m) across a mass window, generating 10,000 background- only toys to compare empirical tail p-values against Wilks’ asymptotics and verifying the Gross–Vitells global trial factor via upcrossings. Stage 2: Reproducing asymptotic and toy-based discovery p 0 , CL s upper limits, and Brazil bands using pyhf and hepstats ( hypotests ) / RooStats . √
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (Neyman–Pearson optimal test statistic for Poisson counting and Gaussian mean shift, deriving Z A → s/ b √ in the s ≪ b limit and showing where s/ b fails, proving CL s over-covers and never excludes zero-sensitivity signals, deriving the Gross–Vitells trial-factor scaling with mass-window width and detector resolution) + 2 computational problems (Feldman–Cousins belt construction for Poisson n ∼ Pois(s + b) with b = 3.0; Brazil-band CL s limit scan in pyhf comparing asymptotic vs. toy calculators at low counts). Exit criterion: Stage 1 asymptotic CL s limits match pyhf to < 10 −4 and toy-calibrated breakdown of asymptotics at b < 5 is quantitatively demonstrated.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Cowan–Cranmer–Gross–Vitells (arXiv:1007.1727), PDG Statistics (Sec. 40.3–40.5), and Cowan’s Statistics for Searches at the LHC (arXiv:1307.2487). Intermediate: Read (2002) CL s , Junk (1999), Feldman & Cousins (1998), and Gross & Vitells (2010). Advanced/optional: RooStats (Moneta et al.), pyhf JOSS/arXiv papers, and hepstats .

learningOutcomes: Prove the Neyman–Pearson lemma and distinguish p-values, Type-I
error rates α, power 1 − β, and posterior hypothesis probabilities.
Derive the asymptotic distributions of profile likelihood ratio test statistics (t µ , q 0 , q µ , q̃ µ ) using Wilks’ and Wald’s theorems.
Construct Asimov datasets to compute median expected discovery significance and ±1σ, ±2σ exclusion sensitivity bands without running toys.

Compute modified frequentist CL s upper limits and contrast their coverage and physical behavior with Feldman–Cousins unified intervals. Quantify the Look-Elsewhere Effect in resonance searches using the
Gross–Vitells upcrossing formula and calibrate trial factors with pseudo-experiments.
Diagnose when asymptotic formulae break down (low event counts, parameter boundaries) and switch cleanly to toy-based inference.
Execute publication-grade hypothesis tests and limit scans in pyhf , hepstats , and RooStats .

lectures.title: Systematic Uncertainties, Nuisance Parameters, and Profile-Likelihood Modeling

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 3.2 (correlations), Lecture 3.3 (MLE and Bayesian marginalization), and Lecture 3.4 (profile likelihood ratio). Downstream links: Lecture 3.6 (propagating systematics through unfolding), Part 11 (global LHC/FCC statistical combinations, Higgs mass and coupling measurements, and HEPData likelihood preservation).
dependencies.prerequisites: Lecture 3.2 (correlations), Lecture 3.3 (MLE and Bayesian marginalization), and Lecture 3.4 (profile likelihood ratio).

lectures.abstract: At high-luminosity colliders such as HL-LHC and FCC-ee, experimental precision is overwhelmingly limited by systematic rather than statistical uncertainties. This lecture formalizes systematic uncertainties as nuisance parameters θ constrained by auxiliary control measurements in a joint statistical ˆ Q model L(µ, θ) = P (data|µ, θ) k p k ( θ̃ k |θ k ). We compare frequentist profiling (replacing θ by conditional MLEs θ̂(µ)) against Bayesian/Cousins– Highland marginalization, derive the HistFactory modifier algebra ( normsys , histosys , shapesys , staterror ) including piecewise-exponential and polynomial template morphing, and analyze finite-Monte-Carlo template uncertainties via Barlow–Beeston and Conway’s Barlow–Beeston-lite approximations. Finally, we master essential diagnostic plots: nuisance-parameter pulls, constraints, correlation matrices, and ranking/impact plots.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivation of auxiliary-measurement constraint terms (Gaussian, log-normal, Gamma/Poisson) and why log-normal avoids unphysical negative rates; vertical vs. horizontal template morphing ( histosys interpolation codes); exact Barlow–Beeston per-bin per-process profiling vs. Barlow–Beeston-lite (Conway) and symmetric Poisson approximations (Dembinski–Abdelmotteleb); treatment of correlated vs. uncorrelated systematics across channels/experiments (e.g., ATLAS+CMS Higgs mass combination); mathematical definition of nuisance pulls ( θ̂ − θ 0 )/σ 0 , constraints σ θ̂ /σ 0 , and impacts ∆µ̂; worked example: 2-channel signal + control-region fit constraining a background normalization and jet-energy-scale shape systematic.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy/SciPy implementation of a multi-bin Poisson likelihood with a Gaussian-constrained shape-morphing nuisance parameter and Barlow–Beeston-lite MC statistical uncertainties, computing pulls, constraints, and parameter impacts. Stage 2: Building the exact HistFactory JSON workspace in pyhf (with autodiff/JAX or SciPy backend), running fit diagnostics, and comparing against CMS Combine / ATLAS HistFitter conventions.
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (proving Gaussian vs. log-normal constraint equivalence at small σ and divergence at large σ, deriving the exact Barlow–Beeston-lite quadratic equation for per-bin γ i , showing how an in-situ control region constrains a shared background nuisance parameter, comparing profiled vs. marginalized uncertainty on a counting-experiment signal strength) + 2 computational problems (producing a complete nuisance-parameter pull/constraint/impact ranking plot for a 3-channel pyhf model; diagnosing an over-constrained nuisance parameter caused by a two-point theory systematic). Exit criterion: Stage 1 custom profile likelihood matches pyhf MLEs, pulls, and impacts to < 10 −4 and correctly flags an injected mis-modeled systematic via pull diagnostics.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Cranmer’s Practical Statistics for the LHC (arXiv:1503.07622), HistFactory User Guide (CERN-OPEN-2012-016), and PDG Statistics (Sec. 40). Intermediate: Conway (arXiv:1103.0354), Barlow & Beeston (1993), and pyhf documentation (arXiv:2211.15838). Advanced/optional: CMS Combine (arXiv:2404.06614), ATLAS HistFitter (arXiv:1410.1280), Dembinski & Abdelmotteleb (arXiv:2206.12346), and ATLAS+CMS Higgs mass combination (PRL 114, 191803).

learningOutcomes: Formulate joint likelihood models separating parameters of interest µ
from constrained nuisance parameters θ and global observables.
Select and justify Gaussian, log-normal, and Poisson/Gamma constraint terms and vertical vs. horizontal template-morphing schemes.
Implement exact Barlow–Beeston and Barlow–Beeston-lite treatments of finite Monte Carlo template statistical uncertainties (including weighted MC events).
Model correlated and uncorrelated systematic uncertainties across disjoint signal and control regions or independent collider experiments. Compute and interpret nuisance-parameter pulls, constraints,
correlation matrices, and post-fit impacts on parameters of interest.
Contrast frequentist profiling with Bayesian/Cousins–Highland marginalization and identify pathologies such as over-constraining two-point systematics.
Author, serialize (JSON), fit, and validate full HistFactory statistical workspaces using pyhf , iminuit , and CMS Combine /ATLAS HistFitter workflows.

lectures.title: Unfolding, Inverse Problems, and Template-Fit Strategies

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 3.2 (covariance algebra), Lecture 3.3 (regularized MLE/MAP), and Lecture 3.5 (systematic nuisance parameters and template fits). Downstream links: Part 11 (fiducial differential cross-section measurements at LHC/FCC-ee, HEPData preservation, and theory reinterpretation) and Part 12 (machine-learning-based unbinned unfolding).
dependencies.prerequisites: Lecture 3.2 (covariance algebra), Lecture 3.3 (regularized MLE/MAP), and Lecture 3.5 (systematic nuisance parameters and template fits).
dependencies.downstream: Part 11 (fiducial differential cross-section measurements at LHC/FCC-ee, HEPData preservation, and theory reinterpretation) and Part 12 (machine-learning-based unbinned unfolding).

lectures.abstract: Reconstructed collider spectra are distorted by finite detector resolution, limited acceptance, and efficiency losses, turning differential cross-section P measurements into ill-posed Fredholm integral inverse problems ν i = j R ij µ j + b i . This lecture dissects why naive response-matrix inversion amplifies high-frequency statistical noise into wild bin-to-bin oscillations (via the singular-value spectrum and condition number of R) and why bin-by-bin correction factors suffer severe prior bias. We rigorously develop the primary regularized unfolding frameworks used in HEP: Tikhonov / curvature regularization ( TUnfold ), Singular Value Decomposition unfolding (Höcker–Kartvelishvili), Iterative Bayesian Unfolding (D’Agostini / Richardson–Lucy), profile-likelihood template unfolding, and modern unbinned machine-learning unfolding ( OmniFold , conditional invertible neural networks). Emphasis is placed on bias–variance trade-offs, regularization-strength selection (L-curve, global correlation coefficient), covariance estimation, and closure/stress testing.

deliverables.lectureNote: Discretization of the Fredholm integral equation of the first kind, SVD diagnosis of ill-conditioning and noise amplification, full derivations of Tikhonov regularization with curvature matrix L ( TUnfold ), SVD unfolding (Höcker–Kartvelishvili), D’Agostini iterative Bayesian unfolding (showing convergence toward the unregularized MLE as iterations k → ∞), profile-likelihood unfolding with nuisance parameters, and unbinned classifier-reweighting ( OmniFold ); explicit covariance propagation and bias-corrected uncertainty quantification (Kuusela–Panaretos); worked example: unfolding a falling jet-p T spectrum and a bimodal resonance spectrum under Gaussian smearing and non-uniform efficiency.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy/SciPy implementation of response-matrix construction, naive inversion, Tikhonov curvature regularization (with L-curve scan), SVD unfolding, and D’Agostini IBU, measuring bias, variance, mean-squared error, and frequentist coverage across 500 toy experiments. Stage 2: Production unfolding using RooUnfold / TUnfold and a lightweight Python OmniFold / classifier-reweighting benchmark on a multi-observable jet dataset.
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (proving oscillation amplification from small singular values σ k ≪ 1, deriving the Tikhonov normal equations and exact linear error propagation matrix, showing D’Agostini IBU preserves total event count and positivity, comparing forward-folding template fits vs. unfolded differential cross sections for theory reinterpretation) + 2 computational problems (reweighting stress test exposing prior bias when truth data differs from MC prior; comparing covariance matrices from analytical error propagation vs. bootstrap/toy pseudo-experiments). Exit criterion: closure test recovers truth within < 1σ (with χ 2 /ndf ≈ 1), L-curve optimal τ minimizes global MSE, and bias-induced coverage loss under over-regularization is quantified.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Cowan’s Statistical Data Analysis (Ch. 11), Spanò (2013) Unfolding in particle physics, and Höcker & Kartvelishvili (hep-ph/9509307). Intermediate: Adye ( RooUnfold , arXiv:1105.1160) and Schmitt ( TUnfold , arXiv:1205.6201). Advanced/optional: Kuusela & Panaretos (arXiv:1505.04768), OmniFold (arXiv:1911.09107), Tools for Unbinned Unfolding (arXiv:2503.09720), Gaussian-Process unfolding (arXiv:1811.01242), and iterative cINN unfolding (SciPost 2024).

learningOutcomes: Formulate detector smearing, acceptance, and efficiency as a discretized
response matrix R ij and diagnose ill-conditioning via its singular-value spectrum.
Explain why unregularized matrix inversion produces large anti-correlated bin fluctuations and why bin-by-bin correction factors are biased toward the MC prior.
Implement and compare Tikhonov ( TUnfold ), SVD (Höcker–Kartvelishvili), and iterative Bayesian (D’Agostini) unfolding algorithms.
Select regularization parameters systematically using L-curve scans, minimal global correlation, or empirical Bayes criteria, quantifying the bias–variance trade-off.
Propagate statistical, MC-template, and detector-systematic uncertainties into full unfolded bin-to-bin covariance matrices and validate coverage with stress tests.
Contrast forward-folding profile-likelihood template fits with unfolded fiducial cross sections and evaluate when each strategy is optimal.
Apply modern unbinned unfolding ( OmniFold ) alongside classical RooUnfold / TUnfold pipelines.

lectures.title: Monte Carlo Methods, Importance Sampling, and Variance Reduction

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 1 (numerical integration and random-number generation), Lecture 2.3 (relativistic phase space), Lecture 3.1 (probability distributions), and Lecture 3.3 (Bayesian posteriors). Downstream links: Part 5 (perturbative cross-section integration), Part 7 (Geant4 detector simulation), and Part 8 (MadGraph5_aMC@NLO/Pythia 8 event generation, weighted/unweighted events, and neural importance sampling).

lectures.abstract: High-dimensional phase-space integrals, parton-shower evolution, detector transport, and Bayesian posterior marginalization are analytically intractable and numerically defeated by grid quadrature in d ≳ 4 dimensions. This lecture provides a rigorous treatment of Monte Carlo (MC) methods tailored to HEP event generation and statistical inference. We cover pseudorandom number generators (PCG, Mersenne Twister, Ranlux) and reproducibility, √ inverse-transform and Box–Muller sampling, von Neumann accept–reject (hit-or-miss) unweighting, and the O(1/ N ) convergence of crude MC integration. We then derive variance-reduction techniques—stratified sampling, antithetic variates, control variates, and adaptive/multi-channel importance sampling ( VEGAS , resonant Breit–Wigner mapping via s → tan θ)—before introducing Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Metropolis–Hastings, affine-invariant ensemble sampling, Hamiltonian/NUTS) and diagnostics (effective sample size N eff , autocorrelation time τ int , and Kish weight efficiency).

deliverables.lectureNote: Proofs of unbiasedness and O(N −1/2 ) dimension-independent scaling of MC quadrature, inverse-CDF and Box–Muller derivations, accept–reject efficiency and unweighting of weighted collider events, optimal importance-sampling proposal q ∗ (x) ∝ |f (x)|, mathematical derivation of the VEGAS adaptive grid-refinement algorithm + − ∗ + − (Lepage P 2021), Breit–Wigner Jacobian importance mapping for e e → Z → µ µ cross sections, Kish effective sample size N eff = ( w i ) 2 / w i 2 , and detailed balance for Metropolis–Hastings and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo; worked P examples: 6D phase-space integral with a sharp Z-boson pole and MCMC posterior sampling of a correlated 4-parameter model.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure Python/NumPy implementation of inverse-CDF, Box–Muller, accept–reject, Breit–Wigner importance sampling, a 2D adaptive VEGAS -style stratified integrator, and a Metropolis–Hastings sampler with autocorrelation and acceptance-rate diagnostics. Stage 2: High-dimensional cross-section integration with Lepage’s vegas / MadGraph5_aMC@NLO concepts, Bayesian posterior sampling with emcee (Goodman–Weare affine- invariant ensemble) and PyMC (NUTS), and inspecting weighted/unweighted event generation mechanics in Pythia 8 .
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (deriving Box–Muller transformation and Jacobian, proving optimal importance-sampling density minimizes variance, deriving the Breit–Wigner tangent substitution s − M 2 = M Γ tan ρ and its flat Jacobian, proving detailed balance and stationarity of the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance kernel) + 2 computational problems (benchmarking crude MC vs. importance sampling vs. stratified VEGAS variance reduction on a sharply peaked 6D integrand; computing autocorrelation time τ int , R̂, and N eff for Metropolis–Hastings vs. emcee on a strongly correlated Rosenbrock-like posterior). Exit criterion: achieve ≥ 100× variance reduction on the peaked 6D integral via importance sampling and verify MCMC posterior moments agree with exact quadrature within 2σ MC .
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: PDG Monte Carlo Techniques review, Cowan’s Statistical Data Analysis (Ch. 3), and Bielajew’s Fundamentals of the Monte Carlo Method. Intermediate: Lepage VEGAS Enhanced (arXiv:2009.05112) and emcee / PyMC tutorials. Advanced/optional: MadGraph5_ aMC@NLO (arXiv:1405.0301), Pythia / Herwig collider event-generator comparison (arXiv:2509.24567), Metropolis historic perspective, and exact inference from noisy MC simulations (APS).

Combine stratified sampling, multi-channel mappings, and antithetic/control variates for peaked collider phase-space integrands. Derive detailed balance for Metropolis–Hastings and Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo (NUTS) and diagnose chain convergence via autocorrelation times and R̂.
Distinguish weighted vs. unweighted collider event samples and account for negative weights (NLO matching) in statistical variance calculations.
Implement and benchmark production MC integration and Bayesian MCMC pipelines using SciPy , emcee , PyMC , and HEP event-generator tooling ( MadGraph5_aMC@NLO , Pythia ).

parts.abstract: Modern high-energy physics experiments operate as distributed software instruments spanning exabytes of columnar event data, heterogeneous CPU/GPU clusters, and multi-decade collaboration lifetimes. This part builds the complete computational foundation required to move from interactive prototypes to reproducible, high-throughput scientific software deployed across CERN and Future Circular Collider (FCC) infrastructure. Beginning with POSIX environments, SSH workflows on lxplus , and collaborative Git engineering, the sequence advances through vectorized scientific Python, memory-aware Modern C++17/20, declarative CMake/Spack/CVMFS/Apptainer software stacks, automated testing and profiling, next-generation columnar I/O ( ROOT RNTuple , EDM4hep , HDF5, Parquet), and performance-portable parallel computing. Graduates acquire the engineering discipline needed to author, verify, and scale production HEP code.

deliverables.lectureNote: Unified ~160-page monograph (eight chapters, 15–25 pages each) establishing consistent SI/natural-unit conventions, memory- hierarchy models (bytes, cache lines, FLOP/byte operational intensity), formal complexity bounds, and worked end-to-end HEP code comparisons between Python and C++17/20.
deliverables.lab: Progressive eight-module studio moving from Stage 1 Python prototypes (NumPy/SciPy/Uproot/Awkward) to Stage 2 production HEP tooling ( lxplus , GitLab CI, Modern C++, CMake, Spack, CVMFS, Apptainer, Key4hep / EDM4hep , ROOT::RDataFrame / RNTuple , and OpenMP/MPI/CUDA/Kokkos).
deliverables.problemSet: Eight integrated analytical and computational assignments (memory-layout derivations, Roofline bounds, I/O throughput modeling, and reproducible containerized benchmarks) with a capstone exit criterion requiring a tested, CI-verified, containerized RNTuple analysis pipeline achieving ≥ 80% of Roofline memory bandwidth on multi-core hardware.

lectures.abstract: High-energy physics computing takes place almost exclusively on headless Linux clusters accessed remotely over secure shell protocols. This lecture introduces the POSIX process model, filesystem hierarchy, permission bits, standard streams, pipelines, and defensive Bash scripting ( set -euo pipefail , quoting, job control). Students examine the CERN interactive login service ( lxplus ), including Kerberos/AFS/EOS storage quotas ( /afs , / eos ), SSH key management, ControlMaster connection multiplexing, ProxyJump tunneling, and HTCondor batch submission interfaces. Emphasis is placed on automating repetitive data-processing tasks through composable Unix filters ( awk , sed , find , xargs , rsync ) and clean login-environment hygiene so remote scientific workflows remain fast, auditable, and resilient to network drops.

deliverables.lectureNote: 18-page guide covering POSIX file descriptors ( stdin / stdout / stderr ), exit codes, signal handling ( SIGINT / SIGTERM ), quoting rules, SSH cryptographic authentication, ControlMaster / ProxyJump configs, and CERN lxplus /AFS/EOS filesystem semantics with worked command-line recipes.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a local POSIX shell pipeline parsing simulated detector log files and computing rate statistics via awk /Python CLI wrappers; Stage 2 migrates the workflow to remote SSH execution ( ~/.ssh/config with ControlMaster , rsync staging, and lxplus /HTCondor job-submission templates).
deliverables.problemSet: Four analytical/practical tasks (debugging broken quoting and race conditions in batch scripts, analyzing file-descriptor redirections, writing an idempotent POSIX log-archiver, and configuring passwordless multiplexed SSH tunnels); exit criterion: zero shellcheck -style quoting defects and deterministic exit codes across edge-case filenames.

lectures.abstract: Version control in large scientific collaborations is not merely backup storage; it is a content-addressed directed acyclic graph (DAG) enabling concurrent development by hundreds of physicists across decades. This lecture demystifies Git’s object model (blobs, trees, commits, annotated tags) and reflog mechanics before mastering branching, three-way merging, interactive rebasing, cherry-picking, conflict resolution, and git bisect regression hunting. Students contrast trunk-based development, GitHub Flow, and GitLab Flow as practiced in CERN GitLab and Key4hep repositories. Equal weight is given to human collaboration: crafting atomic Conventional Commits, structuring small reviewable merge requests, conducting constructive technical code reviews, and enforcing repository hygiene through hooks and push rules.

deliverables.lectureNote: 18-page treatise covering Git’s SHA-1/SHA-256 content-addressed DAG, index/staging semantics, fast-forward vs. three-way merge vs. rebase graph transformations, git bisect binary search complexity O(log 2 N ), and structured code-review rubrics.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 simulates a two-developer feature branch conflict and interactive history cleanup on a local Python physics script; Stage 2 executes a full fork-and-merge-request workflow on GitHub/GitLab with Conventional Commits, automated pre-commit hooks, and peer code review.

lectures.abstract: Python serves as the interactive orchestration and exploratory analysis language of modern particle physics, provided numerical kernels are delegated to compiled array backends rather than Python bytecode loops. This lecture develops vectorized thinking from first principles: NumPy’s ndarray memory model (data buffers, dtype , shapes, strides, zero-copy views vs. copies), broadcasting algebra, universal functions ( ufuncs ), and numerical algorithms in SciPy (quadrature, ODE integrators, root finding, sparse linear algebra, optimization, and statistical distributions). lectures.abstract: Detector simulation ( Geant4 ), geometry ( DD4hep ), reconstruction, and columnar I/O ( ROOT , PODIO ) rely on Modern C++ to deliver zero-overhead abstractions at hardware speed. This lecture teaches C++17/20 as a type-safe, value-oriented systems language rather than "C with classes." Topics include value semantics, move semantics, Rule of Zero/Five, RAII and smart pointers ( std::unique_ptr ), STL containers and algorithms, templates, constexpr compile-time evaluation, and C++20 std::span /concepts/ranges. Crucially, students connect language semantics to CPU microarchitecture: cache lines (64 B), spatial/temporal locality, branch prediction, Array-of-Structures (AoS) vs. Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) layouts, and inspecting generated x86-64 assembly in Compiler Explorer to verify inlining and auto-vectorization.

deliverables.lectureNote: 24-page technical manual deriving object-size/padding alignment rules, move vs. copy elision guarantees, RAII exception safety, template instantiation mechanics, and quantitative L1/L2/L3 cache-miss models comparing AoS vs. SoA particle-track storage.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 prototypes a 4-momentum Lorentz-boost and calorimeter-clustering kernel in Python; Stage 2 implements both AoS ( std::vector<Particle> ) and SoA ( ParticleSoA with std::span ) versions in C++20, inspects emitted SIMD assembly on godbolt.org , and benchmarks cache-miss rates.
deliverables.problemSet: Four analytical/coding problems (calculating struct padding/alignment, implementing a move-only RAII file-handle wrapper, writing a constexpr /concepts-constrained 4-vector template, and benchmarking AoS vs. SoA SIMD throughput); exit criterion: zero warnings under -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic , zero sanitizer errors, and verified AVX2/SSE vectorization in assembly.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: HSF/CERN C++ Course (Ponce et al.), Stroustrup & Sutter C++ Core Guidelines, and Compiler Explorer ( godbolt.org ); advanced/optional: Ulrich Drepper What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory, Agner Fog Optimizing Software in C++, and ISO C++ FAQ.

compare AoS and SoA memory layouts for HEP particle collections.

lectures.abstract: Reproducible science requires bit-level or environment-level provenance across hundreds of interdependent C++, Fortran, and Python libraries. This lecture covers the complete HEP software-delivery stack: target-based Modern CMake ( target_link_libraries , PUBLIC / PRIVATE / INTERFACE transitive properties, find_package , FetchContent , presets), combinatorial HPC package management with Spack (specs, concretization, environments), global read-only software distribution via CernVM-FS ( /cvmfs , FUSE, Merkle-tree cryptographic verification, /cvmfs/sw.hsf.org/key4hep ), and rootless HPC containerization with Apptainer (SIF images, definition files, bind /cvmfs ). Students learn how Key4hep unifies these layers so identical FCC simulation and analysis environments run seamlessly from laptops to lxplus and Tier-1 supercomputers.

deliverables.lectureNote: 20-page architecture guide detailing compilation/linking stages (ELF symbols, RPATH / RUNPATH , ABI compatibility), Modern CMake target-dependency graphs, Spack DAG concretization, CVMFS Stratum-0/1/Squid caching topology, and Apptainer user-namespace isolation.

lectures.abstract: Scientific conclusions are only as trustworthy as the software that produces them. This lecture establishes production software-engineering practices tailored to numerical physics codes: unit, property-based, and physics-regression testing ( pytest for Python, GoogleTest and CTest for C++); automated Continuous Integration (GitHub Actions and CERN GitLab CI); static analysis ( clang-tidy ); dynamic memory and undefined-behavior diagnostics ( GDB , Valgrind Memcheck, LLVM AddressSanitizer / UBSan ); sampling performance profiling ( Linux perf and Brendan Gregg’s CPU/Off- CPU Flame Graphs); and maintainable API documentation ( Sphinx , Doxygen ). Students adopt a disciplined "measure, don’t guess" workflow that catches subtle numerical regressions and memory corruptions before they contaminate physics results.

deliverables.lectureNote: 20-page engineering handbook detailing test-pyramid design for floating-point code (ULP vs. relative tolerance), CI YAML pipeline architectures, sanitizer instrumentation overhead, hardware performance counters ( perf stat / perf record ), flame-graph reading rules, and docs-as-code workflows.

lectures.abstract: Exabyte-scale collider datasets are frequently I/O-bound rather than compute-bound, making serialization layout a first-order physics-computing constraint. This lecture analyzes columnar vs. row-wise storage, compression codecs ( ZSTD , LZ4 , ZLIB ), split-level schema evolution, and zero-copy in-memory interchange. Students contrast legacy ROOT TTree basket mechanics with ROOT’s next-generation RNTuple subsystem (pages, clusters, sealed envelopes, direct NVMe/object-store readiness) and examine the FCC common Event Data Model ( EDM4hep ) generated by PODIO . Cross-domain scientific formats — HDF5 (hierarchical chunked multidimensional arrays and h5py ) and Apache Parquet/Arrow — are benchmarked head-to-head against RNTuple using both ROOT::RDataFrame and Python’s Uproot / Awkward / PyArrow stack.

deliverables.lectureNote: 22-page comparative specification deriving storage-amplification and read-amplification factors for row vs. columnar layouts, TTree basket vs. RNTuple page/cluster architectures, PODIO YAML-to-C++ code generation for EDM4hep , HDF5 chunk-cache mechanics, and Apache Arrow/Parquet memory/disk schemas.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 reads an FCC-ee EDM4hep sample via Uproot / Awkward and exports selected branches to HDF5 ( h5py ) and Apache Parquet ( pyarrow ); Stage 2 benchmarks multi-threaded read throughput, file size, and decompression CPU cost across TTree , RNTuple , HDF5, and Parquet using ROOT::RDataFrame and podio::RNTupleReader .
deliverables.problemSet: Four quantitative I/O exercises (modeling selective-column read speedup vs. compression ratio, designing a custom PODIO YAML schema for calorimeter clusters, comparing TTree vs. RNTuple cluster-prefetch latency, and zero-copy Arrow-to-Awkward conversion); exit criterion: reproducible benchmark report demonstrating RNTuple throughput and storage savings over TTree .

RNTuple papers (ACAT 2021, CHEP 2024), ROOT::RDataFrame docs, EDM4hep Key4hep tutorial, and Apache Parquet/Arrow docs; advanced/optional: HDF5 User Guide, h5py Parallel HDF5 docs, Pivarski Awkward Array C++/Python papers, and hepconvert .

lectures.abstract: With Dennard scaling ended, future collider computing at HL-LHC and FCC relies on exploiting multi-core CPUs, multi-node clusters, and GPU accelerators simultaneously. This lecture builds a quantitative performance-reasoning framework grounded in Amdahl’s and Gustafson’s laws and the Roofline model (operational intensity vs. peak FLOP/s and memory bandwidth). Students study shared-memory concurrency ( std::thread , data races, false sharing, OpenMP , Intel oneTBB ), distributed-memory message passing ( MPI point-to-point and collective operations), and GPU execution architectures ( CUDA thread hierarchy, warps, coalesced global memory, shared-memory tiling). To avoid vendor lock-in across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel hardware, the lecture introduces performance-portable C++ abstractions adopted in HEP ( Kokkos , Alpaka , and Khronos SYCL ).

deliverables.lectureNote: 24-page monograph deriving Amdahl/Gustafson strong/weak scaling bounds, Roofline ceiling equations (P ≤ min(P peak , I · B peak )), cache-coherence false-sharing costs, MPI collective communication complexity, CUDA warp-divergence/occupancy models, and Kokkos/Alpaka execution/memory-space abstractions.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 prototypes a 2D particle-in-cell / N-body space-charge force solver in NumPy; Stage 2 implements and scales the kernel across OpenMP/ oneTBB (shared memory), MPI (distributed domain decomposition), and CUDA/Kokkos (GPU), plotting measured throughput directly onto the target machine’s empirical Roofline diagram.
deliverables.problemSet: Four analytical and benchmarking problems (deriving Roofline operational intensity for sparse matrix-vector multiply and track propagation, diagnosing false sharing in a multi-threaded histogrammer, analyzing strong vs. weak MPI scaling efficiency, and refactoring a non-coalesced GPU kernel); exit criterion: verified numerical agreement across serial/OpenMP/MPI/GPU backends within 10 −6 relative tolerance and measured ≥ 70% memory-bandwidth utilization on GPU or multi-core CPU.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Williams, Waterman & Patterson (2009) Roofline paper, OpenMP 6.1 Specification, MPI Forum Docs, and NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide; advanced/optional: Kokkos Core Wiki, Khronos SYCL 2020 Spec, Intel oneTBB Guide, and CERN traccc / Alpaka & Awkward Array GPU papers.

parts.abstract: Part 5 develops the complete theoretical edifice of modern elementary particle physics, bridging undergraduate relativistic quantum mechanics to research-grade quantum field theory (QFT) and precision phenomenology at the LHC and Future Circular Collider (FCC). Beginning with the Standard Model (SM) particle spectrum and relativistic collider kinematics, the sequence constructs canonical field quantization, Feynman rules, and tree-level QED amplitudes before advancing to non-Abelian gauge dynamics in QCD and electroweak symmetry breaking. Subsequent lectures treat quark and neutrino flavour physics, loop renormalization and Z-pole precision observables, Higgs couplings and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) portals, and early-Universe cosmology, integrating analytical derivations with production-grade computational HEP workflows.

deliverables.lectureNote: Twelve modular graduate-level monographs (~35–50 pages each) written in natural units (ℏ = c = 1) with explicit dimensional restoration tables to SI units (ℏc = 0.197327 GeV · fm, (ℏc) 2 = 0.389379 GeV 2 · mb), standardized mostly-minus metric η µν = diag(+1, −1, −1, −1), full step-by-step derivations of amplitudes, β-functions, and effective potentials, and worked collider benchmarks spanning LEP, LHC, and FCC- ee/FCC-hh.
deliverables.lab: Twelve two-stage computational notebooks progressing from Stage 1 transparent Python prototypes ( NumPy , SciPy , SymPy , scikit-hep/ vector ) to Stage 2 production HEP software ( FeynCalc 10 , FeynRules 2.0 , MadGraph5_aMC@NLO , PYTHIA 8.3 , LHAPDF6 , FastJet , SMEFTsim 3.0 , and PTPlot / thermal bounce solvers).
deliverables.problemSet: Twelve structured problem sets pairing 4–6 rigorous analytical derivations with 2–3 quantitative computational tasks per lecture; exit criterion requires ≥ 85% accuracy on analytical benchmarks and < 1% numerical agreement between Stage 1 Python prototypes and Stage 2 HEP tooling across all cross sections, decay widths, and RGE trajectories.

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes the complete particle taxonomy and symmetry architecture of the Standard Model. Students classify the three generations of chiral quarks and leptons, the twelve spin-1 gauge bosons of G SM = SU (3) C × SU (2) L × U (1) Y , and the complex scalar Higgs doublet by their Lorentz, color, weak-isospin, and hypercharge quantum numbers. Emphasis is placed on the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation Q = T 3 + Y , exact and accidental symmetries (B, L, B − L), gauge anomaly cancellation per generation, and natural-unit dimensional analysis of couplings and scales. The lecture bridges qualitative particle catalogues to the rigorous gauge-invariant Lagrangian structure developed throughout Part 5.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete representation table of SM fields (R C , R L ) Y ; explicit proof of cubic and mixed gauge-gravitational anomaly cancellation ([SU (3)] 2 U (1) Y , [SU (2)] 2 U (1) Y , [U (1) Y ] 3 , [grav] 2 U (1) Y ); conservation laws and discrete symmetries (C, P , T , CP ); natural units (ℏ = c = 1) conversion table mapping GeV to meters, seconds, kilograms, and barns; worked selection-rule examples for strong, electromagnetic, and weak decays.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python SymPy /dataclass registry of all SM particles implementing automated quantum-number conservation checks, PDG Monte Carlo ID (MCID) lookups, and symbolic gauge-anomaly trace verification. Stage 2: Programmatic querying of the particle (scikit-hep) PDG database and inspection of standard UFO / FeynRules SM model files ( sm.fr ) to cross-verify field quantum numbers and coupling definitions.
deliverables.problemSet: 4 analytical problems (anomaly cancellation with a hypothetical 4th generation; hypercharge quantization from anomaly constraints; allowed/forbidden decay selection rules; natural-unit dimensional analysis of G F , α, and Λ QCD ) + 2 computational problems (automated reaction- vertex validator in Python; comparison against FeynRules SM vertices). Exit criterion: 100% pass rate on a 50-process reaction-validity benchmark suite.

Distinguish exact gauge symmetries from global accidental symmetries (B, L e , L µ , L τ , B − L) and identify where each is violated. Convert physical quantities (masses, lifetimes, cross sections, lengths)
accurately between natural units (ℏ = c = 1) and SI units.
Apply conservation laws and discrete symmetry (C, P, CP ) selection rules to classify whether candidate particle decays proceed via strong, EM, or weak interactions.

lectures.abstract: Reconciling quantum mechanics with special relativity reveals both the necessity of spin-1/2 matter and the breakdown of single-particle wave mechanics. This lecture derives the Klein–Gordon equation and diagnoses its negative-probability pathology before constructing the Dirac equation from the Clifford algebra {γ µ , γ ν } = 2η µν . Students analyze Lorentz covariance of spinors, bilinear covariants, the Feynman–Stückelberg antiparticle interpretation, Weyl chiral projections P L,R = 12 (1 ∓ γ 5 ), Majorana spinors, and the distinction between Lorentz-invariant chirality and frame-dependent helicity. Two-component Weyl spinor notation is introduced alongside four-component Dirac algebra to prepare for modern helicity-amplitude calculations.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivation of Klein–Gordon and Dirac equations in natural units (ℏ = c = 1, with explicit Compton wavelength λ C = ℏ/(mc) SI Weyl (chiral) and Dirac representations of γ µ ; construction of plane-wave spinors u s (p) and v s (p), spin-sum completeness scale analysis); P s explicit s relations s u ū ≠ p + m; Gordon identity and magnetic moment g = 2; C, P , T transformations of Dirac bilinears; worked helicity-suppression calculation for π − → e − ν̄ e vs. π − → µ − ν̄ µ .

Stage 2: Symbolic Dirac-trace and spinor-contraction verification using FeynCalc 10 (Mathematica/Wolfram or FeynCalc benchmark scripts) and two-component spinor cross-checks following Dreiner–Haber–Martin. µ µν ψ; derive the

Exit criterion: All 16 Dirac bilinear Lorentz-transformation identities verified symbolically to zero residual.

lectures.abstract: This lecture builds the operational machinery of perturbative quantum field theory from first principles. Starting from classical field Lagrangians and Noether currents, students perform canonical quantization of real and complex Klein–Gordon fields, Dirac fermion fields (deriving the spin-statistics connection via anticommutators), and the Maxwell gauge field in covariant R ξ gauges. Using the interaction picture, Dyson’s series, Wick’s theorem, and the LSZ reduction formula, the lecture derives Feynman propagators with the causal iϵ prescription and extracts exact position- and momentum-space Feynman rules for ϕ 4 theory, Yukawa theory, and spinor QED, emphasizing symmetry factors and Grassmann sign conventions.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete canonical quantization of spin-0, spin-1/2, and spin-1 fields in natural units (ℏ = c = 1, mass dimensions [ϕ] = 1, [ψ] = 3/2, [A µ ] = 1); derivation of microcausality [ϕ(x), ϕ(y)] = 0 for spacelike intervals; contour-integral derivation of the Feynman propagator D F (x − y) and S F (x − y); proof of Wick’s theorem and LSZ reduction; complete Feynman rules and symmetry-factor catalog for ϕ 4 , Yukawa, and QED; brief bridge to functional path-integral quantization. 4
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python symbolic Wick-contraction and Feynman-diagram generator for ϕ and Yukawa theories computing connected Green’s functions and verifying symmetry factors and fermion-loop minus signs up to 2-loop order. Stage 2: Automated Lagrangian-to-Feynman-rules generation using FeynRules 2.0 ( UFO export) and diagram/amplitude inspection in FeynCalc 10 .

lectures.abstract: This lecture converts Feynman diagrams into quantitative collider predictions by mastering Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) and relativistic phase-space integration. Students derive the master formulas for differential cross sections dσ and partial decay widths dΓ, master Casimir’s trick and Dirac gamma- matrix trace identities, and verify crossing symmetry and the QED Ward identity k µ M µ = 0. Canonical 2 → 2 QED processes—e + e − → µ + µ − , Bhabha scattering (e + e − → e + e − ), Møller scattering, and Compton scattering (Klein–Nishina formula)—are evaluated analytically and via spinor-helicity methods, alongside n-body phase-space factorization and numerical Monte Carlo integration.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact derivations of Fermi’s Golden Rule in relativistic normalization, two-body phase space dΠ 2 = 16π 2 f E dΩ, three-body phase-space cm 2 recursion, Casimir’s trick and d = 4 trace theorems, full worked calculations of e + e − → µ + µ − (σ = 4πα ), Bhabha scattering (illustrating 3s s-/t-channel interference relevant to FCC-ee luminometry), Compton scattering, and polarized helicity amplitudes; explicit conversion from GeV −2 to nb/pb via (ℏc) 2 = 0.389379 GeV 2 · mb.

Stage 2: Automated matrix-element and cross-section validation in FeynCalc 10 and MadGraph5_aMC@NLO (with fiducial | cos θ| cuts for t-channel Bhabha regulation). + − → µ + µ − retaining m ; derive Bhabha scattering amplitude

lectures.abstract: Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) governs strong interactions across every energy scale at hadron and lepton colliders. Starting from local SU (3) C Yang–Mills invariance, this lecture derives non-Abelian gluon self-interactions, color factors (C F = 4/3, C A = 3, T R = 1/2), and the one-loop QCD β-function demonstrating asymptotic freedom and infrared confinement (Λ QCD ≈ 200–300 MeV). Bridging perturbation theory to collider data, the lecture develops deep inelastic scattering (DIS), collinear factorization, DGLAP evolution of Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs), infrared and collinear (IRC) safety, sequential recombination jet algorithms (k t , Cambridge/Aachen, anti-k t ), parton showers, and Lund string hadronization.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete SU (3) C Lagrangian and Faddeev–Popov ghost structure; color-factor trace algebra; derivation of 1-loop running α s (µ 2 ) and R(s) = σ(e + e − → hadrons)/σ(e + e − → µ + µ − ) = N c Q q (1 + α s /π); collinear factorization theorem for Drell–Yan pp → ℓ + ℓ − X; P 2 Altarelli–Parisi splitting kernels P qq , P qg , P gq , P gg and DGLAP evolution; IRC-safety proofs for thrust and anti-k t clustering; overview of Sudakov form factors and Lund string fragmentation.

Stage 2: Production workflow querying NNPDF/MSHT PDF sets via LHAPDF6 , showering e + e − → q q̄ and pp → jj events with PYTHIA 8.3 , and clustering jets with FastJet (comparing k t , C/A, and anti-k t jet areas).
deliverables.problemSet: 5 analytical problems (evaluate SU (N c ) color factors for q q̄ → gg and qq → qq; solve 1-loop α s (Q) and compute α s (m Z ) from Λ QCD ; verify momentum sum rule 0 1 dx x f i (x, Q 2 ) = 1 under DGLAP; prove why seeded cone algorithms fail IRC safety whereas anti-k t succeeds; R P compute LO Drell–Yan partonic cross section) + 2 computational problems (benchmark Python anti-k t against FastJet on 1,000 PYTHIA 8.3 events; quantify PDF uncertainty bands for pp → Z at 13.6 TeV and 100 TeV FCC-hh using LHAPDF6 ). Exit criterion: Exact jet-constituent match with FastJet (∆R < 10 −6 ) and α s (m Z ) within 0.5% of LHAPDF6 .

lectures.abstract: This lecture constructs the Glashow–Weinberg–Salam SU (2) L × U (1) Y electroweak theory and the Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB). Motivated by maximal parity violation in charged weak currents and perturbative unitarity violation in longitudinal W L W L scattering, students derive Goldstone’s theorem, the Abelian Higgs model, and the non-Abelian breaking SU (2) L × U (1) Y → U (1) em . The lecture derives the gauge boson mass eigenstates (W ± , Z, γ), the Weinberg angle θ W , the tree-level custodial relation ρ = m 2 W /(m 2 Z cos 2 θ W ) = 1, Yukawa fermion mass generation, R ξ vs. unitary gauge fixing, and the Goldstone Boson Equivalence Theorem.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivation of L EW = L YM + L fermion + L Higgs + L Yukawa in natural units (v = ( f f (W µ 3 , B µ ) → (Z µ , A µ ); derivation of vector/axial-vector Zf f ¯ couplings (g V ); tree-level partial widths Γ(W → f f ¯ ′ ) and Γ(Z → f f ¯ ); custodial , g A SU (2) L × SU (2) R → SU (2) V symmetry proof; high-energy unitarity restoration in W L + W L − → W L + W L − via Higgs exchange.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python SymPy symbolic diagonalization of the electroweak neutral-boson mass matrix, automated computation of all tree-level W and Z + − − + partial widths and branching ratios, and numerical demonstration of high-energy unitarity √ cancellation in e e → W W (γ, Z, ν e interference) and W L W L → W L W L . Stage 2: Generation and comparison of e + e − → W + W − ( s = 161–365 GeV) and Z-pole fermion pair production in MadGraph5_aMC@NLO , verifying gauge cancellation by selectively disabling s-channel Z or γ diagrams. ± ′
deliverables.problemSet: 5 analytical problems (derive W , Z masses and ρ = 1 for a doublet vs. a triplet Higgs representation; prove e = g sin θ W = g cos θ W f f and compute g V , g A for all SM fermions; compute tree-level Γ Z , Γ W , and R b ; show how the hW W coupling restores s-wave unitarity in W L + W L − → W L + W L − for m H ≲ 1 TeV; verify the Goldstone Boson Equivalence Theorem for h → W L + W L − ) + 2 computational problems (plot √ σ(e + e − → W + W − ) with/without Z-exchange to display unitarity violation; compute A fF B across s ∈ [60, 250] GeV). Exit criterion: Tree-level W/Z branching ratios and e e → W W threshold cross section match MadGraph5_aMC@NLO to < 0.2%. − − + +

explain why explicit fermion and gauge-boson mass terms violate chiral gauge invariance.
Derive Goldstone’s theorem and the Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism, demonstrating how three Goldstone modes become the longitudinal polarizations of W ± and Z. 2
Diagonalize the electroweak gauge sector to obtain m W , m Z , sin θ W , f f and the exact neutral-current couplings (g V , g A ).
Explain custodial SU (2) V symmetry and predict how non-doublet scalar representations modify ρ = m 2 W /(m 2 Z cos 2 θ W ).
Derive tree-level partial widths and branching ratios of the W and Z bosons and the forward-backward asymmetry A fF B in e + e − → f f ¯ . 2 )
Prove how triple gauge couplings and Higgs exchange cancel O(s/m W unitarity-violating growth in e + e − → W + W − and W L W L scattering.

lectures.title: Flavour Physics, CKM/PMNS Mixing, CP Violation, and Neutrino Oscillations

lectures.abstract: Flavour physics accounts for the majority of the Standard Model’s free parameters and provides indirect sensitivity to new physics up to Λ ∼ 10 2 –10 5 TeV. This lecture derives quark and lepton mass diagonalization from general Yukawa matrices, constructing the unitary CKM matrix, its Wolfenstein parameterization, the Jarlskog invariant J, and the Unitarity Triangle. Students analyze the Glashow–Iliopoulos–Maiani (GIM) suppression of flavour- changing neutral currents (FCNCs), neutral meson mixing (K 0 – K̄ 0 , B d,s 0 – B̄ 0 ), and direct/indirect CP violation. The second half develops neutrino d,s oscillations in vacuum and matter (MSW effect), the PMNS matrix (including Majorana phases), and Dirac versus seesaw (Type I/II/III) mass-generation mechanisms.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact parameter counting for N -generation quark and lepton mixing matrices (N (N − 1)/2 angles, (N − 1)(N − 2)/2 Dirac phases, plus N − 1 Majorana phases); GIM mechanism proof and ∆F = 2 box-diagram scaling; time-dependent B 0 – B̄ 0 oscillation and CP asymmetry S ψK S = sin 2β; weak effective Hamiltonian for rare decays (b → sγ, b → sℓ + ℓ − , B s → µ + µ − ); exact 3-flavour neutrino oscillation probability −1 P (ν α → ν β ; L/E) in vacuum and MSW matter Hamiltonian; Type-I seesaw diagonalization m ν ≃ −m T D M R m D and Weinberg dimension-5 operator. 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python global Unitarity Triangle (ρ̄, η̄) χ -fitter using PDG inputs (|V ub /V cb |, ∆m d /∆m s , sin 2β, γ, ϵ K ), paired with a 3-flavour neutrino oscillation simulator ( SciPy matrix exponentiation) computing DUNE/Hyper-K ν µ → ν e appearance probabilities with Earth-crust matter effects and δ CP variation. Stage 2: Reproducing rare-decay Wilson-coefficient constraints and FCC-ee Tera-Z flavour benchmarks (e.g., B s → τ + τ − , b → sν ν̄) using flavio / wilson Python HEP packages.
deliverables.problemSet: 5 analytical problems (prove N -generation CKM phase counting and Jarlskog rephasing invariance; derive GIM suppression in K L → µ + µ − ; derive time-dependent CP asymmetry A CP (t) in B d 0 → J/ψK S ; derive two-flavour MSW resonance density n res e in the Sun; diagonalize the 2 × 2 Type-I seesaw matrix and relate to the dimension-5 Weinberg operator) + 2 computational problems (reconstruct the 95% CL (ρ̄, η̄) apex and check SM consistency; map ν µ → ν e oscillation probability vs. E ν for normal vs. inverted ordering). Exit criterion: Fitted (ρ̄, η̄) agrees with PDG 2024 central values within 1σ and oscillation probabilities conserve unitarity to < 10 −14 .

learningOutcomes: Diagonalize general Yukawa matrices via bi-unitary transformations to
derive the CKM matrix and prove why three generations are the minimum required for CP violation.
Construct the Wolfenstein parameterization, Jarlskog invariant, and Unitarity Triangle constraints from tree-level and loop-level meson observables.

Explain the GIM mechanism and evaluate why FCNC processes (B d,s mixing, b → sℓ + ℓ − ) probe BSM mass scales far beyond direct collider reach. Distinguish CP violation in decay, in mixing, and in interference
between decay with and without mixing.
Derive three-flavour neutrino oscillation probabilities in vacuum and matter (MSW effect) and analyze sensitivity to mass ordering and δ CP .
Contrast Dirac versus Majorana neutrino masses, derive the Type-I seesaw mechanism, and connect lepton-number violation to 0νββ decay.

lectures.title: Renormalization, Loop Corrections, and Precision Electroweak Physics at the Z Pole

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 5.4, 5.5, 5.6, 5.7. Downstream: Lectures 5.10, 5.11, Part 11, Part 13.

lectures.abstract: Precision electroweak measurements test the Standard Model at the quantum loop level and indirectly predicted the top-quark and Higgs-boson masses prior to their direct discoveries. This lecture develops one-loop renormalization in dimensional regularization (d = 4 − 2ϵ), contrasting on-shell and MS subtraction schemes, deriving the Callan–Symanzik renormalization group equation (RGE), and computing the QED vacuum polarization ∆α(m 2 Z ) and electron anomalous magnetic moment a e = α/(2π). Applying these techniques to the electroweak sector, students derive the ∆r relation linking (G F , α, m Z ) to m W , the Peskin–Takeuchi oblique parameters (S, T, U ), and the Z-pole pseudo-observables (Γ Z , R ℓ , A ℓ , sin 2 θ eff ℓ ) that anchor the FCC-ee Tera-Z precision program.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete dimensional-regularization toolkit (Feynman parameters, Wick rotation, Γ(ϵ) expansion); explicit one-loop calculations of 3G m 2 Π γγ (q 2 ), QED β-function, and Schwinger’s g − 2; derivation of Veltman’s quadratic top-mass correction ∆ρ ≃ √ F 2 t and logarithmic Higgs-mass 8 2π dependence ∝ ln(m H /m W ); exact definitions of Peskin–Takeuchi (S, T, U ) from gauge-boson self-energies; complete dictionary of LEP/SLD and FCC-ee Z-pole observables and two-loop theory-uncertainty budgets. 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python numerical one-loop Passarino–Veltman (A 0 , B 0 ) integrator and global electroweak precision χ -fitter predicting m W and ℓ from (m , m , m , ∆α (5) , α ) and generating (S, T ) 68%/95% CL ellipses for LEP vs. FCC-ee projected uncertainties. Stage 2: Automated sin 2 θ eff t s Z H had one-loop self-energy and oblique-parameter calculation in FeynCalc 10 (with Package-X /Passarino–Veltman reduction) and cross-validation against published Gfitter / FCC-ee EWPO benchmarks.
deliverables.problemSet: 5 analytical problems (compute 1-loop QED vacuum polarization in d = 4 − 2ϵ and extract β(e); derive ∆ρ from a heavy chiral fermion doublet with mass splitting ∆m; show how (S, T, U ) shift m W , Γ Z , and sin 2 θ eff ℓ ; prove why a degenerate heavy scalar doublet gives T = 0; evaluate the impact of δm t and δ(∆α had ) on indirect m H bounds) + 2 computational problems (reproduce the LEP/LHC vs. FCC-ee (S, T ) error ellipses; compute m W (m t , m H ) contours). Exit criterion: Indirect SM prediction of m W matches PDG/Gfitter central value within 5 MeV and (S, T ) ellipse semi-axes match literature within 5%.

lectures.abstract: Precision characterization of the 125 GeV Higgs boson is the centerpiece of HL-LHC and FCC physics. This lecture derives all major Higgs pro- duction modes (ggF , VBF, V H, tt̄H at hadron colliders; Higgsstrahlung e + e − → ZH and W W -fusion at lepton colliders) and decay channels (bb̄, W W ∗ , gg, τ τ, ZZ ∗ , γγ), including loop-induced hgg and hγγ amplitudes and the Higgs trilinear self-coupling λ hhh probed via di-Higgs pro- duction (hh) and single-Higgs NLO EW loops. Students then transition from the leading-order κ-framework to the gauge-invariant, systematically improvable Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) in the 59-operator Warsaw basis, examining operator matching, RGE mixing, and global Higgs+EW+diboson fits.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact derivations of h → f f ¯ , h → V V ∗ , and one-loop h → gg, γγ form factors (A 1/2 , A 1 ) in the heavy-top limit; Higgs potential V (h) = 12 m 2 H h 2 + λ hhh vh 3 + 14 λ hhhh h 4 and destructive box–triangle interference in gg → hh; formal definition and limitations (gauge invariance, P C i kinematic dependence) of the LHCHWG κ-framework; complete introduction to L SMEFT = L SM + i Λ 2 O i in the Warsaw basis, mapping key operators (O H , O H□ , O HD , O HW B , O HG ) to Higgs/EW observables. f
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python Higgs branching-ratio and signal-strength (µ i ) calculator implementing the full κ-framework (κ W , κ Z , κ t , κ b , κ τ , κ γ , κ g , κ λ ) and computing linearized SMEFT Wilson-coefficient Fisher information matrices combining HL-LHC and FCC-ee inputs. Stage 2: Monte Carlo generation of e + e − → ZH and pp → hh with dimension-6 operators turned on in MadGraph5_aMC@NLO using the SMEFTsim 3.0 UFO model, comparing linear O(Λ −2 ) vs. quadratic O(Λ −4 ) cross-section scaling.
deliverables.problemSet: 5 analytical problems (derive Γ(h → bb̄) and Γ(h → γγ) in the m t → ∞ limit; prove why κ V ̸ = 1 violates perturbative unitarity at high energy; count independent baryon-conserving dimension-6 Warsaw-basis operators; derive the shift to λ hhh from O H = (H † H) 3 and O H□ ; demonstrate a flat direction between O HD , O HW B and how FCC-ee Z-pole + ZH breaks it) + 2 computational problems (reproduce the m hh invariant-mass shift for κ λ ∈ {−1, 1, 5}; perform a 4-parameter SMEFT Fisher-matrix forecast for HL-LHC + FCC-ee). Exit criterion: SM branching ratios match LHCHWG Vol. 4 within 3% (LO+QCD-corrected) and SMEFTsim 3.0 linear coefficients match analytical shifts to < 1%.

lectures.title: Beyond the Standard Model — Supersymmetry, Dark Matter, Feebly-Interacting Portals, and Long-Lived Particles

lectures.abstract: Despite its precision triumphs, the Standard Model leaves unresolved the electroweak hierarchy problem, dark matter, neutrino masses, and the strong CP problem. This lecture surveys the principal theoretical paradigms and experimental signatures of Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) physics across both the high-mass energy frontier and the low-coupling intensity frontier. Students study the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM)—covering quadratic-divergence cancellation, soft SUSY breaking, R-parity, and neutralino dark matter—alongside simplified dark matter portal models (Higgs, vector, and pseudoscalar portals), Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs), Axion-Like Particles (ALPs), and displaced Long-Lived Particle (LLP) topologies targeted by LHC, Physics Beyond Colliders, and FCC-ee/FCC-hh detectors.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivation of quadratic Higgs-mass divergence cancellation via stop loops in the MSSM; superpotential, R-parity, and sparticle mass- spectrum taxonomy; classification of renormalizable portals (Higgs, dark photon, sterile-neutrino/HNL) and dimension-5 ALP effective Lagrangian c γγ aF µν F̃ µν ; derivation of proper decay length cτ = ℏc/Γ and laboratory displacement L lab = βγcτ for HNLs (Z → νN ) and ALPs L ALP ⊃ − 4f a (Z → γa, h → aa) across FCC-ee and LHC detector volumes. 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python decay-width and displaced-vertex geometric-acceptance simulator computing cτ (m N , |U αN | ) for HNLs and cτ (m a , g aγγ ) for ALPs, projecting 95% CL exclusion contours for FCC-ee Tera-Z (5 × 10 12 Z bosons) vs. LHC/SHiP. Stage 2: Implementing a benchmark BSM portal (ALP or HNL) via FeynRules -> UFO -> MadGraph5_aMC@NLO + PYTHIA 8.3 with displaced-vertex lifetime sampling and reconstructing radial decay distributions L xy . 2 in δm 2 between top and stop loops; show why R-parity stabilizes the LSP

Exit criterion: Simulated HNL lifetime scaling matches analytical τ ∝ m −5 −2 to < 1% and FCC-ee sensitivity reaches |U | 2 ∼ 10 −11 for m N |U | N ∼ 30 GeV.

lectures.abstract: The early Universe functions as the ultimate high-energy laboratory, directly linking collider measurements of the Higgs potential and dark sectors to cosmological relics. This capstone lecture develops thermal quantum field theory in the imaginary-time (Matsubara) formalism to compute the one-loop Coleman–Weinberg and finite-temperature Higgs effective potential V eff (ϕ, T ) with Daisy resummation. Students examine why the minimal SM undergoes a smooth crossover at T c ≈ 160 GeV, how BSM scalar extensions (real singlet, SMEFT O 6 ) restore a strongly first-order electroweak phase transition (SFOEWPT, v c /T c ≳ 1) satisfying the Sakharov conditions for electroweak baryogenesis, how Boltzmann equations govern thermal WIMP freeze-out and freeze-in, and how bubble nucleation parameters (α, β/H ∗ , T ∗ , v w ) generate stochastic gravitational-wave backgrounds detectable by LISA alongside FCC Higgs self-coupling measurements.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivation of FLRW thermal history (H(T ) ≃ 1.66 g ∗ T 2 /M Pl ), Boltzmann equation for dark-matter thermal freeze-out (Ω χ h 2 ≃ 0.12 for ⟨σv⟩ ≈ 3 × 10 −26 cm 3 /s), Sakharov’s three conditions and electroweak sphaleron rate, one-loop thermal effective potential V eff (ϕ, T ) = V 0 + V CW + V T + V Daisy in natural units (with explicit conversion of T ∗ ∼ 100 GeV to LISA peak frequencies f peak ∼ mHz), O(3)-symmetric Euclidean bounce action S 3 (T )/T , and sound-wave/turbulence/bubble-collision GW power spectra Ω GW (f )h 2 .

Stage 2: Production phase-transition and GW spectrum pipeline comparing Stage 1 results against CosmoTransitions / PTPlot (LISA Cosmology Working Group) and correlating LISA SNR with FCC-ee/FCC-hh δκ λ sensitivity. −1 and the Lee–Weinberg lower mass bound; derive 2

parts.abstract: Particle physics at the energy and precision frontiers is inseparable from the accelerator physics that delivers colliding beams. This part develops circular and linear collider physics from first principles and applies it directly to the Future Circular Collider (FCC) integrated programme. Starting from Courant–Snyder transverse/longitudinal optics, synchrotron radiation damping, and quantum equilibrium emittances, the curriculum advances to high-luminosity beam–beam dynamics (beamstrahlung, large Piwinski angle, crab-waist collisions), spin-precession physics for parts-per-million resonant depolarization energy calibration, and the tightly coupled Machine–Detector Interface (MDI) and background mitigation. The final modules synthesize the staged FCC programme (FCC-ee, FCC-hh, FCC-eh) from the 2019 CDR through the 2025 Feasibility Study Report and benchmark it quantitatively against HL-LHC, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and the Muon Collider.

deliverables.lectureNote: ~170-page graduate accelerator-physics monograph (seven chapters) using standard accelerator conventions (magnetic rigidity Bρ = p/q, Twiss functions α, β, γ, synchrotron radiation integrals I 1 –I 5 , Piwinski angle ϕ, beamstrahlung parameter Υ, spin tune ν s = a e γ), complete with worked numerical tables for FCC-ee (Z, W W, ZH, tt̄) and FCC-hh (100 TeV).
deliverables.lab: Seven-module simulation sequence pairing Stage 1 Python/NumPy first-principles prototypes (FODO transfer matrices, Sands radiation- integral solvers, crab-waist overlap integrals, Thomas–BMT spin tracking) with Stage 2 production codes ( MAD-X , Xsuite , Guinea-Pig++ , DD4hep , BDSIM / FLUKA ).
deliverables.problemSet: Seven quantitative problem sets linking analytical derivations to FCC design margins (dynamic aperture, 100 MW synchrotron-radiation power cap, ∆E cm ∼ 100 keV at the Z pole, MDI pair-background rates); exit criterion: end-to-end parameter-consistency audit reproducing the FCC Feasibility Study luminosity and energy-uncertainty tables within 5%.

lectures.abstract: Charged-particle transport in circular colliders is governed by periodic magnetic lattices that confine relativistic beams over billions of turns. This lecture derives the Frenet–Serret curvilinear equations of motion, magnetic rigidity (Bρ = p/q), multipole expansions (dipoles, quadrupoles, sextupoles), and Hill’s equation for alternating-gradient focusing. Students construct transfer matrices, Floquet solutions, Courant–Snyder (Twiss) parameters (α, β, γ), betatron phase advance and tune Q, geometric vs. normalized emittance, dispersion D(s), and natural/sextupole-corrected chromaticity ξ. In the longitudinal plane, the lecture derives the momentum compaction factor α c , phase slip factor η, transition energy γ t , RF bucket separatrix, and synchrotron tune Q s , culminating in FODO cell and dispersion-suppressor design using MAD-X and Xsuite .

deliverables.lectureNote: 26-page analytical derivation of linear and weakly nonlinear single-particle dynamics: symplectic transfer matrices (det M = 1), stability condition |Tr M | < 2, Courant–Snyder invariant γx 2 + 2αxx ′ + βx ′2 = ϵ, dispersion matching, chromaticity sextupoles, and longitudinal pendulum Hamiltonian.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a pure-Python 2D/4D symplectic FODO-cell transfer-matrix solver computing β(s), D(s), Q x , Q y , and phase-space ellipses; Stage 2 translates the lattice into MAD-X and Xsuite ( Xtrack ), matches tunes and chromaticities, and tracks 1,000 turns to map dynamic aperture.
deliverables.problemSet: Five analytical/computational problems (thin-lens FODO stability diagram, dipole-kick closed-orbit distortion, quadrupole-error tune β∆K ds, RF bucket height/area for FCC-ee vs. LHC, and chromaticity correction with two sextupole families); exit criterion: MAD-X 1 H shift ∆Q = 4π and Xsuite Twiss tables agreeing with the Stage 1 Python solver to < 10 −6 relative error.

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 6.1 (Courant–Snyder optics, dispersion, RF longitudinal dynamics) and relativistic electrodynamics. Downstream: sets the equilibrium beam sizes, energy spread, RF power budget, and sawtooth orbit tapering governing Lectures 6.3–6.6.

lectures.abstract: For ultra-relativistic electrons and positrons in circular rings, synchrotron radiation transforms single-particle motion from Hamiltonian to dissipative- stochastic dynamics. Starting from the relativistic Liénard power formula, this lecture derives the energy loss per turn U 0 = C γ E 4 /ρ, critical photon energy u c , classical radiation damping rates in all three degrees of freedom, and Robinson’s damping-partition sum rule (J x +J y +J ε = 4). Incorporating quantized photon emission as a stochastic diffusion process yields the equilibrium energy spread σ δ , bunch length σ z , and horizontal emittance ε x via the five synchrotron radiation integrals I 1 –I 5 . Students examine how the 100 MW total synchrotron-radiation power cap dictates FCC-ee beam currents from Z (45.6 GeV) to tt̄ (182.5 GeV), necessitating magnet-strength tapering to compensate the energy sawtooth and driving the high-energy luminosity cliff.

deliverables.lectureNote: 24-page monograph deriving Liénard radiation power, critical photon spectrum, damping times (τ x , τ y , τ ε ), Robinson’s theorem, quantum excitation via the curly-H dispersion invariant, Helm’s radiation integrals I 1 –I 5 , quantum lifetime, and FCC-ee energy-sawtooth tapering.

lectures.abstract: Achieving 10 36 cm −2 s −1 at the FCC-ee Z pole requires colliding ultra-flat nanobeams where collective electromagnetic fields of the opposing bunch dominate beam stability. This lecture derives the general 4D luminosity overlap integral, geometric crossing-angle reduction, hourglass effect, and σ z tan θ 2 c ≫ 1) combined with Raimondi’s linear/nonlinear beam–beam tune shifts (ξ x , ξ y ). Students analyze how the large Piwinski angle (ϕ = σ x crab-waist sextupole transformation suppresses synchro-betatron resonances and unlocks sub-millimeter β y ∗ . At high beam energies, radiation in the opposing bunch’s collective field — beamstrahlung — lengthens the bunch, broadens the center-of-mass energy spread, and imposes Telnov’s fundamental lifetime limit on circular e + e − colliders, necessitating careful beam-parameter optimization and top-up injection.

lectures.abstract: Measuring the Z boson mass and width to ∼ 100 keV and the W boson mass to ∼ 0.3 MeV at FCC-ee requires calibrating the beam energy to the part-per-million (∼ 10 −6 ) level. This lecture develops relativistic spin dynamics in storage rings via the Thomas–BMT equation, showing how the spin tune ν s = a e γ = E beam /0.4406486 GeV directly encodes the average beam energy. Students study radiative self-polarization (the Sokolov–Ternov effect, asymptotic 92.4%, and polarization wigglers), depolarizing spin-orbit resonances (Derbenev–Kondratenko–Mane formula), and the technique of resonant depolarization (RDP) using an RF kicker and Compton polarimetry on non-colliding pilot bunches. Finally, students construct the full center-of-mass √ energy ( s) uncertainty budget, translating ring-averaged beam energies to each interaction point by correcting for RF energy sawtooth, opposite-sign vertical dispersion, tidal/geological circumference drifts, and collision-induced energy-spread shifts measured via e + e − → µ + µ − acollinearity.

deliverables.lectureNote: 22-page monograph deriving the Thomas–BMT spin-precession equation, spin tune ν s , Sokolov–Ternov build-up time τ ST ∝ ρ 3 /E 5 , √ Derbenev–Kondratenko depolarization balance, LEP1/LEP2 calibration lessons (earth tides, TGV rail leakage currents), and the complete FCC-ee s systematic error table at Z and W W energies.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 implements a Python Thomas–BMT spin-precession integrator simulating a frequency-swept RF depolarizer across ν s and fitting the depolarization step; Stage 2 models the FCC-ee RF sawtooth, dispersion-induced CM energy shift, and e + e − → µ + µ − acollinearity estimator to propagate systematic uncertainties into δm Z and δΓ Z .
deliverables.problemSet: Five analytical/numerical problems (computing τ ST at 45.6 and 80 GeV with and without wigglers, evaluating integer and synchrotron sideband spin-resonance spacings, translating a 10 µm tidal circumference change into ∆E beam , deriving the opposite-sign dispersion CM energy shift, and auditing the FCC-ee Z-pole energy budget); exit criterion: simulated RDP frequency scan recovering E beam to < 50 keV statistical precision.

lectures.abstract: The Machine–Detector Interface (MDI) is the tightly constrained volume within ±10 m of the interaction point where accelerator optics and detector acceptance physically overlap. To achieve β y ∗ ≈ 0.8–1.6 mm at FCC-ee, superconducting final-focus quadrupoles sit inside the detector volume at L ∗ = 2.2 m, requiring anti-solenoid shielding to cancel the 2 T detector solenoid field and prevent vertical emittance blow-up from the 30 mrad crossing angle. This lecture analyzes the mechanical, thermal, and radiation engineering of the central beryllium beam pipe (r = 10 mm), precision luminosity calorimeter (LumiCal), synchrotron-radiation masks, and beam-induced backgrounds — dominated by incoherent e + e − pair creation (IPC), radiative Bhabha losses, beam-gas scattering, and synchrotron-radiation photons — simulated end-to-end with Guinea-Pig++ , DD4hep , BDSIM , and FLUKA .

deliverables.lectureNote: 22-page technical specification covering FCC-ee IR geometry (L ∗ = 2.2 m, 30 mrad crossing angle, 100 mrad dead cone), solenoid- coupling emittance blow-up and anti-solenoid compensation, incoherent pair-creation kinematic envelopes (p T vs. θ in a 2 T field), SR-masking ray tracing, and wakefield/HOM heating in the central beam pipe. + − pairs inside a 2 T solenoid to size

lectures.abstract: The Future Circular Collider (FCC) is conceived as a multi-generation research infrastructure modeled on the LEP-to-LHC paradigm, reusing a single ∼ 90.7 km underground tunnel in the Geneva–Annecy basin across the 21st century. This lecture synthesizes the complete technical architecture from the 2019 Conceptual Design Report (CDR Volumes 1–3) through the landmark 2025 FCC Feasibility Study Report (Volumes 1–3). Students analyze Stage 1 (FCC-ee: four-IP layout, full-energy top-up booster in the same tunnel, 15-year staged run plan across Z, W W, ZH, tt̄), Stage 2 (FCC-hh: ∼ 85–100 TeV pp collider driven by high-field Nb 3 Sn or HTS dipole magnets, synchrotron-radiation beam-screen cryogenics, and heavy-ion operation), and the optional Energy-Recovery Linac electron–hadron extension (FCC-eh). Equal attention is given to civil engineering, geology, electrical grid power, waste-heat recovery, and environmental sustainability.

deliverables.lectureNote: 24-page systems-engineering overview mapping the 90.7 km ring placement (8 surface sites, 4 experiment caverns), FCC-ee 15-year integrated-luminosity schedule (Z, W W, ZH, tt̄), FCC-hh dipole-field vs. energy scaling (E cm ∝ Bρ), FCC-eh ERL architecture, and 2025 Feasibility Study updates relative to the 2019 CDR.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a Python integrated-luminosity and energy-consumption simulator modeling the 15-year FCC-ee run plan (turnaround, top-up efficiency, shutdowns, annual TWh electricity draw); Stage 2 performs a parametric dipole-field/tunnel-circumference trade study comparing Nb 3 Sn (14–16 T) vs. HTS (17–20 T) FCC-hh configurations and synchrotron-radiation cryo-load.
deliverables.problemSet: Four systems-engineering problems (deriving the FCC-hh beam energy and proton synchrotron-radiation power per meter for 14 T vs. 16 T dipoles, sizing the FCC-ee booster ramp cycle for top-up injection, comparing 2-IP vs. 4-IP integrated luminosity yields, and estimating FCC-eh ERL power recovery); exit criterion: quantitative reconciliation of 2019 CDR vs. 2025 Feasibility Study baseline parameters.

(2022) FCC overview ( arXiv:2204.10029 ), Brüning et al. (2022) Electron–Hadron Colliders (EIC/LHeC/FCC-eh), and Abelleira Fernandez et al. (2012) LHeC CDR.

lectures.abstract: Selecting the next flagship particle collider requires weighing fundamental physical scaling laws against technological readiness, wall-plug power, cost, and discovery reach. This lecture places the FCC programme in the global post-LHC landscape by conducting a first-principles comparative analysis of six major machine paradigms: the near-term High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC: 11–12 T Nb 3 Sn triplet magnets, crab cavities, 3–4 ab −1 ), circular Higgs/EW factories (FCC-ee and China’s 100 km CEPC), linear e + e − colliders (ILC superconducting 1.3 GHz niobium RF at 250–1000 GeV and CLIC normal-conducting 12 GHz two-beam X-band acceleration up to 3 TeV with longitudinal beam polarization), and the 10 TeV Muon Collider (IMCC: negligible synchrotron radiation, 6D ionization cooling, rapid cycling synchrotrons, and neutrino-flux/decay-background mitigation). Students evaluate luminosity-per-MW curves, partonic vs. leptonic energy reach, and R&D timelines.

deliverables.lectureNote: 24-page comparative synthesis deriving the crossover energy ( luminosity per MW, the parton-luminosity equivalence between a 10 TeV µ + µ − collider and a ∼ 100 TeV pp collider, and comprehensive parameter matrices across HL-LHC, FCC-ee/hh, CEPC, ILC, CLIC, and IMCC. √

parts.abstract: This part bridges microscopic radiation–matter interactions and macroscopic collider instrumentation, establishing the physical and engineering foundations required to design, simulate, calibrate, and operate next-generation detectors at the Future Circular Collider in its electron–positron mode (FCC-ee). Beginning with electromagnetic and hadronic energy loss, multiple scattering, and optical radiation mechanisms, the curriculum progresses through charge transport, Shockley–Ramo signal induction, and low-noise CMOS front-end electronics. It then examines gaseous and silicon tracking systems, electromagnetic and hadronic calorimetry (including dual-readout and high-granularity imaging), particle identification, muon spectrometers, superconducting solenoids, triggerless data acquisition, and in-situ calibration and alignment across the IDEA, CLD, and ALLEGRO detector concepts.

deliverables.lectureNote: Unified 14-chapter graduate monograph (~350 pages) maintaining explicit dimensional transparency between natural units (ℏ = c = 1), atomic/nuclear units (MeV cm 2 g −1 , X 0 , λ I ), and electrical engineering units (fF, e − ENC, mW cm −2 ), with end-to-end worked design budgets comparing IDEA, CLD, and ALLEGRO subdetectors.
deliverables.lab: Progressive 14-module computational laboratory pairing Stage 1 transparent Python/NumPy/SciPy first-principles prototypes (Monte Carlo straggling, 2D weighting-field Laplace solvers, CR–RC n noise integrators, toy Kalman/Millepede aligners) with Stage 2 production HEP toolchains ( Geant4 , Garfield++ , Allpix^2 , DD4hep , Key4hep , PandoraPFA , Millepede-II , and ngspice ).
deliverables.problemSet: Fourteen graded analytical–computational assignments (~60 problems total) culminating in a capstone subsystem trade-off audit; exit criterion requires deriving and validating a complete FCC-ee detector subsystem performance budget within 5% of published DD4hep / Geant4 benchmarks.

lectures.abstract: This lecture develops the microscopic theory of electronic energy loss by heavy charged particles (M ≫ m e ) traversing condensed and gaseous media. Starting from the classical Bohr impulse approximation and progressing to the quantum-mechanical Bethe–Bloch stopping-power formula, we derive the maximum single-collision energy transfer W max , the mean excitation energy I, shell corrections at low βγ, and the Fermi–Sternheimer density effect δ(βγ) arising from transverse field polarization in dielectric media. We then formulate energy-loss straggling in thin absorbers via the Landau–Vavilov–Bichsel distributions, distinguishing mean stopping power from most probable energy loss (∆ p ), restricted energy loss, and δ-ray knock-on spectra in thin silicon and gas layers.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivation of the Bethe–Bloch equation in mass stopping-power units (MeV cm 2 g −1 ), exact kinematics of W max , Sternheimer parameterization of δ(βγ), Landau–Vavilov κ = ξ/W max regime classification, and worked calculations of ∆ p and FWHM in 50 µm MAPS silicon vs. 1 cm He/iC 4 H 10 drift cells.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python notebook implementing Bethe–Bloch with Sternheimer density corrections, Bragg’s additivity rule for gas mixtures, and numerical Laplace inversion / SciPy Landau–Vavilov convolution for thin silicon; Stage 2 validation against Geant4 ( G4UrbanMscModel / G4PAIModel photo-absorption ionization) and Garfield++ / Heed straggling spectra in 50 µm Si and Ar/CO 2 .
deliverables.problemSet: Four analytical/computational problems: (1) derive W max relativistically and identify where the m e /M correction breaks down for muons and pions; (2) compute the relativistic rise and Fermi plateau in gaseous He vs. solid Si; (3) fit ∆ p and truncated-mean resolution vs. sample thickness; (4) compare G4PAIModel vs. Landau in 20 µm silicon. Exit criterion: reproduce PDG MIP stopping power and Bichsel ∆ p for 300 µm Si within 2%.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: PDG Ch. 34.2, Grupen & Shwartz Ch. 1, Leo Ch. 2, Knoll Ch. 2. Advanced/optional: Bichsel (1988) Rev. Mod. Phys. on thin-silicon straggling, Allison & Cobb (1980) on relativistic rise and PAI, and recent shell-correction studies in silicon.

learningOutcomes: Derive the relativistic kinematics of W max and explain the mass
independence of ⟨−dE/dx⟩ as a function of βγ in the Bethe region.
Quantify the physical origin of the minimum-ionizing point (βγ ≈ 3–3.5), the relativistic rise, and its saturation via the density-effect correction δ(βγ).
Distinguish total stopping power from restricted energy loss and compute δ-ray production rates above an energy threshold T cut .

Classify thin, intermediate, and thick absorber straggling regimes using the Vavilov parameter κ = ξ/W max and evaluate ∆ p via the Landau–Vavilov–Bichsel formalism. Explain why Bichsel’s atomic-shell convolution outperforms pure
Landau theory in thin (≲ 300 µm) silicon sensors and low-pressure gases.
Apply Bragg’s additivity rule to compute stopping power and primary ionization yields (W -value, Fano factor) in composite detector gases and compounds.
Benchmark Python Bethe–Bloch and Landau–Vavilov implementations against Geant4 PAI and Heed microscopic ionization simulations.
