dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 5 (QED Cross Sections), Lecture 7.1 (Ionization Energy Loss). Downstream: Lectures 7.7 (Material Budget & Conversions), 7.8 (Electromagnetic Calorimetry), 7.9 (EM Component of Hadronic Showers), 7.11 (Radiative Muon Losses).

lectures.abstract: This lecture treats high-energy electromagnetic interactions of electrons, positrons, and photons with matter, connecting QED radiative cross sections to macroscopic shower morphology. We derive bremsstrahlung and pair-production cross sections in the Bethe–Heitler screened-nucleus approximation, defining the radiation length X 0 , the photon conversion mean free path 97 X 0 , and the Rossi critical energy E c separating radiative from collisional dominance. Low-energy photon processes (photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering) and ultrahigh-energy suppression (Landau–Pomeranchuk– Migdal effect) are also analyzed. Finally, we build the Heitler–Rossi toy cascade model alongside gamma-function longitudinal profiles and the Molière radius R M governing transverse shower containment.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivations of Bethe–Heitler complete-screening X 0 , photon attenuation µ(E) across photoelectric/Compton/pair regimes, Rossi’s E c parameterization for solids and gases, the Heitler exponential branching model (t max ∝ ln(E 0 /E c )), Longo–Sestili gamma-function longitudinal profiles, and Molière radius R M = X 0 E s /E c with worked examples for PbWO 4 , LAr/Pb, and Si/W.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python 3D Monte Carlo EM shower simulator (sampling bremsstrahlung, pair production, Compton, photoelectric, and multiple scattering) computing longitudinal dE/dt and radial containment curves; Stage 2 Geant4 ( FTFP_BERT / G4EmStandardPhysics_option4 ) shower library in PbWO 4 and W/Si sampling stacks to extract t max , t 95% , and R 90% vs. E 0 . 7
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) derive the ratio between asymptotic pair-production and bremsstrahlung cross sections; (2) compute X 0 and R M 9 for a composite W/Si sampling calorimeter using weight-fraction mixing; (3) calculate longitudinal depth required for 99% containment of 100 GeV electrons at FCC-ee; (4) evaluate LPM suppression onset energy in Pb vs. air. Exit criterion: match Geant4 longitudinal shower maximum t max and 90% radial containment radius to within 10% across 1–100 GeV.

with Thomas–Fermi atomic screening and evaluate X 0 for elemental and composite materials. + − pair
Contrast photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering, and e e production cross-section scalings with Z and photon energy E γ .
Define the critical energy E c (Rossi and Berger–Seltzer conventions) and compute the transition from ionization-dominated to radiation-dominated electron energy loss.

Derive the Heitler cascade scaling laws for shower maximum t max , total track length T ∝ E 0 /E c , and intrinsic stochastic fluctuations. Parameterize longitudinal EM shower profiles via gamma distributions
and compute transverse containment radii in units of the Molière radius R M .
Explain the physical mechanism and onset scale of the Landau–Pomeranchuk–Migdal (LPM) suppression of bremsstrahlung and pair production.
Validate simplified Monte Carlo EM cascades against full Geant4 electromagnetic physics lists in homogeneous crystal and sampling geometries.

lectures.abstract: This lecture covers three non-ionizing interaction mechanisms central to tracking precision, calorimetry, and particle identification: multiple Coulomb scattering (MCS), inelastic hadron–nucleus interactions, and coherent optical/X-ray radiation. We derive Molière’s multiple-scattering angular distribution, its Gaussian core via the Highland–Lynch–Dahl formula, non-Gaussian Rutherford tails, and lateral–angular correlations (y plane , θ plane ). We then formulate nuclear collision and interaction lengths (λ T , λ I ∝ A 1/3 ) and contrast spallation, nuclear evaporation, and π 0 production in hadronic cascades. Finally, we derive the Frank–Tamm Cherenkov photon spectrum and threshold condition (βn > 1), together with Ginzburg–Frank transition radiation across dielectric interfaces (γ-threshold X-ray emission).

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of Molière theory and Highland’s θ 0 , correlated (y, θ) covariance matrix for Kalman track propagation, nuclear interaction length λ I vs. X 0 scaling across the periodic table, Frank–Tamm photon yield d 2 N/(dx dλ), and multi-foil transition radiation interference conditions (formation zone Z 1 , Z 2 and threshold γ th ).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python simulation of Molière scattering through layered tracker material (extracting θ 0 and non-Gaussian tail fractions) plus numerical integration of Cherenkov yields in aerogel/quartz/C 4 F 10 and multi-foil TR X-ray spectra; Stage 2 Geant4 test-beam material-imaging study ( G4UrbanMscModel vs. G4GoudsmitSaundersonMscModel , plus G4Cerenkov and G4VXTRenergyLoss in straw-tube radiators).
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) prove why combining thin slabs in quadrature underestimates Highland’s θ 0 due to the logarithmic term; (2) compute the impact-parameter multiple-scattering term b for the FCC-ee AlBeMet beam pipe (0.68% X 0 ) and inner MAPS layer (0.3% X 0 ); (3) calculate λ I /X 0 for Cu, W, Pb, and Fe and explain its role in EM/hadron separation; (4) optimize polypropylene foil thickness and spacing for a 10 GeV e/π TRD. Exit criterion: extract fractional radiation length x/X 0 of a simulated silicon module from MCS angles to better than 3%.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: PDG Ch. 34.3 & 34.7, Grupen & Shwartz Ch. 1 & 9, Leo Ch. 2. Advanced/optional: Lynch & Dahl (1991) MCS approximations (via ATLAS/CMS material-imaging papers), Geant4 hadronic physics overview, and straw-tube XTR optimization studies.

learningOutcomes: Derive the Highland–Lynch–Dahl Gaussian approximation to Molière
multiple Coulomb scattering and quantify the correlated transverse displacement–angle covariance.
Explain how non-Gaussian single-scattering tails bias track fits and how test-beam MCS tomography maps detector material budgets in x/X 0 .
Define nuclear collision length λ T and interaction length λ I , and explain the A 1/3 scaling of λ I relative to the A/Z 2 scaling of X 0 .
Summarize the microscopic components of inelastic hadron–nucleus interactions (intranuclear cascade, spallation, nuclear binding energy loss, and π 0 → γγ production).
Derive the Cherenkov emission angle cos θ c = 1/(nβ) and Frank–Tamm photon yield per unit path length and wavelength.
Derive the transition radiation total energy W ∝ αγℏω p and formation-zone interference conditions for multi-foil X-ray radiators.
Simulate and benchmark multiple scattering, optical Cherenkov transport, and X-ray transition radiation in Geant4 .

lectures.title: Charge Transport, Avalanche Multiplication, and the Shockley–Ramo Theorem

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 1 (Green’s Functions & PDEs), Part 2 (Electrostatics & Boltzmann Transport), Lecture 7.1 (Primary Ionization). Downstream: Lectures 7.5 (Front-End Signal Convolution), 7.6 (Gaseous Detectors), 7.7 (Silicon Detectors & LGADs).

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes the universal electrodynamic framework linking moving charge carriers to measurable electrode currents in both gaseous and semiconductor detectors. We derive drift velocity and longitudinal/transverse diffusion tensors from Langevin and Boltzmann transport in crossed electric and magnetic fields (E × B, Lorentz angle), followed by Townsend avalanche multiplication, Polya gain fluctuations, attachment, and space-charge distortion. We then prove the Shockley–Ramo theorem from Green’s reciprocity and energy conservation, extending it to multi-electrode segmented sensors (the small-pixel effect) and weakly conductive or resistive media (RPCs, resistive Micromegas) via time-dependent weighting potentials.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous proof of i k (t) = −q v(t) · E w,k (x(t)) and Q k = −q ∆ϕ w,k , explicit weighting-field solutions for parallel-plate, coaxial wire, and segmented strip/pixel geometries, Langevin E × B drift equations, Townsend α(E) and Polya gain statistics, and Riegler’s generalization to resistive layers.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python 2D finite-difference Laplace/Poisson solver computing operating fields E and weighting potentials ϕ w for a segmented silicon pixel sensor and a cylindrical drift tube, integrating electron/hole/ion trajectories to synthesize induced current pulses i(t); Stage 2 Garfield++ (gas avalanche + weighting field in a wire tube) and Allpix^2 ( TransientPropagation + PulseTransfer ) simulations benchmarked against Stage 1.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) prove from Shockley–Ramo why the signal in a wire proportional chamber is dominated by drifting positive ions rather than electrons; (2) derive the small-pixel weighting potential and show how it achieves single-polarity sensing; (3) compute the Lorentz angle in a 2 T FCC-ee solenoid for silicon electrons/holes and He/iC 4 H 10 drift gas; (4) compute Polya avalanche gain variance and its impact on single-electron efficiency. Exit criterion: match Garfield++ and Allpix^2 induced-charge pulse integrals to theoretical q ∆ϕ w within 1%.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: He (2001) NIM A Shockley–Ramo review, Blum–Riegler–Rolandi Ch. 2–6, Spieler Ch. 2, Sauli Ch. 3–5. Advanced/optional: Riegler (2016) arXiv:1602.07949 on resistive-medium weighting fields and Allpix^2 carrier-transport documentation.

learningOutcomes: Prove the Shockley–Ramo theorem using Green’s reciprocity theorem
and verify that stationary space charge alters trajectories but not the weighting field.
Compute analytical and numerical weighting potentials ϕ w (x) for planar, coaxial, and fine-pitch segmented electrodes, demonstrating the small-pixel effect.
Derive electron and ion drift velocities, mobility, and anisotropic diffusion (D L , D T ) in electric and magnetic fields, including the Lorentz angle tan θ L .
Analyze Townsend impact ionization, Polya avalanche gain fluctuations, electron attachment, and space-charge feedback in gases and silicon gain layers.
Distinguish the physical timescales of electron vs. ion/hole current components in gaseous proportional chambers, parallel-plate RPCs, and depleted silicon diodes.
Formulate time-dependent weighting fields and resistive charge spreading in detectors incorporating resistive layers (RPCs, resistive MPGDs).
Synthesize and validate transient induced-current waveforms using both Python finite-difference solvers and Garfield++ / Allpix^2 .

lectures.abstract: This lecture develops the signal-processing and microelectronic foundations connecting raw sensor currents to digitized energy and time measurements. We analyze charge-sensitive preamplifiers (CSAs) and transimpedance amplifiers (TIAs), pole-zero cancellation, ballistic deficit, and CR–RC n / trapezoidal pulse shaping. Using spectral noise densities, we derive the Equivalent Noise Charge (ENC) from series thermal (e 2 n ∝ k B T /g m ), 1/f flicker, and parallel shot (i 2 n = 2qI leak ) noise sources, optimizing the shaping time τ opt and transistor capacitance matching. We then examine time-walk, jitter (σ t ≈ σ n /(dV /dt)), ADC/TDC architectures (SAR, pipelined, Vernier/DLL, ToT), and modern deep-submicron (65 nm CMOS) HEP ASIC design trade-offs (RD53, H2M, lpGBT).

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivation of CSA transfer function and closed-loop input impedance, complete ENC formula ENC 2 = F v C d 2 τ n + F vf C d 2 A f + F i τ i 2 n with noise indices (F v , F vf , F i ), timing jitter vs. time-walk correction (CFD, ToT), ADC ENOB/INL/DNL metrics, and 65 nm CMOS power/area/radiation-hardening budgets. n
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python frequency- and time-domain front-end simulator convolving Lecture 7.4 Shockley–Ramo pulses with CR–RC shapers, computing ENC vs. τ s curves, ballistic deficit, and jitter vs. threshold; Stage 2 ngspice transistor-level/behavioral CSA + shaper + comparator transient/noise simulation coupled to Allpix^2 CSADigitizer for a 65 nm MAPS pixel.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) derive τ opt minimizing ENC for a given C d , I leak , and g m , and evaluate how radiation-induced leakage shifts τ opt ; (2) calculate time-walk and jitter for a 50 µm LGAD vs. planar pixel; (3) size a 12-bit SAR ADC and 20 ps TDC for calorimeter/timing readout; (4) compare power consumption of continuous FCC-ee Z-pole readout vs. linear-collider power pulsing. Exit criterion: match Python analytical ENC and ngspice .noise integral within 5% across three decades of shaping time.

Advanced/optional: RD53A/CROCv1 65 nm pixel ASIC papers, H2M 65 nm MAPS paper, and CMS HL-LHC ECAL dual-gain TIA/160 MHz ADC electronics.

learningOutcomes: Derive the transfer function, dynamic input capacitance, and
charge-collection efficiency of a charge-sensitive preamplifier (CSA) vs. a current-sensitive transimpedance amplifier (TIA).
Formulate the Equivalent Noise Charge (ENC) from series thermal, 1/f flicker, and parallel shot noise, and compute the noise-optimal shaping time τ opt and detector–transistor capacitance match.
Quantify ballistic deficit, pile-up distortion, and baseline shift at high hit rates, and design pole-zero cancellation and baseline restoration circuits.
Derive timing resolution limits from electronic jitter (σ n /(dV /dt)), Landau shape fluctuations, and time-walk, comparing leading-edge, ToT, and constant-fraction discriminators.
Compare ADC (flash, SAR, pipelined, Σ∆) and TDC (counter, Vernier, tapped delay line) architectures in terms of resolution, latency, power, and radiation tolerance.
Analyze deep-submicron CMOS ASIC constraints (weak/moderate inversion g m /I D , serial powering, SEU triple modular redundancy, and continuous vs. power-pulsed operation at FCC-ee).
Verify analytical ENC and timing-jitter predictions using ngspice noise analysis and Allpix^2 digitization modules.

lectures.abstract: This lecture examines the physics, electrostatic design, and operational limits of gaseous tracking and amplification detectors from classical Multi-Wire Proportional Chambers (MWPCs) and cylindrical drift chambers to Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) and Micro-Pattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs). We analyze wire-chamber electrostatics, electrostatic stability, gas-mixture selection (noble gases plus molecular quenchers), ion backflow (IBF), and space-charge distortions at high collision rates. Special emphasis is placed on the IDEA ultra-lightweight helium-based drift chamber (He/iC 4 H 10 90:10) and its cluster-counting (dN cl /dx) technique, which overcomes Landau-tail degradation by resolving individual primary ionization clusters with GHz waveform digitization and real-time peak-finding / edge-ML algorithms.

deliverables.lectureNote: Detailed electrostatic derivations for MWPCs and stereo-wire drift cells, Gluckstern momentum-resolution scaling (σ p T /p 2 T ) for continuous vs. discrete gaseous trackers, GEM and Micromegas amplification/IBF physics, TPC E × B distortion analysis at the FCC-ee Z-pole, and Poisson vs. Landau resolution proofs for dN/dx cluster counting.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python drift-cell waveform generator simulating Poisson primary clusters, drift/diffusion arrival times, single-electron avalanche pulses, and derivative/peak-finding cluster-counting estimators; Stage 2 Garfield++ + Magboltz + Heed simulation of an IDEA 1.2 cm He/iC 4 H 10 (90:10) drift cell and a triple-GEM stack, quantifying drift velocity, diffusion, spatial resolution, and cluster-counting efficiency.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) derive the wire-chamber gain sensitivity to mechanical wire radius and voltage tolerances; (2) calculate the IBF-induced space-charge distortion in a 2 m TPC at the FCC-ee Z-pole (50 kHz Z rate) vs. ZH running; (3) show analytically why Poisson cluster counting improves π/K separation by ∼ 2× over truncated-mean dE/dx; (4) compute total radiation length x/X 0 of the IDEA drift chamber gas and wires. Explain the operating principles, amplification geometries, spark protection, and ion-backflow (IBF) mitigation mechanisms of GEM, Micromegas, and µ-RWELL MPGDs.

lectures.abstract: This lecture presents the device physics and system architecture of modern silicon trackers from planar microstrips and hybrid pixels to CMOS Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), 3D sensors, and Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs). We derive p–n junction depletion voltage, capacitance, charge sharing, and spatial resolution (binary vs. analog centroiding). We then examine bulk displacement damage via Non-Ionizing Energy Loss (NIEL) scaling—leakage-current increase (∆I = αΦV ), effective doping evolution/type inversion, and carrier trapping—alongside surface Total Ionizing Dose (TID) oxide charge accumulation. Finally, we analyze FCC-ee vertex-detector engineering: curved wafer-scale 65 nm MAPS targeting ∼ 3 µm hit resolution, ≲ 0.3% X 0 /layer (down to ∼ 0.05% X 0 curved), and ≲ 50 mW cm −2 air-cooled operation.

deliverables.lectureNote: Full derivations of full-depletion voltage V fd , strip/pixel spatial resolution vs. pitch and Lorentz drift, NIEL damage parameterization (α, Hamburg annealing model, double-junction electric field), LGAD gain-layer avalanche physics and Landau-limited ∼ 20–30 ps timing, and FCC-ee impact-parameter resolution σ d 0 = a ⊕ b/(p sin 3/2 θ).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python 1D/2D Poisson depletion & LGAD gain-layer solver computing V fd , C(V ), and charge-collection efficiency under NIEL trapping; Stage 2 Allpix^2 full simulation of a 50 µm 65 nm MAPS pixel sensor (comparing modified-process depleted vs. epitaxial collection) and a 50 µm LGAD, extracting hit efficiency, cluster size, spatial residuals, and timing jitter. ◦ ◦ 16 n cm −2 ) vs. FCC-ee Z-pole
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) calculate V fd and leakage power density at 20 C vs. −20 C after HL-LHC (10 eq (few × 10 13 n eq cm −2 /yr) fluences; (2) optimize pixel pitch vs. diffusion charge sharing for σ x < 3 µm; (3) compare IDEA single-hit ultra-thin VXD vs. CLD double-sided VXD σ d 0 (p) from 1 to 50 GeV; (4) quantify Landau jitter floor in 50 µm vs. 20 µm LGADs. Exit criterion: match Allpix^2 cluster-size and spatial-resolution curves to test-beam benchmarks within 10%.

Advanced/optional: Sadrozinski–Seiden–Cartiglia (2018) on LGAD 4D tracking, Moll (RD50) radiation damage lectures, ALICE ITS3 stitched 65 nm MAPS, and RD53A/3D sensor beam-test results.

learningOutcomes: Derive the depletion depth, full-depletion voltage, and junction
capacitance of p–n silicon diodes and evaluate how sensor thickness trades signal amplitude against material budget.
Contrast hybrid pixel detectors, planar microstrips, 3D silicon sensors, and depleted/epitaxial CMOS MAPS in terms of capacitance, pitch, material budget, and radiation tolerance.
Derive the physical mechanisms of LGAD internal gain (M ≈ 10–30) and show how thin (30–50 µm) LGADs achieve 20–30 ps 4D tracking resolution.

Quantify bulk radiation damage via NIEL scaling (∆I = αΦV , space-charge sign inversion, acceptor removal, trapping) and surface TID damage (Q f , N it , p-stop/p-spray isolation). Compute the asymptotic (a) and multiple-scattering (b) terms of
transverse impact-parameter resolution σ d 0 for FCC-ee vertex detector geometries (IDEA, CLD, curved ITS3-like MAPS).
Evaluate the interplay between FCC-ee Z-pole hit rates (∼ 200–370 MHz cm −2 from incoherent pairs), integration time (≲ 1 µs), and air-cooling power limits (≲ 50 mW cm −2 ).
Configure and run Allpix^2 simulations for MAPS and LGAD sensors to extract spatial resolution, timing resolution, and charge-collection efficiency.

lectures.title: Electromagnetic Calorimetry: Homogeneous Crystals, Noble Liquids, and Sampling Architectures

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 7.2 (EM Showers, X 0 , R M ), 7.4 (Charge/Light Collection), 7.5 (Noise & Dynamic Range). Downstream: Lectures 7.9 (Hadronic & PFA Calorimetry), 7.12 (Cryostats & Coil Placement), 7.14 (In-Situ ECAL Calibration).

lectures.abstract: This lecture provides a quantitative analysis of electromagnetic calorimeter architectures and their energy, position, and timing resolution limits. We √ decompose the fractional energy resolution σ E /E = a/ E ⊕ b/E ⊕ c into stochastic (sampling and photostatistics), electronic/pile-up noise, and constant (non-uniformity, intercalibration, longitudinal leakage) terms. We compare homogeneous inorganic scintillating crystals (PbWO 4 , BGO, LYSO) read out by APDs or SiPMs against noble-liquid ionization calorimeters (LAr/Pb inclined-plate PCB readout in ALLEGRO) and high-granularity Si/W sampling calorimeters (CLD, CMS HGCAL). Key design trade-offs—upstream dead material, π 0 → γγ separation, shower-pointing granularity, and dynamic range—are evaluated for FCC-ee Higgs, flavor, and electroweak physics.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of sampling-fraction and sampling-frequency scaling of the stochastic term a ∝ t/f samp , photostatistics and SiPM saturation/excess-noise corrections, bipolar shaping for LAr triangular current pulses, shower centroiding and π 0 /γ separation vs. cell size/R M , and comparative engineering table of IDEA Crystal ECAL, ALLEGRO LAr/Pb ECAL, and CLD Si/W ECAL.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python sampling-calorimeter resolution model sweeping absorber thickness, active gap, and electronic noise to fit (a, b, c); Stage 2 Geant4 + DD4hep simulation of electron and photon beams (1–100 GeV) in a homogeneous PbWO 4 matrix vs. a 40-layer Si/W sampling ECAL and an inclined-plate LAr/Pb module, extracting (a, b, c) and π 0 two-photon separation efficiency.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) derive how sampling fluctuations scale with absorber thickness d and critical energy E c ; (2) compute the impact of 0.5 X 0 upstream tracker/cryostat material on 5 GeV photon energy resolution; (3) calculate the maximum π 0 energy for resolved γγ clusters in ALLEGRO vs. CLD ECAL at R = 2.1 m; (4) model SiPM dynamic-range non-linearity in a high-light-yield LYSO crystal at 100 GeV. Exit criterion: fit Geant4 resolution curves for Si/W and PbWO 4 to recover stochastic terms within 10% of CLD/IDEA specifications.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Fabjan & Gianotti (2003), Wigmans Ch. 3–5, PDG Ch. 35.8, Grupen & Shwartz Ch. 8. Advanced/optional: ALLEGRO noble-liquid ECAL papers, CMS ECAL HL-LHC upgrade, SiPM fundamentals (Gundacker & Heering 2020), and ALICE PHOS crystal calibration.

learningOutcomes: Derive the stochastic, noise, and constant contributions to
electromagnetic √ calorimeter energy resolution σ E /E = a/ E ⊕ b/E ⊕ c and identify which physics observables each term limits.
Quantify sampling fluctuations as a function of sampling fraction, sampling frequency, and e/mip ratio in Pb/LAr and W/Si calorimeters.
Contrast inorganic crystal scintillators (PbWO 4 , BGO, LYSO) on density, X 0 , R M , light yield, decay time, temperature coefficient, and radiation-induced transparency loss.
Explain the physics of noble-liquid ionization calorimetry (LAr/LKr drift, triangular induced current, bipolar shaping, cryogenic feedthroughs, and intrinsic uniformity/stability in ALLEGRO).
Analyze photodetector technologies (PMTs, APDs, SiPMs) including quantum efficiency, Geiger-mode microcell saturation, dark-count rate, optical crosstalk, and magnetic-field immunity.
Evaluate the trade-offs between homogeneous crystal ECALs (IDEA), noble-liquid ECALs (ALLEGRO), and ultra-granular Si/W ECALs (CLD) for γ/π 0 separation and H → γγ / B → K ∗ γ physics at FCC-ee.
Simulate and extract energy and position resolutions of homogeneous and sampling ECAL geometries using Geant4 and DD4hep .

lectures.title: Hadronic Calorimetry, Non-Compensation, Dual-Readout, and Imaging Particle Flow

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 7.3 (Nuclear Interactions & λ I ), 7.8 (EM Calorimetry). Downstream: Part 9 (Particle Flow & Jet Reconstruction), Part 11 (FCC-ee W/Z/H → q q̄ Boson Mass Separation).
dependencies.prerequisites: Lectures 7.3 (Nuclear Interactions & λ I ), 7.8 (EM Calorimetry).
dependencies.downstream: Part 9 (Particle Flow & Jet Reconstruction), Part 11 (FCC-ee W/Z/H → q q̄ Boson Mass Separation).

lectures.abstract: This lecture analyzes the physics of hadronic cascades and the two leading paradigms designed to achieve the FCC-ee jet-energy resolution benchmark (σ E /E ≈ 3–4% for W/Z → q q̄ separation). We derive why conventional hadronic calorimeters suffer from non-compensation (e/h ̸ = 1), invisible nuclear binding energy losses, and large event-by-event fluctuations in the electromagnetic shower fraction f em (which induce non-linearity and a non-Gaussian constant term). We then examine hardware compensation (ZEUS U/scintillator), software local-density weighting, dual-readout calorimetry (simultaneous scintillation S and Cherenkov C measurement in IDEA copper/brass fiber and crystal systems to extract f em event-by-event), and 5D high-granularity imaging calorimetry coupled to Particle Flow (CLD, CALICE, CMS HGCAL, PandoraPFA).

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact derivation of the hadronic response R π = f em e + (1 − f em )h, non-linearity vs. ⟨f em (E)⟩, the dual-readout master equation 1−(h/e) E = S−χC 2 = σ 2 + σ 2 + σ 2 + σ 2 with χ = 1−(h/e) S , and the Particle Flow jet-resolution decomposition σ jet (confusion term). tr γ h 0 conf 1−χ C
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python dual-readout and PFA resolution simulator demonstrating how χ-reconstruction removes f em non-Gaussian tails and how confusion scales with cell granularity and magnetic field B; Stage 2 Geant4 simulation of 10–100 GeV charged pions in (a) a dual-readout Cu/scintillator+quartz-fiber module and (b) a CALICE-like Fe/scintillator or W/Si imaging stack, comparing raw, dual-readout-corrected, and software-compensated energy resolutions.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) derive the dual-readout estimator E(S, C) and propagate uncorrelated photon-statistics uncertainties in S and C into σ E /E; (2) show why e/h > 1 causes hadronic response non-linearity with energy; (3) compute the ideal vs. confusion-limited PFA jet resolution for a √ 100 GeV dijet √ event (65% charged, 25% photon, 10% neutral hadron); (4) compare W/Z hadronic invariant-mass separation at σ E /E = 30%/ E vs. 50%/ E. Exit criterion: demonstrate > 2× resolution improvement and restored linearity (< 1%) on Geant4 pion showers using dual-readout reconstruction.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Lee, Livan & Wigmans (2018) Rev. Mod. Phys. on Dual-Readout, Thomson (2009) PandoraPFA, Fabjan & Gianotti (2003), Wigmans Ch. 6–8. Advanced/optional: CALICE experimental PFA tests ( arXiv:1507.05893 ), CMS HGCAL 5D imaging and GNN reconstruction ( arXiv:1802.05987 , arXiv:2203.01189 ), and information-theoretic shower limits ( arXiv:2610.41894 ).

learningOutcomes: Explain the microscopic origins of invisible energy (nuclear binding,
recoils, delayed neutrons, neutrinos) and why non-compensation (e/h ̸ = 1) degrades linearity and creates a constant resolution term.

Derive the dual-readout reconstruction formula relating scintillation (S) and Cherenkov (C) signals to true hadron energy E and event-by-event f em , and evaluate the role of Cherenkov photostatistics.
Contrast hardware compensation (hydrogenous neutron detection), software compensation (local hit-density reweighting), dual-readout calorimetry (IDEA), and Particle Flow imaging (CLD/ILD/CMS HGCAL).
Decompose Particle Flow jet-energy resolution into tracking, ECAL, HCAL, and confusion terms, identifying how R M , cell granularity, B-field, and coil placement control confusion.
Analyze 5D imaging calorimetry (3D space + energy + ∼ 30 ps timing) and graph/set neural-network reconstruction for overlapping showers and hadron PID.
Quantify longitudinal containment requirements (in λ I ) for hadronic showers from 10 to 175 GeV at FCC-ee (Z-pole through tt̄ threshold).
Implement and benchmark dual-readout and software-compensated pion reconstruction on Geant4 hadronic shower simulations ( FTFP_ BERT ).

lectures.title: Particle Identification: Ionization, Time-of-Flight, Cherenkov Imaging, and Global Likelihoods

lectures.abstract: This lecture develops the physics and statistical combination of charged-hadron (e/π/K/p) particle identification (PID) across the full FCC-ee momentum spectrum (0.2–50 GeV/c). We derive the mass-separation power N σ (p) for four complementary techniques: specific ionization (dE/dx truncated mean) and primary cluster counting (dN/dx) in gaseous trackers, Time-of-Flight (ToF) with MRPCs, LGADs, or quartz Cherenkov timing (TORCH), Ring Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) counters with dual aerogel/gas radiators, and Detection of Internally Reflected Cherenkov light (DIRC / Belle II TOP). Finally, we formulate multi-detector log-likelihood ratios (∆ ln L Kπ ) and Bayesian posterior probabilities that seamlessly bridge the dE/dx crossover blind spot around 1 GeV/c.

deliverables.lectureNote: Analytical N σ (p) derivations for dE/dx, dN/dx, ToF (∆t = 2c ), and RICH (σ θ c / N pe including chromatic, emission-point, p 2 and pixel errors), TORCH chromatic-dispersion correction, and multi-subsystem global PID likelihood construction with correlated track-momentum uncertainties.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python global PID workbench generating synthetic π/K/p responses across 0.2–40 GeV/c for combined IDEA dN/dx + 50 ps ToF vs. compact dual-radiator RICH, producing N σ (p) and ROC (kaon efficiency vs. pion mis-ID) curves; Stage 2 Geant4 optical-photon ray-tracing of a proximity-focusing aerogel/C 4 F 10 RICH and a quartz DIRC/TORCH bar with SiPM/MCP-PMT photodetectors, reconstructing Cherenkov rings via maximum likelihood.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) compute the flight path L and timing resolution σ t required for 3σ π/K separation at 3 GeV/c and 10 GeV/c; (2) derive the chromatic error σ θ,chrom for fused silica vs. C 4 F 10 and optimize photodetector spectral window; (3) show how combining 100 ps Si-wrapper ToF with IDEA dN/dx closes the ∼ 1 GeV/c crossover blind spot; (4) evaluate impact of K/π mis-ID on B s 0 → D s − K + vs. B s 0 → D s − π + background suppression. Exit criterion: achieve > 3σ π/K separation continuously from 0.5 to 30 GeV/c in the combined likelihood simulation.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Wilkinson (2021) Particle Identification at FCC-ee ( arXiv:2106.01253 ), PDG Ch. 35.5, Grupen & Shwartz Ch. 9, Allison & Cobb (1980). Advanced/optional: Nappi & Seguinot RICH review, ALICE Run 3 MRPC TOF performance ( arXiv:2511.10311 ), IDEA cluster counting ( arXiv:2211.04220 ), and calorimeter-assisted hadron PID ( arXiv:2608.19064 ).

learningOutcomes: Derive the momentum scaling of N σ (p) for ToF (∝ p −2 ), RICH (∝ p −2
above threshold), and dE/dx / dN/dx (relativistic rise and crossover blind spots).
Analyze the error budget of a RICH detector (chromatic dispersion, emission-point uncertainty, pixel granularity, track-direction error, and N pe = N 0 L sin 2 θ c ).
Explain the optical principles of DIRC and TORCH quartz-bar Cherenkov detectors and how time-of-propagation resolves chromatic dispersion to achieve ∼ 10–15 ps per-track timing.
Evaluate the performance and operational requirements of MRPC, LGAD, and LYSO+SiPM Time-of-Flight systems for intermediate-momentum (0.5–5 GeV/c) PID.
Formulate multi-subsystem log-likelihood ratios and calibrated Bayesian PID probabilities, accounting for species priors and track-parameter correlations.
Quantify the global detector impact (radial space, material budget in front of ECAL, and channel count) of integrating dedicated PID systems into FCC-ee detector concepts.
Simulate optical Cherenkov photon transport and perform maximum-likelihood ring reconstruction in Geant4 and Python.

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lectures 7.1 (Ionization), 7.2 (Radiative Losses), 7.3 (MCS & λ I ), 7.6 (Gaseous Chambers & MPGDs). Downstream: Lectures 7.12 (Magnet Return Yoke Integration), 7.14 (Z → µ + µ − Momentum-Scale Calibration).

lectures.abstract: This lecture examines muon interaction physics from 1 GeV to multi-TeV energies and the design of large-area muon spectrometers and taggers. We derive the muon stopping-power equation −⟨dE/dx⟩ = a(E) + b(E)E, quantifying ionization, direct e + e − pair production, bremsstrahlung, and photonuclear interactions, along with the muon critical energy E µc (e.g., ∼ 160 GeV in PbWO 4 , ∼ 340 GeV in Fe). We analyze large-area gaseous detector technologies embedded in iron return yokes or air-core toroids—Drift Tubes (MDTs/DTs), Cathode Strip Chambers (CSCs), Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs), and µ-RWELL / GEM stations (as in IDEA and CLD)—evaluating momentum resolution, hadronic punch-through suppression vs. absorber depth in λ I , decay-in-flight backgrounds, and displaced long-lived particle (LLP) vertexing.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivation of a(E) and b(E) muon stopping-power terms and stochastic catastrophic energy-loss tails, range-energy tables, standalone vs. combined inner-tracker + muon-system momentum resolution, punch-through probability parameterization P pt (E, λ I ), and comparative architecture of ATLAS/CMS vs. IDEA (µ-RWELL) and CLD (RPC) muon systems.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python muon transport and punch-through model integrating −⟨dE/dx⟩ = a + bE through calorimeter + yoke layers and computing multiple-scattering degradation of standalone muon momentum resolution; Stage 2 Geant4 simulation of 5–200 GeV muons and pions traversing an ECAL + HCAL + segmented iron return yoke (8–14 λ I ), measuring muon tagging efficiency, radiative shower-induced hit multiplicity, and pion punch-through rates.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) compute the muon critical energy E µc in Fe and PbWO 4 from Groom–Mokhov–Striganov parameters and compare with the CMS cosmic-ray measurement (160 GeV); (2) calculate the minimum muon momentum needed to penetrate 10 λ I of Fe; (3) estimate the π ± → µ ± ν decay-in-flight fake rate inside a 2.1 m FCC-ee tracking volume at p = 10 GeV/c; (4) design a 3-station µ-RWELL yoke layout for IDEA to tag displaced LLP decays. Exit criterion: reproduce Geant4 pion punch-through fraction vs. depth (λ I ) and muon critical energy in PbWO 4 within 10%.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: PDG Ch. 34.6 & 35.6, CMS cosmic-ray muon stopping-power measurement ( arXiv:0911.5397 , citing Groom– Mokhov–Striganov 2001), Grupen & Shwartz Ch. 11. Advanced/optional: ATLAS/CMS Run 2 muon performance papers ( arXiv:1603.05598 , arXiv:2012.00578 ), IDEA µ-RWELL muon system ( arXiv:2502.21223 ), and Riegler RPC physics.

learningOutcomes: Decompose high-energy muon energy loss into ionization a(E) and
radiative b(E)E (pair production, bremsstrahlung, photonuclear) contributions and calculate the muon critical energy E µc .
Explain why stochastic catastrophic radiative losses create secondary electromagnetic showers inside muon chambers and degrade high-p T standalone tracking.
Compare large-area muon chamber technologies (DT/MDT, CSC, RPC, GEM, µ-RWELL) across spatial resolution, timing resolution, rate capability, cost per m 2 , and gas-system sustainability.
Quantify hadronic punch-through probability as a function of calorimeter + yoke depth in interaction lengths λ I and distinguish punch-through from π/K decays in flight.
Contrast combined tracker–muon momentum reconstruction at hadron colliders (ATLAS/CMS) with muon tagging, tail-catching, and far-displaced LLP vertexing at FCC-ee (IDEA/CLD/ALLEGRO).
Evaluate the impact of magnetic-field return-yoke geometry on muon bending, fringe fields, and mechanical access.
Simulate muon radiative energy loss and pion punch-through in a segmented calorimeter-plus-yoke stack using Geant4 .

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 2 (Magnetostatics & Thermodynamics), Part 6 (FCC-ee MDI & Final-Focus Quadrupoles), Lectures 7.7–7.9. Downstream: Lecture 7.14 (Magnetic Field Mapping & Thermal-Mechanical Stability).

lectures.abstract: This lecture bridges detector physics and systems engineering, analyzing how superconducting magnets, cooling plants, mechanical supports, and electrical/optical services shape real-world physics performance. We derive superconducting solenoid scaling laws—stored magnetic energy E mag , hoop stress σ θ = B 2 R/(2µ 0 t), the energy-to-mass ratio E/M governing quench protection, and the transparency budget (x/X 0 ) of thin Al-stabilized NbTi or HTS coils placed inside the HCAL (IDEA, ALLEGRO: ∼ 0.8 X 0 coil + cryostat) vs. outside (CLD). We then analyze the FCC-ee Machine–Detector Interface (MDI) constraint capping the central field at 2 T with a −5 T compensating solenoid, together with two-phase evaporative CO 2 microchannel cooling, forced-air vertex cooling, and low-mass carbon-fiber mechanics.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of solenoid field uniformity, hoop stress and E/M quench enthalpy balance, thin-coil material-budget optimization (X 0 of Al stabilizer vs. NbTi/HTS conductor), two-phase CO 2 vs. air-cooling heat-transfer equations (thermal figure of merit K cm 2 W −1 ), thermal-runaway stability criterion for irradiated silicon, and FCC-ee MDI integration geometry (ℓ ∗ = 2.2 m, 15 mrad crossing angle).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python magnetics & thermal-budget script computing solenoid B(r, z) via Biot–Savart, hoop stress, E/M quench temperature rise, and 1D stave thermal profile (including thermal-runaway feedback); Stage 2 DD4hep material-scan ( materialScan in Key4hep ) of the IDEA and CLD detector models across cos θ, decomposing x/X 0 and x/λ I by subdetector, cryostat, beam pipe, cooling pipes, and cabling.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) calculate stored energy, hoop stress, and E/M for the IDEA 2 T (R = 2.1 m) thin solenoid vs. CMS 3.8 T (R = 3 m); (2) explain R why the 30 mrad crossing angle at FCC-ee Z-pole limits the detector solenoid to 2 T and compute the required compensating solenoid integral B z dz; (3) compare the radiation-length overhead of silicon microchannel evaporative CO 2 cooling vs. forced-air cooling at 50 mW cm −2 ; (4) compute the thermal contraction differential between lead–steel absorber plates cooled from 300 K to 87 K in ALLEGRO LAr. Exit criterion: generate a full DD4hep polar-angle material budget breakdown matching IDEA/CLD specifications within 5%.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Yamamoto (2023) & Deelen (2022) CERN Indico magnet reviews, FCC-ee Detector Requirements ( arXiv:2505.06781 ), IDEA MDI & mechanics ( arXiv:2502.21223 ). Advanced/optional: LHCb VELO evaporative CO 2 microchannel cooling ( arXiv:1211.1176 , arXiv:2404.13615 ), CMS Phase-1 Pixel CO 2 upgrade, ATLAS IBL integration, and ALLEGRO cryogenic contraction tests.

learningOutcomes: Derive superconducting solenoid stored energy, magnetic pressure,
hoop stress, and the E/M enthalpy criterion governing quench protection and coil thickness.
Evaluate the physics and engineering trade-offs of placing an ultra-thin (∼ 0.8 X 0 ) solenoid between ECAL and HCAL (IDEA, ALLEGRO) vs. a larger solenoid outside the HCAL (CLD).
Explain how the FCC-ee beam crossing angle, emittance preservation, and final-focus quadrupoles (ℓ ∗ = 2.2 m) constrain the 2 T detector solenoid and require compensating/screening solenoids.

Compare cooling technologies for tracking detectors (forced air/helium convection, demineralized water, and two-phase evaporative CO 2 in silicon microchannels) via thermal figure of merit and material budget. Formulate the thermal-runaway condition in irradiated silicon sensors
and calculate the cooling margins required to maintain mechanical and thermal stability.
Quantify the material-budget impact of non-active services (power cables, serial powering, optical fibers, carbon-fiber staves, and cryostat walls) using DD4hep material scans.
Analyze cryogenic thermal-contraction and vibration (CFD/FEA) tolerances for noble-liquid calorimeters and ultra-light air-cooled vertex staves.

lectures.title: Trigger, Continuous Data Acquisition, and Real-Time Analysis Architectures

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 3 (Statistical Selection & Efficiency), Lectures 7.5 (Front-End Buffering & Serialization), 7.6–7.9 (Subdetector Channel Counts & Occupancies). Downstream: Lecture 7.14 (Online Calibration & DQM), Part 9 (Real-Time Reconstruction).

lectures.abstract: This lecture analyzes the architecture of Trigger and Data Acquisition (TDAQ) systems across both hadron-collider (multi-level hardware + software triggers) and next-generation continuous-readout regimes (LHCb Run 3, ALICE Run 3, and FCC-ee). We derive dead-time models (paralyzable vs. non-paralyzable), FIFO buffer overflow probabilities via queueing theory, optical-link bandwidth budgets, and event-building network topologies. Contrasting the 40 MHz LHC environment with the FCC-ee Z-pole (40–50 MHz continuous bunch crossings, ∼ 50–60 kHz Z decays, ∼ 100–200 kHz total physics + Bhabha + γγ rate, and incoherent-pair backgrounds), we evaluate zero-suppression, FPGA middle-layer data concentrators, GPU/CPU software trigger farms, and Real-Time Analysis (RTA) paradigms that eliminate irreversible hardware-trigger biases.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of dead-time loss formulas, Poisson buffer-sizing and latency constraints, link-rate and power-per-Gbps budgets (lpGBT / high-speed optical transceivers), full FCC-ee Z-pole vs. ZH/tt̄ data-rate table by subsystem (MAPS VXD, IDEA drift chamber waveforms, high-granularity ECAL/HCAL), and architectural comparison of ATLAS/CMS L1+HLT vs. LHCb triggerless RTA.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python discrete-event TDAQ simulator modeling Poisson + bursty beam-background hit arrivals, front-end zero-suppression, FIFO buffer occupancy, dead-time vs. readout rate, and optical-link saturation for an FCC-ee Z-pole vertex stave; Stage 2 Key4hep / EDM4hep streaming throughput benchmark analyzing simulated Z-pole event sizes and implementing a lightweight online event-selection / data-scouting filter in C++/Python.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) derive dead-time fractions for paralyzable and non-paralyzable front-ends at 200 kHz event rate with 2 µs readout time; (2) compute raw vs. zero-suppressed data bandwidth (in Tbps) for the IDEA vertex detector and drift chamber at the FCC-ee Z-pole; (3) calculate the minimum FIFO depth to keep buffer-overflow loss below 10 −6 at 80% link utilization; (4) evaluate why triggerless full-rate software selection is essential for unbiased FCC-ee Z-lineshape and displaced-LLP searches. Exit criterion: validate Python queueing-model buffer-overflow rates against discrete-event simulation within 5% and produce a complete FCC-ee Z-pole bandwidth budget.

FCC-ee bunch structure & rates ( arXiv:2505.06781 ). Advanced/optional: LHCb Real-Time Analysis ( arXiv:1903.01360 ), triggerless 4D detectors ( arXiv:2607.01496 ), and ALICE Run 3 continuous readout ( arXiv:2511.10311 ).

non-paralyzable trigger/readout stages and size front-end buffers via queueing theory.
Contrast multi-level hardware-plus-software triggers (ATLAS/CMS L1 FPGA + HLT) with continuous, triggerless readout architectures (LHCb Run 3, ALICE Run 3, FCC-ee).
Compute per-subsystem hit rates, occupancies, zero-suppression factors, and off-detector optical bandwidth budgets (Gbps to Tbps) at the FCC-ee Z-pole, W W , ZH, and tt̄ operating points.

Analyze the role of FPGA middle-layer concentrators, high-speed event-building networks, and heterogeneous CPU/GPU online farms in Real-Time Analysis (RTA). Quantify the impact of FCC-ee continuous bunch crossings (no
bunch-train gaps) on front-end powering, latency, and thermal budgets compared to linear colliders.
Design unbiased physics-quality online selection and scouting streams that preserve acceptance for both precision electroweak benchmarks and exotic long-lived signatures.
Simulate front-end buffering, zero-suppression, and event-size scaling using Python discrete-event models and Key4hep / EDM4hep data structures.

lectures.title: Track-Based Alignment, In-Situ Calibration, and Real-Time Data Quality Monitoring

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 3 (Linear Least Squares, Schur Complements & Hypothesis Testing), Lectures 7.6–7.13. Downstream: Part 9 (Precision Track & Calorimeter Reconstruction), Part 11 (FCC-ee m Z , Γ Z , m W , m H Systematic Uncertainty Control).

lectures.abstract: At the FCC-ee Z-pole (∼ 10 12 Z bosons), statistical uncertainties become negligible and physics reach is governed by systematic control of detector geometry, energy/momentum scales, and long-term stability. This lecture formulates the mathematical and operational machinery of detector alignment, calibration, and Data Quality Monitoring (DQM). We derive global track-based alignment via Blobel’s Millepede-II block-matrix reduction (simultaneously solving local track and O(10 5 –10 6 ) global alignment parameters) and analyze "weak modes" (sagitta twist, curl, radial expansion) constrained by Z → µ + µ − , J/ψ → µ + µ − , cosmic rays, and E/p. We then cover in-situ calorimeter intercalibration (ϕ-symmetry, π 0 /η → γγ, Z → e + e − , radiative Z decays), luminosity metrology (10 −4 absolute, 10 −5 relative), and automated real-time DQM anomaly detection.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete linear-algebra derivation of Millepede-II Schur-complement reduction and Lagrange constraints, formal taxonomy of tracker weak-mode deformations and their p T /d 0 biases, multi-step EM calorimeter calibration chain (intercalibration, multivariate response, absolute Z → e + e − scale, non-linearity), and statistical DQM control charts / automated online calibration loops.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 Python global track-based alignment solver (exact Schur complement on a misaligned 6-layer silicon telescope + barrel tracker) demonstrating weak-mode emergence with collision tracks alone and weak-mode suppression when adding cosmic-ray / invariant-mass constraints; Stage 2 Millepede-II C++/Python execution on simulated misaligned DD4hep tracker hits plus an in-situ Z → e + e − & π 0 → γγ calorimeter intercalibration fit.
deliverables.problemSet: Four problems: (1) prove the Schur-complement elimination in Millepede-II reduces an (N global +N tracks ×5) system to an N global ×N global matrix; (2) construct a curl/twist weak-mode transformation that leaves χ 2 of collision tracks invariant while shifting opposite-charge p T by δ(q/p T ) = ±0.1 TeV −1 ; (3) calculate the LumiCal inner-radius mechanical metrology tolerance required for 10 −4 absolute luminosity precision at FCC-ee; (4) derive the intercalibration statistical precision of a 50,000-channel ECAL using π 0 → γγ vs. Z → e + e − at the Z-pole. Exit criterion: recover injected 50 µm sensor misalignments to < 2 µm RMS with Millepede-II and eliminate sagitta bias to < 0.1 TeV −1 .
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Blobel Millepede-II documentation & NIM A (2006), ATLAS Run 2 Inner Detector alignment ( arXiv:2007.07624 ), CMS Run 3 Tracker alignment ( arXiv:2401.01261 ), ATLAS Run 2 e/γ energy calibration ( arXiv:2309.05471 ). Advanced/optional: ALICE PHOS π 0 /η calibration ( arXiv:1902.06145 ), LHCb Real-Time Alignment & Calibration ( arXiv:2412.05041 ), and FCC-ee systematic-stability considerations ( arXiv:2606.07564 ).

learningOutcomes: Derive the global least-squares Millepede-II block-matrix reduction
separating local track parameters from hundreds of thousands of global alignment degrees of freedom.

Identify tracker weak modes (twist, curl, radial/z-scaling, elliptical distortion) and design orthogonal constraints (cosmic rays, Z/Υ/J/ψ → µ + µ − , E/p, survey metrology) to remove sagitta and impact-parameter biases.

Formulate the complete in-situ electromagnetic calorimeter calibration hierarchy: electronic gain, time-dependent transparency/temperature monitoring, ϕ-symmetry and π 0 /η intercalibration, and absolute Z → e + e − scale setting. Quantify how alignment and calibration uncertainties propagate into
benchmark FCC-ee electroweak and Higgs observables (m Z , Γ Z , m H recoil mass, A FB ).
Analyze the metrology and alignment requirements of FCC-ee luminosity calorimeters (LumiCal) needed for 10 −4 absolute and 10 −5 relative luminosity precision.
Design real-time calibration loops and automated Data Quality Monitoring (DQM) pipelines capable of detecting channel drifts, fill-to-fill mechanical movements, and dead modules online.
Execute and validate a global track-based alignment workflow using Millepede-II on misaligned simulated tracking data.

parts.abstract: Part 8 establishes the end-to-end simulation chain connecting first-principles quantum field theory to realistic detector readouts for both hadron colliders (LHC/FCC-hh) and precision lepton colliders (FCC-ee). Students progress from collinear factorization, DGLAP evolution, and multi-leg NLO matrix-element matching through parton showers, non-perturbative hadronization, and QED initial-state radiation resummation. The second half bridges particle-level event records (LHE, HepMC3, EDM4hep) into full Geant4 detector transport via DD4hep geometries, parametric and machine-learning fast-simulation surrogates, electronic digitization with beam-induced background overlay, and test-beam validation. Upon completion, students can independently construct, validate, and assign rigorous modeling systematics to full-chain collider Monte Carlo pipelines.

deliverables.lectureNote: Unified 160-page graduate monograph deriving factorization, Sudakov form factors, NLO matching/merging subtraction terms, Bethe–Bloch and electromagnetic/hadronic cascade transport, and digitization noise models, standardized in natural units (ℏ = c = 1, energies in GeV, lengths in mm, cross sections in pb/fb) with worked FCC-ee (e + e − → ZH, Z → q q̄) and LHC (pp → Z/γ ∗ + jets) benchmarks.
deliverables.lab: Eight-module progressive pipeline moving from Stage 1 standalone Python/NumPy prototypes (toy DGLAP solver, veto-algorithm parton shower, 1D EM shower, Gaussian smearing, noise overlay) to Stage 2 production Key4hep/HEP workflows ( LHAPDF6 , Pythia8 , Sherpa , KKMCee , WHIZARD , MadGraph5_aMC@NLO , DD4hep , ddsim / Geant4 , k4SimDelphes , Allpix 2 , Rivet ).
deliverables.problemSet: Eight graded analytical and computational problem sets (40 problems total) culminating in a capstone end-to-end simulation-to- validation audit; exit criterion requires reproducing benchmark cross sections within 1%, passing DD4hep overlap/material checks, and quantifying generator plus Geant4 physics-list systematics on a target observable.

(2011), Geant4/DD4hep manuals, and FCC-ee CDR Vol. 2; advanced progression branches into NLO multi-jet merging, CaloChallenge generative surrogates, FCC-ee MDI beamstrahlung backgrounds, and CALICE test-beam validation papers.

evaluate PDF and scale uncertainties using LHAPDF6 .
Construct and tune parton-shower and hadronization chains in Pythia8 and Sherpa , and configure precision QED ISR generators ( KKMCee , WHIZARD ) for FCC-ee.
Execute automated NLO matrix-element generation and matching/merging ( MadGraph5_aMC@NLO , FxFx, POWHEG) and validate LHE/HepMC3 event records.

Author, visualize, and audit DD4hep compact XML detector geometries, readout segmentations, and radiation/interaction-length material budgets. Configure and run Geant4 full detector simulations via ddsim ,
optimizing physics lists, production range cuts, and multithreaded throughput.
Benchmark parametric fast simulation ( Delphes / k4SimDelphes ) and generative ML calorimeter surrogates against full Geant4 shower observables.
Model front-end digitization noise and overlay FCC-ee beam-induced backgrounds (incoherent e + e − pairs, synchrotron radiation) onto physics events.
Quantify simulation-to-test-beam discrepancies and propagate generator, tune, and hadronic-model uncertainties into analysis-level systematic envelopes.

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Part 5 (Perturbative QFT, Running α s and QCD). Downstream links: Lecture 8.2 (Initial-State Showers), Lecture 8.3 (NLO Matrix Elements & LHE), Lecture 10.6 (Cross-Section Normalization in FCCAnalyses).

lectures.abstract: This lecture formulates the perturbative calculation of hard-scattering cross sections in hadronic and leptonic collisions. Starting from the QCD collinear factorization theorem, we separate short-distance partonic cross sections σ̂ ab (ŝ, µ F , µ R ) from universal non-perturbative parton distribution functions f i (x, µ 2 F ). We derive the Dokshitzer–Gribov–Lipatov–Altarelli–Parisi (DGLAP) integro-differential evolution equations from collinear singularities, evaluate leading-order splitting kernels P ij (z) with plus-distribution regularization, and contrast Hessian (CT18, MSHT20) versus Monte Carlo replica (NNPDF4.0) PDF uncertainty prescriptions. We conclude with electron structure functions for e + e − colliders and precision scale-variation envelopes.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous derivation of Drell–Yan dσ/dM 2 dy, collinear factorization, Altarelli–Parisi splitting functions P qq , P qg , P gq , P gg , momen- tum/valence sum rules, Mellin-space DGLAP solution, and MS scale conventions (µ R , µ F in GeV, cross sections in pb). 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Implement a Python/NumPy x-space Runge–Kutta DGLAP solver evolving toy valence/gluon PDFs from Q 2 2 0 = 2 GeV to M Z and verifying momentum sum-rule conservation to 10 −4 . Stage 2: Query LHAPDF6 ( NNPDF40_nnlo_as_01180 , CT18NNLO , MSHT20nnlo_as118 , PDF4LHC21_40 ) in Python/C++ to compute pp → Z parton luminosities and 7-point (µ R , µ F ) plus PDF uncertainty bands.
deliverables.problemSet: Derive P qq (z) including the δ(1 − z) virtual term via fermion-number conservation; prove Mellin diagonalization of non-singlet DGLAP; √ compute and compare Hessian vs. Monte Carlo replica 68% CL bands for gg → H luminosity at s = 13.6 TeV and 100 TeV (FCC-hh); exit criterion: numerical DGLAP evolution matches LHAPDF6 non-singlet u v (x, Q 2 ) within 2% across 10 −2 < x < 0.7.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Ellis–Stirling–Webber Ch. 4, Altarelli–Parisi (1977), Buckley et al. LHAPDF6 (2015), Gao–Harland-Lang–Rojo (2018); Advanced: PDF4LHC21 combination, NNPDF4.0/CT18/MSHT20 global-fit methodology papers.

learningOutcomes: State the collinear factorization theorem and identify its
power-suppressed O(Λ 2 QCD /Q 2 ) corrections.
Derive the leading-order DGLAP evolution equations and regularize z → 1 soft singularities with plus distributions.
Verify flavor-valence and longitudinal-momentum sum rules analytically and numerically across evolution scales. Distinguish Hessian eigenvector sets ( CT18 , MSHT20 ) from Monte Carlo
replica ensembles ( NNPDF ) when propagating PDF uncertainties. 2
Compute parton-parton luminosities L ij (τ, µ ) and 7-point (µ R , µ F ) F scale-variation envelopes using LHAPDF6 .
Contrast hadronic PDFs with QED electron structure functions governing initial-state radiation at FCC-ee.

lectures.abstract: This lecture bridges hard partonic configurations to observable hadronic final states via Markovian parton showers and non-perturbative hadronization models. We derive the Sudakov no-emission form factor ∆(t 1 , t 2 ), formulate the veto algorithm for exact sampling with running α s (p 2 ⊥ ), and compare p ⊥ -ordered dipole showers ( Pythia8 , Sherpa ) against angular-ordered coherent showers ( Herwig 7 ), including backward initial-state evolution. We contrast the Lund string fragmentation model against color-singlet cluster hadronization, examine generator tuning ( Monash 2013 , Rivet benchmarks), and detail FCC-ee-specific precision generators: YFS coherent exclusive exponentiation in KKMCee and multi-particle electroweak/beamstrahlung simulation in WHIZARD with CIRCE2 .

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of Sudakov form factors, color coherence and angular ordering, the Sudakov veto algorithm, backward ISR evolution weights, Lund symmetric fragmentation function f (z), cluster fission kinematics, and Yennie–Frautschi–Suura (YFS) QED exponentiation for e + e − → f f ¯ (nγ). 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Write a standalone Python final-state q → qg dipole shower using the veto algorithm with running α s (p ) and verify thrust/broadening √ ⊥ distributions in e + e − → q q̄ at s = 91.2 GeV. Stage 2: Run Pythia 8.3 , Sherpa 3 , KKMCee , and WHIZARD (via k4Gen / Key4hep) for e + e − → Z → q q̄ and e e → ZH, exporting HepMC3 and comparing event shapes against LEP data in Rivet . − +
deliverables.problemSet: Prove exactness of the Sudakov veto algorithm for an arbitrary overestimate kernel g(t) ≥ f (t); compute the leading-log mean gluon multiplicity in a q q̄ shower; compare Pythia8 √ Lund vs. Sherpa / Herwig cluster hadronization on LEP Z-pole thrust and charged multiplicity; evaluate KKMCee vs. Pythia8 ISR lineshape shifts at s = 91.2 GeV; exit criterion: LEP thrust distribution reproduced within 5% across 0.05 < 1 − T < 0.35.

branching-scale sampling via the veto algorithm.
Contrast p ⊥ -ordered dipole recoil schemes with angular-ordered parton showers and explain soft-gluon color coherence.
Explain backward initial-state radiation evolution and its dependence on PDF ratios f a (x/z, t)/f b (x, t). Compare the physical assumptions, parameterizations, and failure

Configure and compare generator tunes ( Monash 2013 , Sherpa defaults) against LEP/LHC reference data using Rivet .

lectures.abstract: This lecture covers automated tree-level and next-to-leading order (NLO) event generation and the theoretical machinery required to combine fixed-order matrix elements with parton showers without double-counting. We analyze helicity-amplitude recursion, FKS/Catani–Seymour infrared subtraction, and one-loop reduction as automated in MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and WHIZARD . We derive the subtractive MC@NLO and multiplicative POWHEG NLO+PS matching formalisms, explain the origin and statistical cost of negative event weights, and compare LO ( MLM , CKKW-L ) and NLO ( FxFx ) multi-jet merging prescriptions. Finally, we dissect the Les Houches Event ( LHE v3) XML schema, multi-weight systematic blocks, and UFO 2.0 BSM model interfaces.

deliverables.lectureNote: Explicit derivations of FKS subtraction, MC@NLO S-event/H-event decomposition, POWHEG hardest-emission Sudakov factor, FxFx merging scale Q cut diagnostics, effective sample size N eff = ( w i ) 2 / w i 2 under negative weights, and LHE v3 XML specification. P P
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Build a Python pylhe parser and diagnostic suite that computes N eff , negative-weight fractions, and differential jet-rate (d 01 , d 12 ) smoothness histograms from LHE v3 files. Stage 2: Run MadGraph5_aMC@NLO to generate pp → Z + 0, 1, 2 jets at LO ( MLM ) and NLO ( FxFx ) plus e + e − → ZH with UFO 2.0 SMEFT operators, shower in Pythia8 , and inspect merging-scale stability in Rivet .
deliverables.problemSet: Prove cancellation of O(α s ) double-counting in MC@NLO and POWHEG using a 1D toy emission model; derive the statistical penalty factor (1 − 2f neg ) −2 from negative-weight fraction f neg ; audit an FxFx merged Z + jets sample across Q cut ∈ {15, 25, 40} GeV using differential jet-resolution distributions y 01 , y 12 ; exit criterion: smooth d n,n+1 transitions with < 5% discontinuity across Q cut .

amplitudes, perform FKS infrared subtraction, and handle adaptive multi-channel phase-space integration.
Contrast subtractive ( MC@NLO ) and multiplicative ( POWHEG ) NLO+PS matching methods, including their treatment of the hardest emission and negative weights.
Quantify the statistical impact of negative weights via effective sample size N eff and evaluate mitigation strategies. Configure LO ( MLM / CKKW-L ) and NLO ( FxFx ) multi-jet merging and
diagnose double-counting or phase-space gaps via differential jet rates (d n,n+1 ).
Parse, validate, and manipulate Les Houches Event ( LHE v3) XML records, including <initrwgt> scale/PDF/EFT reweighting blocks, using pylhe and HepMC3 .
Import custom BSM/SMEFT Lagrangians into MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and WHIZARD via the UFO 2.0 standard.

lectures.abstract: Accurate detector simulation and reconstruction require a single source of truth for geometry, materials, sensitive volumes, and alignment. This lecture introduces the Detector Description Toolkit for High Energy Physics ( DD4hep ) and its Generic Detector Description Model built atop ROOT TGeo . We examine the dual hierarchy of geometric Volume / PlacedVolume trees and logical DetElement trees, compact XML parameterization, C++ detector constructor plugins, and DDSegmentation bitfield encoding ( CellID ) for trackers and granular calorimeters. Students learn systematic geometry verification: overlap checking, 3D visualization, and ray-tracing material budget scans (X/X 0 , X/λ I ) on FCC-ee detector concepts ( CLD , IDEA ).

deliverables.lectureNote: Architectural specification of DD4hep ( DDCore , DDRec , DDSegmentation ), CellID bitfield arithmetic, radiation-length and interaction- w i /X 0,i ), coordinate/unit conventions (mm, rad, Tesla), and worked CLD_o2_v07 vertex-tracker and SiW-ECAL P length mixture formulas (1/X 0 = geometry walkthrough.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Prototype a Python ray-tracer over cylindrical/conical shell primitives computing X/X 0 (η, ϕ) and validating against analytical thin-shell limits. Stage 2: Load CLD_o2_v07.xml from k4geo in Key4hep, write a custom compact XML + C++ plugin for a 4-layer silicon barrel with Cartesian grid segmentation, run checkOverlaps.py and materialScan , and plot X/X 0 (θ) and λ/λ I (θ).
deliverables.problemSet: Derive composite X 0 and λ I for a Si–W–PCB–glue sampling ECAL layer; design a 64-bit CellID bitfield for a 30-layer, 5 × 5 mm 2 granular ECAL without overflow; diagnose and fix three injected geometry overlaps in a provided compact XML; exit criterion: zero overlaps reported by TGeoManager::CheckOverlaps at 10 −3 mm tolerance and material scan agreeing with analytical calculation within 1%.

geoDisplay to eliminate extruded or colliding volumes.

lectures.abstract: This lecture examines microscopic Monte Carlo particle transport through complex detector geometries using Geant4 and the DD4hep simulation interface DDG4 / ddsim . We analyze the stepping loop, electromagnetic processes (ionization with Landau–Vavilov straggling, bremsstrahlung, pair production, Urban/Wentzel multiple scattering), and modular hadronic physics lists ( FTFP_BERT , QGSP_BERT , QGSP_BERT_HP , EMZ options) spanning intranuclear cascades to parton-string fragmentation. We rigorously connect production range cuts to material-dependent energy thresholds, dissect ddsim steering files, sensitive-detector hit scoring, EDM4hep output ( SimTrackerHit , SimCalorimeterHit ), and CPU/memory profiling of multithreaded Geant4-MT jobs.

deliverables.lectureNote: Detailed walkthrough of Geant4 transport equations, mean free path sampling, multiple-scattering step limitations, range-cut-to-energy conversion E cut (R, Z, A), hadronic model energy-transition regimes (Bertini cascade, Fritiof, Quark-Gluon String), and DDG4 action sequences.

lectures.abstract: Full Geant4 calorimeter transport dominates collider computing budgets, motivating fast-simulation architectures that accelerate event generation by 10 2 –10 4 × while preserving physics fidelity. This lecture covers both parametric fast simulation ( Delphes 3 and Key4hep’s k4SimDelphes with FCC-ee IDEA cards) and modern machine-learning calorimeter surrogates. We derive analytical helix propagation, Gluckstern track-covariance parameterization, and calorimeter tower smearing, then examine deep generative shower models: CaloGAN , ATLAS AtlFast3 , normalizing flows ( CaloFlow ), and score-based diffusion models ( CaloDiffusion ) benchmarked on CaloChallenge 2022 . Emphasis is placed on conditioning on incident (E, θ, PID), energy conservation, and high-level classifier metrics for detecting surrogate mismodeling.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of Gluckstern momentum-resolution formulas, covariance-matrix track smearing ( TrackCovariance ), particle-flow emulation in Delphes , and mathematical formulations of conditional GAN, normalizing-flow, and denoising-diffusion loss functions for sparse 3D calorimeter voxel grids.

Stage 2: Run DelphesPythia8_EDM4HEP ( k4SimDelphes ) using delphes_card_IDEA.tcl on e + e − → ZH → µ + µ − bb̄ and compare recoil-mass resolution against ddsim full simulation.

lectures.abstract: Energy depositions ( SimTrackerHit , SimCalorimeterHit ) from Geant4 must be transformed into realistic electronic signals incorporating charge drift, diffusion, Lorentz-angle deflection, front-end shaping, ADC/TDC quantization, dead-time, and electronic noise. This lecture develops microscopic semiconductor digitization (Ramo–Shockley induced currents, Allpix 2 ) alongside fast parametric digitizers used in Key4hep. We then address machine-detector interface (MDI) beam-induced backgrounds (BIB) at FCC-ee: beamstrahlung photons simulated with GUINEA-PIG++ , incoherent e + e − pair creation (Bethe–Heitler, Breit–Wheeler, Landau–Lifshitz), synchrotron radiation, and radiative Bhabha losses. Students implement bunch-crossing time-window overlay pipelines and quantify vertex-detector hit occupancies and tracking degradation.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of charge-cloud drift-diffusion and Lorentz angle tan θ L = µ H B, Ramo–Shockley weighting potentials, equivalent noise charge (ENC) and zero-suppression thresholds, Poisson bunch-crossing overlay statistics, and FCC-ee beamstrahlung parameter Υ and incoherent-pair rates across Z, W W , ZH, and tt̄ working points.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Write a Python silicon pixel digitizer (charge deposition → diffusion + Lorentz shift → pixel charge sharing → Gaussian ENC noise + 4-bit ToT quantization) and overlay synthetic Poisson background hits to measure cluster-splitting and occupancy curves. Stage 2: Simulate a monolithic CMOS pixel sensor in Allpix 2 , and run Key4hep/ CLDConfig digitization + background overlay ( Overlay / k4MarlinWrapper ) with GUINEA-PIG++ incoherent e + e − pairs at the FCC-ee Z-pole.
deliverables.problemSet: Derive the optimal zero-suppression threshold balancing fake-hit rate against MIP detection efficiency for a 50 µm silicon sensor with ENC = 150 e − ; calculate vertex-detector barrel occupancy at FCC-ee Z-pole given a 200 MHz/cm 2 incoherent-pair hit rate and 1 µs integration window; evaluate impact-parameter resolution (d 0 ) degradation before and after BIB overlay; exit criterion: simulated pixel cluster-size distribution and occupancy match FCC-ee vertex-detector benchmarks within 15%.

lectures.abstract: Precision collider measurements are ultimately limited by how faithfully Monte Carlo simulations reproduce nature and how rigorously residual modeling uncertainties are quantified. This lecture establishes systematic validation methodologies spanning both physics-generator truth ( Rivet , HEPData comparisons to LEP/LHC unfolded spectra) and detector-transport benchmarks (CALICE granular calorimeter and CMS/ATLAS test-beam comparisons to Geant4 hadronic/EM models). We construct complete modeling systematic budgets—decomposing perturbative scale, PDF, parton-shower, hadronization/tune, color-reconnection, and Geant4 physics-list variations—and formulate principled correlation models and nuisance-parameter prescriptions that avoid double-counting or ad-hoc envelope inflation.

deliverables.lectureNote: Statistical goodness-of-fit metrics for validation (χ 2 /ndf, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Anderson–Darling, pull distributions), decomposition of two-point vs. continuous nuisance variations (eigen-tunes, ME/PS scale weights, FTFP_BERT vs. QGSP_BERT hadronic shower shifts), and case studies from CALICE SiW-ECAL/AHCAL/DHCAL test beams and LEP Z-pole event shapes. 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Implement a Python validation harness computing bin-by-bin pull tables, χ covariance tests, and systematic covariance matrices from multi-weight histogram ensembles. Stage 2: Execute an automated Rivet 3/4 validation suite comparing Pythia 8.3 (nominal + shower/tune variations) and Sherpa 3 against HEPData LEP Z → q q̄ measurements, paired with a ddsim hadronic-shower comparison ( FTFP_BERT vs. QGSP_ BERT vs. FTFP_BERT_EMZ ) for 10–80 GeV π ± in CLD HCAL.
deliverables.problemSet: Analyze CALICE test-beam vs. Geant4 longitudinal/radial pion shower discrepancies and derive an effective hadronic energy-scale systematic; build a full modeling uncertainty breakdown (PDF, µ R /µ F , ISR/FSR α s , hadronization, Geant4 physics list) for e + e − → ZH → ν ν̄bb̄ jet mass; distinguish statistical MC fluctuations from true model differences via Barlow–Beeston / bootstrap tests; exit criterion: complete systematic covariance matrix and validation report passing all closure checks.

parts.abstract: Part 9 establishes the mathematical, algorithmic, and software foundations of collider event reconstruction, tracing the complete transformation from digitized detector hits to calibrated four-momenta and global event observables. Spanning classical estimation theory and modern deep learning, the module develops charged-particle tracking (helix kinematics, Kalman filtering, combinatorial pattern recognition, gaseous and silicon trackers), vertex reconstruction, topological and density-based calorimeter clustering, and the Particle Flow (PF) paradigm. Detailed treatments of PandoraPFA, sequential recombination jets, heavy-flavour and jet-origin tagging, lepton/tau/missing-energy reconstruction, software compensation, graph- and transformer-based ML reconstruction, and 4D timing prepare students to engineer and benchmark full-simulation reconstruction chains for FCC-ee (CLD, IDEA) and HL-LHC/FCC-hh detectors.

deliverables.lectureNote: Integrated 14-chapter monograph (~280 pages, natural units c = ℏ = 1 with explicit conversion factors to SI/mm/ns/GeV/T for detector geometry and Lorentz transport) containing first-principles derivations of Kalman filtering, multiple-scattering covariance transport, Gluckstern resolution scaling, PF confusion decomposition, IRC-safe jet metrics, and set-to-set neural losses, paired with worked numerical benchmarks on CLD, IDEA, and CMS-like geometries.
deliverables.lab: Two-stage progressive computational track across all 14 lectures: Stage 1 builds transparent, from-scratch NumPy/PyTorch prototypes on synthetic and toy-detector datasets; Stage 2 migrates each algorithm into production Key4hep/EDM4hep workflows interfacing ACTS, k4Clue, PandoraPFA, FastJet, LCFIPlus, and ONNX/PyTorch ML inference.
deliverables.problemSet: 14 graded problem sets (each combining 2–3 analytical derivations with 1–2 quantitative coding benchmarks) culminating in a capstone end-to-end reconstruction benchmark comparing jet energy resolution (RMS 90 ) and W/Z dijet separation across rule-based and ML-based PF pipelines; exit criterion requires ≥ 80% accuracy on analytical derivations and reproducible benchmark plots within 5% of reference full-simulation targets.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine anchored by Strandlie & Frühwirth (2010), Thomson (2009), Cacciari–Salam–Soyez (2012), and FCC-ee/Key4hep design papers; advanced/optional track covering ACTS GPU/non-linear filtering, Pandora SDK internals, Jet-Origin Identification, MLPF/HGPflow, and 4D LGAD timing TDRs.

Quantify the resolution decomposition of Particle Flow reconstruction and diagnose the confusion term as a function of jet energy, magnetic field, and calorimeter granularity.
Configure, run, and benchmark production reconstruction frameworks (ACTS, PandoraPFA, FastJet, LCFIPlus) inside the Key4hep software stack for CLD and IDEA geometries.

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes the architectural blueprint of modern collider event reconstruction, mapping the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of data transformations from raw digitized sensor hits to calibrated physics objects. Students examine how detector geometry descriptions (DD4hep), conditions databases, and column-oriented event data models (PODIO/EDM4hep) decouple physics algorithms from hardware specifics while enabling thread-safe, concurrent execution in Gaudi-based frameworks such as Key4hep. Emphasis is placed on object provenance, Monte Carlo truth-linking ( MCRecoParticleAssociation ), coordinate-frame conventions, and the architectural contrasts between e + e − Higgs-factory reconstruction (CLD, IDEA, ILD) and high-pileup hadron-collider pipelines (ATLAS, CMS).

deliverables.lectureNote: Formal DAG specification of reconstruction stages (hit digitization → clustering/seeding → track/vertex fitting → calorimeter clustering → PF linking → jet/flavour/MET reconstruction), explicit coordinate and unit conventions (Cartesian (x, y, z) in mm, cylindrical (r, ϕ, z), pseudorapidity η = − ln tan(θ/2), four-momenta in GeV), and memory-layout analysis of PODIO Plain-Old-Data (POD) collections.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python/Awkward-Array script parsing a synthetic event record to construct a minimal hit-to-particle DAG with truth-link matrices and energy-flow closure checks. Stage 2: Running a full Key4hep k4run Gaudi steering workflow on a simulated FCC-ee e + e − → ZH EDM4hep file, inspecting TrackerHit , CalorimeterHit , Track , Cluster , and ReconstructedParticle branches with podio Python bindings. 5
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Derive memory-footprint and cache-locality scaling of Structure-of-Arrays (PODIO) vs. Array-of-Structures event records for N = 10 hits; (2) construct the exact truth-linking adjacency graph for a simulated event with bremsstrahlung and K S 0 decay; (3) write a Key4hep/Python diagnostic verifying four-momentum conservation and acceptance losses across CLD vs. IDEA. Exit criterion: zero dangling references in truth-link graph and energy closure within 1% on ideal truth-matched events.

lectures.title: Charged-Particle Tracking I — Helix Models, the Kalman Filter & Process Noise

dependencies.raw: Prerequisites: Lecture 9.1 (EDM4hep Hits & Coordinates), Part 7 (Multiple Coulomb Scattering & Energy Loss), Part 1 (Linear Algebra). Downstream: Lecture 9.3 (Pattern Recognition, CKF & ACTS), Lecture 9.4 (Vertexing), Lecture 9.10 (GSF for Electrons).

lectures.abstract: This lecture develops the statistical estimation theory of charged-particle track fitting from first principles. Starting from the Lorentz equation of motion in solenoidal magnetic fields, students derive the five-parameter perigee helix representation (d 0 , z 0 , ϕ 0 , tan λ, Ω) and its analytical transport Jacobians. We formulate the discrete Kalman Filter (prediction, filtering, and Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoothing) following Frühwirth (1987) and Billoir (1984), explicitly incorporating multiple Coulomb scattering (Highland–Lynch–Dahl process noise) and Bethe–Bloch/Bethe–Heitler energy loss. The lecture derives the Gluckstern momentum-resolution scaling laws, generalizes to non-Gaussian noise via the Gaussian Sum Filter (GSF) and Deterministic Annealing Filter (DAF), and establishes pull-distribution and χ 2 validation diagnostics.

deliverables.lectureNote: Rigorous derivations of: (i) helix equations with p T [GeV] = 0.299792458 |q|B[T]R[m]; (ii) exact equivalence between global least squares and recursive Kalman filtering; (iii) process-noise covariance Q k from projected scattering angle θ 0 = 13.6 MeV p z x/X 0 [1+0.038 ln(x/X 0 )]; βcp √ (iv) Gluckstern formula σ(p T )/p 2 T ∝ σ rϕ /(BL 2 N + 4) and multiple-scattering floor; (v) GSF mixture-weight update for radiative electron energy loss.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Pure-Python 5-parameter Extended Kalman Filter + smoother on a 10-layer cylindrical silicon tracker with configurable B, layer x/X 0 , and hit resolution σ rϕ ; verify unit-normal pulls and Gluckstern scaling across p T ∈ [0.5, 100] GeV. Stage 2: Execute the ACTS KalmanFitter (and compare against GaussianSumFitter for electrons) on single-muon and single-electron samples inside Key4hep/ACTS.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Prove mathematically that the Kalman smoother yields the exact minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of the full trajectory; (2) derive the 5 × 5 transport Jacobian F k between two concentric cylinders in a uniform field B = B ẑ; (3) numerically compare EKF vs. GSF momentum bias and tail resolution for 20 GeV electrons traversing 0.1 X 0 of silicon. Exit criterion: all five track-parameter pull distributions satisfy |µ| < 0.05 and σ ∈ [0.95, 1.05] with χ 2 /ndf matching theory.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Frühwirth (1987), Strandlie & Frühwirth (2010) Secs. II–IV, Gluckstern (1963), and Lynch & Dahl (1991). Advanced/optional: Blobel’s General Broken Lines (GBL), Non-Linear Kalman Filter in ACTS, and Gaussian Mixture Regression for track fitting.

learningOutcomes: Parameterize a helical trajectory in perigee and curvilinear frames and
convert between curvature Ω = q/R, q/p, and transverse momentum p T with exact sign and unit conventions.
Derive the Kalman prediction, gain matrix, state update, covariance update, and backward smoothing equations and explain their O(N ) complexity advantage over global matrix inversion.
Compute the multiple-scattering process-noise covariance matrix Q k in local detector coordinates from the Highland–Lynch–Dahl formula. Apply the Gluckstern scaling relations to separate
measurement-dominated (∝ p T ) and multiple-scattering-dominated (constant) regimes of σ(p T )/p T .
Explain why single-Gaussian Kalman filtering degrades for electrons experiencing bremsstrahlung and formulate the multi-component Gaussian Sum Filter (GSF) update.
Diagnose covariance miscalibration, material-budget errors, and outlier hits using normalized residual pulls and χ 2 probability distributions.
