lectures.abstract: While Lecture 9.2 assumes hits are already grouped into tracks, real collider events present a combinatorial pattern-recognition challenge across 10 3 –10 5 hits per event. This lecture covers the full track-finding pipeline: triplet seeding, cellular automata, conformal mapping for all-silicon FCC-ee/CLIC trackers, and the Combinatorial Kalman Filter (CKF) with branching, hole handling, and ambiguity resolution. Students study the thread-safe geometry navigation and material-mapping architecture of ACTS, alongside heterogeneous GPU parallelization strategies. The second half addresses continuous gaseous trackers—the IDEA ultra-light stereo drift chamber (left–right ambiguity, dN/dx cluster counting) and the ILD/ALICE Time Projection Chamber (space-charge distortions and low-p T looper reconstruction).

deliverables.lectureNote: Algorithmic complexity analysis of seeding (O(n 3 ) naive vs. spatial-binned triplet search), derivation of the conformal transformation (u, v) = (x, y)/(x 2 + y 2 ) mapping circles through the origin to straight lines, CKF branching tree pruning and shared-hit ambiguity scoring, drift-circle tangent geometry and stereo-angle z-reconstruction, and mirror-rotation parameterization for TPC loopers.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Implement a 2D conformal-mapping + cellular-automaton track finder and a branching CKF in Python on noisy multi-track toy events (with 5% hit inefficiency and 20% background noise hits). Stage 2: Run the ACTS CKF pipeline on the Open Data Detector / CLD geometry in Key4hep, tuning seeding and branching parameters and measuring tracking efficiency, fake rate, and duplicate rate versus p T and η.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Derive how a non-zero transverse impact parameter d 0 perturbs a conformal-space straight line into a parabola and compute the maximum d 0 tolerated by linear cellular-automaton seeding; (2) solve the 2D left–right drift-circle ambiguity for a 4-wire stereo cell; (3) benchmark CKF CPU scaling and efficiency vs. fake rate as a function of maximum branching factor on a dense jet core. Exit criterion: tracking efficiency > 98% for p T > 1 GeV with fake rate < 1% in the CLD benchmark.

Advanced/optional: GPU-based Kalman filtering, heterogeneous CMS pixel tracking, ACTS hyperparameter optimization, and large-TPC looper tracking.

Explain how the Combinatorial Kalman Filter unifies pattern recognition and statistical fitting via χ 2 -gated branching trees. Navigate ACTS architecture: tracking geometry, surface material maps,

lectures.abstract: Precision vertex reconstruction transforms individual track trajectories into spatial maps of hard-scatter interaction points, heavy-flavour decay chains (B → D → X), strange-hadron decays (K S 0 , Λ), photon conversions, and long-lived BSM signatures. This lecture derives the Kalman vertex filter and smoother (with and without beamspot constraints), kinematic mass-constrained V 0 fits, and robust adaptive multi-vertex fitters (AMVF) employing deterministic annealing to suppress outlier tracks and pileup merging. Students analyze the exact definitions of signed 2D and 3D impact parameters (d 0 , z 0 ) and their significances (S d 0 , S z 0 ), and dissect the build-up/tear-down secondary vertexing architecture of LCFIPlus and ATLAS/CMS heavy-flavour pipelines.

lectures.abstract: Reconstructing localized energy depositions from millions of noisy, granular calorimeter cells is the gateway to both electromagnetic precision and hadronic Particle Flow. This lecture contrasts fixed-window/sliding-window clustering with noise-adaptive 3D topological clustering (ATLAS 4-2-0 topo-clusters), density-peak parallel clustering (CMS HGCAL CLUE and Key4hep k4Clue ), and tree/branch-based shower clustering (Arbor). Students derive local-maximum splitting algorithms for overlapping π 0 → γγ and hadron showers, formulate principal-component and longitudinal/lateral shower-shape moments (R 90 , depth, λ center , f EM ), and analyze noise-suppression trade-offs, zero-suppression bias, and cell-granularity scaling (R M vs. cell pitch).

deliverables.lectureNote: Mathematical formulation of 4-2-0 topological clustering thresholds (|E cell |/σ noise > S, N, P ), CLUE local density ρ i = j E j Θ(d c − d ij ) and nearest-higher-density distance δ i with O(N ) fixed-grid complexity, iterative Gaussian-mixture / shared-cell splitting weights, and complete taxonomy of 3D shower-shape moments (centroid, inertia tensor eigenvalues, longitudinal shower-max t max ).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python implementation of both 3D topological clustering (4-2-0 with local-maxima splitting) and 2D/3D CLUE on synthetic overlapping EM and hadronic showers with electronic noise. Stage 2: Execute k4Clue inside Key4hep on simulated FCC-ee CLD SiW-ECAL single-photon and π 0 → γγ events, quantifying cluster-splitting efficiency versus opening angle ∆θ γγ . 0
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Compute the minimum π energy at which the two decay photons merge within one Molière radius R M in a tungsten-silicon ECAL at R ECAL = 2.15 m; (2) derive the energy bias induced by one-sided vs. two-sided noise thresholds in topological clustering; (3) evaluate CLUE parameter sensitivity (d c , ρ c , δ c ) on cluster purity and energy containment. Exit criterion: π 0 two-photon splitting efficiency > 85% at E π 0 = 20 GeV and linear runtime scaling verified up to 10 5 hits.

lectures.abstract: Particle Flow (PF) revolutionized collider jet reconstruction by replacing purely calorimetric summation with individual particle reconstruction across all subdetectors. Starting from the typical jet energy partition—approximately 60% charged hadrons, 30% photons, and 10% long-lived neutral hadrons—this lecture derives the exact PF jet energy resolution budget, separating intrinsic tracking, ECAL, and HCAL stochastic terms from the dominant algorithmic bottleneck: the confusion term σ conf . Students analyze the three physical mechanisms of confusion (photon merging, neutral-hadron merging, and charged-hadron fragment splitting), derive the figure-of-merit scaling with magnetic field B, inner ECAL radius R, and granularity, and contrast historical ALEPH Energy Flow with CMS, ATLAS, and future FCC-ee PF designs.

deliverables.lectureNote: Complete derivation of the PF jet variance decomposition σ E thresh + σ conf , quantitative evaluation of why γ h 0 trk 3–4% jet energy resolution is required for W/Z → q q̄ separation (∆m ZW /m̄ ≈ 12%), and scaling laws for charged-neutral spatial separation ∆r ∝ BR 2 /p T inside a jet.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Toy PF simulator in Python taking truth jets (E j ∈ [45, 250] GeV), projecting tracks and neutral showers onto an ECAL/HCAL cylinder with configurable (B, R, cell size), and implementing an oracle ("perfect PFA") vs. nearest-neighbor linking to directly measure σ conf (E j ). Stage 2: √ Run truth-assisted vs. full PF reconstruction in Key4hep/CLD on e + e − → Z(→ q q̄) at s = 91.2, 240, 365 GeV, decomposing RMS 90 (E j )/E j into intrinsic and confusion components. √ √
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Derive the ideal "perfect PFA" jet energy resolution for a 100 GeV jet given σ ECAL /E = 16%/ E, σ HCAL /E = 50%/ E, and negligible tracking error; (2) calculate the crossover energy where σ conf overtakes intrinsic HCAL resolution; (3) quantify how placing the solenoid coil inside vs. outside the calorimeter degrades σ conf and low-energy photon containment. Exit criterion: numerical reproduction of the Thomson (2009) confusion-term energy scaling curve within 10%.

purely calorimetric reconstruction from the 60%/30%/10% particle-species energy budget.

Categorize and quantify the distinct modes of PF confusion: track-cluster mis-association, charged-shower fragment splitting (fake neutrals), and neutral-shower absorption into charged clusters. Relate detector engineering parameters (B-field, ECAL radius R, R M ,
transverse/longitudinal segmentation, coil placement) to PF pattern-recognition performance.
Contrast track-subtraction PF (ATLAS) with global block-linking PF (CMS) and high-granularity imaging PF (PandoraPFA at ILC/CLIC/FCC-ee).
Design an "oracle/perfect PFA" study to isolate hardware limits from algorithmic confusion in simulation.

lectures.abstract: PandoraPFA is the canonical rule-based Particle Flow framework for high-granularity imaging calorimeters at ILC, CLIC, and FCC-ee (CLD). This lecture dissects the software engineering and physics logic of the Pandora SDK and its Linear Collider ( LCContent ) algorithm chain: isolated-hit filtering, cone-based forward clustering designed to err on the side of splitting, topological cluster-merging rules (track-segment, mip-stub, neutral- fragment, photon-recovery), track-cluster association, and the hallmark statistical reclustering loop driven by track–cluster energy compatibility 0 /neutron leakage, back-scattering, and split χ = (E clus − p trk )/σ E . Students learn to diagnose failure modes—high-energy jet-core saturation, K L charged fragments—and profile XML steering parameters.

deliverables.lectureNote: Architectural walkthrough of Pandora SDK ( PandoraManager , named object lists, client application DDMarlinPandora / k4Pandora , persistency .pndr files), exact decision criteria for cone clustering and topological association algorithms, mathematical formulation of the χ-driven reclustering figure of merit, and systematic failure-mode atlas with visual event-display diagnostics.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python prototype of a two-stage "split-first + χ-guided reclustering" PF engine on synthetic overlapping charged/neutral showers, demonstrating how varying the clustering cone angle resolves merged showers when E clus −p trk > 3σ E . Stage 2: Configure and execute PandoraPFA inside Key4hep on CLD Z → q q̄ samples, modifying XML steering parameters (cone angle, topological merge thresholds, reclustering triggers) and inspecting Pandora monitoring trees and event displays.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Derive the statistical test χ = (E clus − p trk )/σ(E clus ) and determine optimal split/merge trigger thresholds balancing fake neutrals against absorbed photons; (2) perform a controlled ablation study in Key4hep/PandoraPFA disabling (a) topological merging, (b) statistical reclustering, and (c) fragment removal, quantifying the impact on RMS 90 (E j )/E j at E j = 45, 125, 250 GeV; (3) identify and classify the top 3 confusion failure modes in E j = 250 GeV jets. Exit criterion: quantitative ablation table and verified XML steering patch improving RMS 90 or matching CLD baseline within 2%.

clustering parameters when track momentum and cluster energy are incompatible (|χ| > χ cut ).

lectures.abstract: Jets bridge partonic QCD calculations and experimental particle-flow collections. This lecture presents the theoretical and algorithmic foundations of infrared- and collinear-safe (IRC-safe) sequential recombination algorithms: the generalized k t , Cambridge/Aachen, and anti-k t metrics (p = +1, 0, −1) for hadron colliders, alongside exclusive e + e − algorithms—Durham (e + e − k t ), generalized e + e − k t , and the beam-background-resilient Valencia (VLC) algorithm. Students derive jet areas, back-reaction suppression, and N -subjettiness (τ N ) / Soft Drop (z cut , β) grooming for boosted W/Z/H/t topologies, and master factorized Jet Energy Scale (JES) and Jet Energy Resolution (JER) calibration chains (MC truth response, γ + jet / Z + jet / dijet in-situ balance).

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact distance metrics for longitudinally invariant (d ij = min(p T i , p T j )∆R ij ij i j = 2 min(E i 2β , E j 2β )(1 − cos θ ij )/R 2 , d VLC = E i 2β sin 2γ θ i ) clustering; IRC safety proofs; Soft Drop declustering condition cos θ ij ), d VLC ij iB min(p T 1 , p T 2 )/(p T 1 + p T 2 ) > z cut (∆R 12 /R 0 ) β ; JES/JER factorized calibration equations. 3
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python implementation of O(N ) sequential recombination supporting anti-k t , Durham, and Valencia metrics, verified against analytic 3-parton test cases and IRC-safety perturbations. Stage 2: Production FastJet (via C++/Python fastjet and Key4hep FCCAnalyses ) clustering on FCC-ee e + e − → ZH → q q̄bb̄ (exclusive N = 4 Durham vs. VLC) and LHC boosted W/t samples (anti-k t R = 1.0 + Soft Drop + τ 21 , τ 32 ), deriving MC JES/JER curves.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Prove analytically that anti-k t produces conical hard jets with zero area anomalous dimension while iterative cones with split– merge fail collinear safety at NNLO; (2) compare Durham vs. Valencia (R, β, γ) invariant-mass resolution on 4-jet W W/ZZ events with overlaid γγ → hadrons background; (3) compute Soft Drop groomed mass and τ 2 /τ 1 ROC curves for boosted W vs. QCD jets. Exit criterion: exact constituent agreement (100%) between Stage 1 prototype and FastJet on 10 3 test events, plus validated JES closure within 0.5%.

lectures.abstract: Identifying the initiating parton of a hadronic jet is decisive for Higgs-factory measurements (H → bb̄, cc̄, ss̄, gg) and electroweak asymmetries. This lecture traces the evolution from classical likelihood-ratio and BDT taggers (LCFIPlus, CSV) built on impact-parameter significances, secondary-vertex flight distances, and corrected vertex masses to modern deep architectures treating jets as unordered particle clouds: DeepJet, ParticleNet (Dynamic Graph CNN / EdgeConv), and Particle Transformer (ParT) with pairwise Lorentz-invariant interaction matrices. We culminate with 11-class Jet- ¯ g), demonstrating how charged-hadron PID (dN/dx, ToF) and jet-charge weighting unlock s-tagging and Origin Identification (b, b̄, c, c̄, s, s̄, u, ū, d, d, quark/antiquark separation at FCC-ee.

deliverables.lectureNote: Physics of b/c/s/g fragmentation (cτ B ≈ 450 µm, cτ D ≈ 120–300 µm, leading K ± /K S 0 in s-jets, Casimir colour factor C /C = 9/4 A F for gluon multiplicity), mathematical formulation of LCFIPlus BDT inputs, EdgeConv message passing in ParticleNet, pairwise interaction bias U ij = (ln ∆, ln k T , ln z, ln m 2 ) in ParT, and 11-class confusion-matrix and ROC/mis-ID evaluation metrics.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: PyTorch implementation of a lightweight ParticleNet (EdgeConv) and Particle Transformer block trained on particle-cloud features (p T , ∆η, ∆ϕ, d 0 , z 0 , S d 0 , S z 0 , PID) from simulated Z → q q̄ jets. Stage 2: Run LCFIPlus and the FCC-ee ONNX/Weaver ParT flavour tagger inside Key4hep/FCCAnalyses on IDEA/CLD ZH(H → jj) samples, comparing b-, c-, and s-tagging efficiencies with and without K/π PID. κ P
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Compute the expected jet-charge flip rate Q κ = i q i (p T i /p T,jet ) as a function of κ ∈ [0.1, 1.0] for b vs. u jets; (2) perform a feature-ablation study quantifying the drop in s-tagging rejection when removing dN/dx and ToF PID from the FCC-ee tagger; (3) derive the calibration scale-factor propagation from Z-pole tag-and-probe data to H → cc̄ branching-ratio uncertainty. Exit criterion: trained Stage 1 tagger achieves > 80% b-efficiency at < 1% light-jet mistag and reproduces the PID ablation trend of Bedeschi et al. (2022).

lectures.abstract: Rigorous, reproducible performance methodology is essential to prevent biased comparisons between detector concepts or reconstruction algorithms. This lecture formalizes truth-to-reconstructed matching protocols across tracks (hit-share purity), calorimeter clusters (energy-weighted truth links), PF candidates (Hungarian/bipartite matching), and jets (∆R matching with neutrino treatment). Students derive robust, non-Gaussian resolution estimators—RMS 90 (the standard ILC/CLIC/FCC-ee jet-resolution metric), interquartile range (IQR), and double-sided Crystal Ball fits—and learn to separate efficiency, fake rate, duplicate rate, and response linearity. The lecture concludes with canonical FCC-ee/ILC physics benchmarks (W/Z → jj separation, ZH recoil mass, H → µ + µ − ) and full-simulation vs. Delphes fast-simulation validation.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact mathematical definitions of RMS 90 (smallest interval containing 90% of events, with conversion factor RMS 90 ≈ 0.789 σ for a pure Gaussian), Double-Sided Crystal Ball (DSCB) PDF, bipartite Hungarian matching cost functions for set-to-set PF evaluation, effi- ciency/fake/duplicate definitions with Clopper–Pearson uncertainties, and standardized FCC-ee detector benchmark tables (CLD vs. IDEA vs. ILD).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python statistical validation suite implementing RMS 90 , IQR, DSCB maximum-likelihood fitting, and Hungarian truth-matching on synthetic heavy-tailed response distributions, demonstrating how outlier tails distort standard RMS vs. RMS √ 90 . Stage 2: Build an automated Key4hep benchmark dashboard evaluating CLD full simulation vs. Delphes fast simulation on Z → q q̄ (uds) at s = 91.2, 240, 365 GeV and W W/ZZ dijet mass separation.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Prove analytically that for a unit Gaussian, the central 90% truncated RMS equals 0.789, and compute the bias of RMS 90 under a 5% Gaussian tail contamination of width 4σ; (2) design a truth-matching protocol for Z → bb̄ jets that properly accounts for semileptonic neutrino energy loss; (3) audit a fast-simulation (Delphes) card against full simulation (Key4hep/CLD) and identify three kinematic regimes where parametric smearing breaks down. Exit criterion: reproducible benchmark report with Clopper–Pearson error bars and RMS 90 matching published CLD/ILD values within 3%.

lectures.abstract: Non-compensating calorimeters (e/h > 1) suffer from invisible nuclear binding-energy losses and event-by-event fluctuations in the electromagnetic shower fraction f em , degrading single-hadron energy resolution and biasing PF track–cluster energy matching. This lecture derives the complete calibration hierarchy: MIP-scale inter-calibration, electromagnetic scale anchoring (Z → e + e − , π 0 → γγ), hadronic scale calibration, and local/global software compensation (SC) that reweights individual calorimeter cells by local energy density ρ i to restore effective e/h ≈ 1. Students examine how integrating SC directly inside PandoraPFA improves both neutral-hadron resolution (by ∼ 13–26%) and reclustering accuracy, alongside dual-readout (S, C) compensation and in-situ LHC E/p single-hadron tuning.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivation of the e/h non-compensation response R π (E) = R e [f em (E) + (1 − f em (E))(h/e)], local software-compensation energy estimator E SC = bins k ω k (E raw ) i∈k E i with polynomial weight parameterization ω k (E) = p 1,k + p 2,k E + p 3,k E 2 , dual-readout analytical P P compensation E = (S − χC)/(1 − χ) where χ = (1 − (h/e) S )/(1 − (h/e) C ), and CMS/ATLAS E/p isolated-hadron calibration methodology.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Python optimization of local and global software-compensation weights ω k (E) via constrained least-squares minimization on simulated 0 /π ± shower hit-energy-density histograms, quantifying linearity and σ /E improvement from 10 to 100 GeV. Stage 2: Extract EM, single-K L E hadronic, and software-compensation calibration constants for a Key4hep/CLD calorimeter geometry and inject them into PandoraPFA , comparing single-particle and dijet RMS 90 before and after SC.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Derive the constant term induced by e/h ̸ = 1 and f em fluctuations in a non-compensating Fe/scintillator HCAL; (2) derive the exact dual-readout energy estimator and propagate scintillation/Cherenkov photostatistics into σ E /E; (3) quantify how mis-calibrating the hadronic scale by ±5% biases PandoraPFA’s χ-based reclustering and increases confusion. Exit criterion: Stage 1 SC reduces single-hadron stochastic term by ≥ 15% with linearity within ±3% over 10–90 GeV.

lectures.abstract: Rule-based Particle Flow relies on hundreds of hand-tuned heuristics that scale poorly on heterogeneous GPUs and struggle in dense, high-granularity HL-LHC and FCC environments. This lecture formulates Particle Flow as an end-to-end, permutation-equivariant set-to-set learning problem over irregular detector geometries. Students derive three foundational paradigms: (1) distance-weighted graph networks (GravNet/GarNet) paired with Object Condensation (Kieseler 2020), which learns attractive/repulsive physics potentials in latent space to condense arbitrary numbers of particles without fixed grids; (2) Machine-Learned Particle Flow (MLPF, Pata et al.), using scalable GNNs and linear-complexity transformers to map tracks and clusters directly to particles in a single pass; and (3) Hypergraph Particle Flow (HGPflow), representing particles as hyperedges over detector nodes for physically interpretable energy-conserving reconstruction.

deliverables.lectureNote: Mathematical derivations of: (i) GravNet learned spatial projection S i with Gaussian distance-weighted message passing V (d ij ) = exp(−d 2 ij ); (ii) Object Condensation loss L OC = L V + L β + L p with charge q i = arctanh 2 β i + q min and attractive/repulsive hinge potentials; (iii) MLPF multi-task classification + regression objective and O(N log N ) locality-sensitive hashing / kernel attention scaling; (iv) HGPflow incidence-matrix learning I ∈ [0, 1] N ×K and proxy-guided property regression.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: PyTorch Geometric implementation of an Object Condensation GravNet model on a synthetic 2D/3D multi-shower calorimeter dataset, visualizing latent-space condensation points β i and cluster separation. Stage 2: Train and evaluate a compact MLPF model on the public FCC-ee CLD/Delphes or CMS-like PF dataset, export to ONNX, and benchmark GPU inference latency and jet RMS 90 against rule-based PandoraPFA in Key4hep.
deliverables.problemSet: (1) Prove that Object Condensation is invariant to input-node permutation and independent of the maximum number of target particles K; (2) compare the asymptotic memory and FLOP complexity of full Transformer self-attention (O(N 2 )) vs. GravNet k-NN and kernel-based attention (O(N )) for N = 10 4 calorimeter hits; (3) test out-of-distribution generalization of an MLPF model trained on tt̄ or Z → q q̄ when evaluated on high-p T boosted jets or displaced decays. Exit criterion: Stage 1 Object Condensation achieves > 90% particle-finding efficiency on overlapping 3-shower events; Stage 2 MLPF runs end-to-end ONNX inference with validated jet response linearity within 2%.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Kieseler (2020) Object Condensation, Qasim et al. (2019) GravNet/GarNet, Pata et al. (2021, 2024) MLPF, and Di Bello et al. (2023) HGPflow. Advanced/optional: Extending HGPflow to full collider events (2024), CMS production MLPF (2025), fine-tuning MLPF across detectors (2025), and GNNs in Particle Physics review (2022).

Explain the MLPF architecture, target-assignment strategy (matching target particles to primary input elements), and linear-scaling attention mechanisms enabling GPU deployment.
Contrast Object Condensation, MLPF, and HGPflow (hypergraph incidence-matrix learning) in terms of physical interpretability, energy conservation, and computational throughput.

lectures.abstract: Adding 10–50 ps time-stamping to spatial hit measurements transforms 3D detector reconstruction into 4D spacetime reconstruction. This lecture develops the detector physics and reconstruction algorithms enabled by Ultra-Fast Silicon Detectors (LGADs, AC-LGADs) and precision timing layers (CMS MTD, ATLAS HGTD, and FCC-ee silicon wrappers/calorimeters). Students derive the 4D Kalman filter and 4D Deterministic Annealing vertexing that slice HL-LHC (⟨µ⟩ ≈ 200) and FCC-hh (⟨µ⟩ ≈ 1000) luminous regions in (z, t) to reduce effective pileup density by a factor of 4–6. At e + e − Higgs factories, we formulate Time-of-Flight (ToF) particle identification (π/K/p separation up to several GeV) and its integration with cluster counting 0 /n) timing inside Particle Flow. Stage 2: Run the FCC-ee IDEA/CLD Time-of-Flight and cluster-counting PID module in Key4hep/Delphes ( TimeOfFlight + ClusterCounting ), measuring the combined > 3σ K/π separation reach and its downstream impact on s-jet tagging.

parts.abstract: Part 10 trains graduate researchers to engineer, operate, and contribute to production high-energy physics software ecosystems centered on the Key4hep turnkey stack and modern scientific Python. Spanning ten lectures, the module dissects Key4hep Spack/CVMFS releases, the EDM4hep / podio event data model, Gaudi multithreaded algorithm scheduling, k4geo detector plugins, and full production workflows integrating k4SimGeant4 , CLDConfig , and Marlin / LCIO legacy bridges. The second half masters high-throughput columnar analysis ( FCCAnalyses / RDataFrame and the Scikit-HEP ecosystem), distributed grid computing ( HTCondor , EOS , CVMFS , DIRAC ), reproducible workflow automation ( Snakemake , REANA , CI/CD), and open-source HEP software maintainership.

lectures.abstract: Future collider studies (FCC, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, EIC, Muon Collider) share a unified turnkey software stack— Key4hep —designed to eliminate duplicated framework engineering across experiments. This lecture dissects the modular Key4hep architecture: common core ( Gaudi , k4FWCore , EDM4hep , podio , DD4hep ), simulation/reconstruction packages ( k4Gen , k4geo , k4SimDelphes , k4SimGeant4 , k4MarlinWrapper ), and analysis tools ( FCCAnalyses ). We analyze how Spack resolves combinatorial C++/Python dependency graphs, manages compiler/ABI compatibility, and deploys pinned releases and nightlies onto /cvmfs/sw.hsf.org/key4hep and /cvmfs/sw-nightlies.hsf.org/key4hep , alongside local overlay development workflows with CMake .

deliverables.lectureNote: Architectural blueprint of Key4hep , Spack concretizer mechanics ( spack.yaml / spack.lock ), environment-variable layering ( CMAKE_ PREFIX_PATH , LD_LIBRARY_PATH , PYTHONPATH ), release vs. nightly lifecycle policies, and troubleshooting ABI/RPATH mismatches.

Stage 2: Source a pinned Key4hep CVMFS release (or Apptainer container), inspect active package versions with k4_local_repo / spack find , and build a local CMake overlay package against the upstream stack without rebuilding dependencies.

lectures.abstract: The event data model (EDM) defines the common language across generation, simulation, reconstruction, and physics analysis. This lecture examines EDM4hep and its underlying code-generation toolkit podio . We analyze podio ’s three-layer architecture—Plain Old Data (POD) structs for contiguous cache-friendly storage, lightweight handle classes enforcing const-correctness, and type-safe collections supporting OneToOneRelations , OneToManyRelations , and VectorMembers without raw pointers. We study the YAML-driven code generation of edm4hep.yaml , the thread-safe podio::Frame container decoupling in-memory access from I/O, schema evolution and embedded metadata ( podio-dump ), and the transition from ROOT TTree to RNTuple backends.

deliverables.lectureNote: Memory-layout analysis of POD arrays vs. polymorphic object graphs, podio three-layer handle/object/collection design, ObjectID (collectionID, index) relational indexing, podio::Frame lifecycle, schema-evolution mechanics, and TTree vs. RNTuple serialization benchmarks.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Implement a minimal Python YAML-to-C++/Python POD-collection generator supporting flat arrays and integer-indexed one-to-many relations. Stage 2: Author a custom podio YAML extension defining a DisplacedVertex datatype, generate C++ bindings with podio_generate_ datamodel , write/read EDM4hep MCParticle / ReconstructedParticle / MCRecoParticleAssociation collections via podio::Frame in C++ and Python, and inspect schemas with podio-dump .
deliverables.problemSet: Compare L1/L2 cache-miss rates and serialization throughput of a pointer-based tree vs. podio POD collections; traverse an EDM4hep MCParticle decay graph and MCRecoParticleAssociation links without dangling references; benchmark ROOT TTree vs. RNTuple file size and read speed on 10,000 simulated e + e − → ZH events; exit criterion: custom podio EDM compiles, passes round-trip I/O equality checks, and demonstrates zero memory leaks under AddressSanitizer.

lectures.abstract: Modern collider data-processing frameworks must coordinate hundreds of reconstruction and simulation modules across multi-core CPUs while guarantee- ing deterministic, thread-safe execution. This lecture presents the Gaudi architecture adopted by LHCb, ATLAS ( Athena ), and Key4hep ( k4FWCore ). We examine core abstractions— Algorithm , AlgTool , Service , and the transient Whiteboard —and emphasize the modern Gaudi::Functional paradigm ( Producer , Transformer , Consumer , MultiTransformer ), which enforces immutable inputs, explicit data-flow declarations, and lock-free inter- and intra-event parallelism via AvalancheScheduler . Students master Python steering configuration via Configurables and k4run , IOSvc Frame I/O, and thread-safety diagnostics.

deliverables.lectureNote: Architectural specification of Gaudi component lifecycle ( initialize , execute , finalize ), Gaudi::Functional type signatures, k4FWCore Transformer / Consumer wrappers for EDM4hep , AvalancheScheduler control-flow vs. data-flow DAG resolution, and k4run CLI/Python configuration mechanics.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Build a minimal Python data-flow task scheduler that resolves producer-consumer dependencies into a DAG and executes stateless functional transforms concurrently with concurrent.futures . Stage 2: Implement a k4FWCore C++ Transformer (calorimeter cluster calibration) and Consumer (invariant-mass monitor) operating on EDM4hep collections, configure them in a k4run Python steering file with IOSvc , and benchmark multi-threaded scaling (1, 2, 4, 8 threads).
deliverables.problemSet: Convert a legacy stateful Gaudi::Algorithm with mutable member variables into a thread-safe k4FWCore::Transformer ; detect and resolve a cyclic data-dependency deadlock in an AvalancheScheduler configuration; measure event-throughput scaling and memory-per-thread overhead across thread counts; exit criterion: k4run executes bit-for-bit identical physics histograms at 1 and 4 threads with zero ThreadSanitizer data races.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Gaudi official docs & architecture guide, k4FWCore GitHub & k4run docs, HSF CWP Data Processing Frameworks paper ( arXiv:1812.07861 ); Advanced: Barrand et al. (2001), FunTuple Gaudi functional case study, Gaussino multithreaded simulation paper.

overrides in Python steering files executed with k4run .

lectures.abstract: While Lecture 8.4 focused on the physics of detector geometry and material budgets, this lecture addresses the software engineering of the geometry stack inside Key4hep . We dissect the k4geo repository structure hosting FCC-ee ( CLD , IDEA , ALLEGRO ), ILC ( ILD , SiD ), and CLIC detector models, version-tagging policies ( o2_v07 ), and GeoSvc integration into Gaudi . Students learn to write, register, and test C++ DD4hep detector constructor plugins ( DECLARE_DETELEMENT ), attach reconstruction extensions ( DDRec::LayeredCalorimeterData , ZPlanarData , tracking surfaces), implement custom DDSegmentation classes, and automate geometry regression tests in CI.

deliverables.lectureNote: Engineering guide to DD4hep plugin factories ( PluginService ), XML::Handle_t parsing, DDRec reconstruction-extension structs, k4geo versioning and directory conventions, GeoSvc service access in Gaudi algorithms, and JSROOT/Phoenix geometry export.

Stage 2: Fork/overlay k4geo , implement a C++ DD4hep detector plugin for a dual-readout or sampling barrel calorimeter attaching DDRec::LayeredCalorimeterData , register it with DECLARE_DETELEMENT , load it via GeoSvc in a k4run algorithm, and verify zero overlaps plus automated CTest regression checks.
deliverables.problemSet: Add a configurable stave tilt angle and cooling-pipe material layer to a silicon tracker plugin while preserving DDRec::ZPlanarData surface normals; write a Gaudi algorithm querying GeoSvc and VolumeManager to map SimCalorimeterHit::getCellID() to global (x, y, z) coordinates; audit IDEA_o2_v01 vs. CLD_o2_v07 compact hierarchies; exit criterion: plugin builds cleanly against Key4hep , passes checkOverlaps and VolumeManager round-trip tests, and exports valid geometry to Phoenix /JSROOT.

lectures.abstract: Bridging decades of mature linear-collider reconstruction ( iLCSoft / Marlin / PandoraPFA ) with modern Key4hep production pipelines requires in- teroperable orchestration. This lecture examines end-to-end full-simulation and reconstruction production workflows across ddsim , k4SimGeant4 (Gaudi-embedded Geant4), and CLDConfig . We dissect k4MarlinWrapper and the in-memory EDM4hep ↔ LCIO converters ( EDM4hep2LcioTool , Lcio2EDM4hepTool ), showing how legacy Marlin XML processors (conformal tracking, DDMarlinPandora particle flow) execute seamlessly inside k4run Python steering scripts without intermediate disk serialization. We also review campaign configuration management, random-seed provenance, and ongoing native-Gaudi migration roadmaps.

deliverables.lectureNote: End-to-end production architecture diagrams comparing standalone ddsim + k4run vs. k4SimGeant4 , exact mapping tables be- tween LCIO and EDM4hep classes/relations, k4MarlinWrapper XML-to-Python translation ( convertMarlinSteeringToGaudi.py ), and CLDConfig production steering reference.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Write a Python steering-file linter and provenance tracker that validates RNG seeds, input/output collection names, and schema consistency across a multi-step √ simulation-reconstruction chain. Stage 2: Execute the complete CLDConfig full-simulation and reconstruction chain on e + e − → Z → q q̄ ( s = 91.2 GeV): ddsim → CLDReconstruction.py via k4run invoking k4MarlinWrapper ( ConformalTracking , DDMarlinPandora ), verifying EDM4hep PandoraPFOs output and comparing against a k4SimGeant4 Gaudi-native job.
deliverables.problemSet: Trace a SimTrackerHit through EDM4hep → LCIO → Marlin digitizer → EDM4hep TrackerHitPlane and verify relation-index integrity; measure CPU and memory overhead introduced by EDM4hep ↔ LCIO conversion; migrate a simple Marlin processor’s steering XML to k4run Python and validate output equivalence; exit criterion: full CLDConfig pipeline produces reconstructed PandoraPFOs with Z-boson invariant mass peak within 1 GeV of m Z and zero dropped truth links.

lectures.abstract: Analyzing tens of millions of simulated FCC-ee events demands declarative, multi-threaded execution without handwritten C++ event-loop boilerplate. This lecture covers ROOT::RDataFrame and its FCC-specific analysis layer, FCCAnalyses . We examine lazy computation-graph construction ( Define , Filter , Histo1D , Snapshot ), implicit multi-threading ( EnableImplicitMT ), JIT-compiled C++ analyzers ( ROOT::VecOps::RVec ), and custom compiled C++ helpers (vertex fitting, flavor tagging, FastJet clustering). Students master the standard three-stage FCCAnalyses workflow— stage1 (n-tuple skimming and derived columns), histmaker (direct single-pass histogramming with cross-section/luminosity weights), and final (cutflows, stacked plots, and datacard exports)—plus HTCondor batch dispatch.

deliverables.lectureNote: Execution model of RDataFrame lazy DAGs, RVec SIMD-friendly operations, memory-safety rules for EDM4hep podio branches inside RDataFrame , FCCAnalyses stage1/histmaker/final architecture, cross-section normalization ( procDict ), and systematic variation booking ( Vary ).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Prototype a lazy columnar query engine in Python supporting Filter , Define , and single-pass Histo1D fusion over NumPy arrays. Stage √ 2: Build a complete FCCAnalyses pipeline for e + e − → ZH → µ + µ − X at s = 240 GeV implementing analysis_stage1.py , histmaker.py , and analysis_final.py , adding a custom compiled C++ analyzer function for recoil mass m recoil , and running multi-threaded via fccanalysis run .
deliverables.problemSet: Optimize an unoptimized FCCAnalyses script by fusing redundant event loops and replacing Python/JIT bottlenecks with compiled C++ RVec analyzers; implement RDataFrame::Vary to book simultaneous muon-momentum-scale systematic histograms in one event-loop pass; benchmark throughput (events/s) across 1, 4, 8, 16 threads; exit criterion: ≥ 5× speedup from single-pass graph fusion + IMT with identical cutflow yields to 10 −6 .
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: FCCAnalyses GitHub & official docs, Piparo et al. RDataFrame (2019), ROOT RDataFrame tutorials, FCC Tutorials ; Advanced: Awkward to RDataFrame bridge ( arXiv:2302.09860 ), FastJet integration, RDataFrame distributed execution.

lectures.abstract: The Scikit-HEP ecosystem brings high-performance, array-oriented HEP data analysis directly into the standard scientific Python and machine- learning stack without requiring a monolithic ROOT installation. This lecture systematically covers the five core analysis libraries: Uproot (pure-Python TTree / RNTuple I/O and Dask lazy chunking), Awkward Array (jagged, variable-length nested structures compiled in C++ and Numba ), Vector (array- oriented 2D/3D/4D Lorentz kinematics), hist / boost-histogram (multi-dimensional named-axis C++-backed histograms with weighted variances), and mplhep (publication-grade Matplotlib HEP styling). We also establish zero-copy interoperability with ROOT RDataFrame , FastJet , and PyTorch/JAX tensors.

deliverables.lectureNote: Memory-layout mechanics of jagged arrays (offsets + content buffers), Awkward broadcasting and combinatorial operators ( ak.combinations , ak.cartesian , ak.argmax ), Vector coordinate-system conversions ( pt/eta/phi/mass ↔ px/py/pz/E ), boost-histogram storage accumulators ( Weight() ), and Uproot / Dask out-of-core scaling.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Implement a minimal Python jagged-array class using (offsets, data) NumPy buffers supporting jagged slicing, per-event sums, and pairwise combinations. Stage 2: Re-implement the Lecture 10.6 e + e − → ZH → µ + µ − bb̄ analysis purely in Scikit-HEP : stream EDM4hep ROOT files with uproot.iterate , apply jagged selections and opposite-sign dimuon pairing with awkward + vector , cluster jets with array-oriented fastjet , fill multi-dimensional named histograms in hist , and render publication-style ratio plots in mplhep .
deliverables.problemSet: Benchmark imperative Python event loops vs. Awkward + Vector vectorized code vs. Numba JIT kernels on 10 events; construct a 6 4D hist.Hist (mass, p T , category, systematic) with Weight storage and perform UHI slicing/rebinning; bridge an Awkward Array directly into ROOT::RDataFrame via ak.to_rdataframe and verify numerical identity; exit criterion: vectorized Scikit-HEP pipeline achieves ≥ 50× speedup over Python loops and matches FCCAnalyses histograms bin-for-bin to machine precision.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Rodrigues et al. Scikit-HEP (2019, 2020), Pivarski et al. Awkward Array (2020), HSF Analysis Essentials Scikit-HEP & Histograms modules; Advanced: ak.to_rdataframe (2023), array-oriented FastJet (2022), boost-histogram SciPy paper (2020), mplhep docs.

histograms using hist and boost-histogram .

lectures.abstract: Future collider campaigns—generating 10 11 + simulated events at FCC-ee and petabytes of reconstructed EDM4hep data—require mastering global distributed computing infrastructure. This lecture examines the four pillars of HEP computing: batch workload scheduling with HTCondor (ClassAds, DAGMan, job flavors, retries), high-throughput disk storage with CERN EOS and XRootD streaming/federation (erasure coding, namespace vs. FST separation, S3/POSIX access), global read-only software distribution with CernVM-FS ( CVMFS HTTP caching, Merkle trees, content-addressable storage), and grid-wide pilot-job orchestration with DIRAC (plus Rucio data management). Students learn storage-tiering economics, job-splitting optimization, and failure-mode resilience.

deliverables.lectureNote: Quantitative modeling of I/O vs. CPU bottlenecks, HTCondor matchmaking ClassAd syntax and DAGMan recovery, EOS MGM/FST architecture and Reed–Solomon erasure-coding overhead, CVMFS Stratum-0/1/Squid cache hierarchy, DIRAC pilot-job + Task Queue + File Catalog ( DFC ) design, and FCC-ee computing resource projections.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Write a Python discrete-event simulator modeling a 100-worker batch pool with job-runtime variance, stragglers, and file-staging bandwidth limits to optimize chunk size. Stage 2: Author an HTCondor submit file and DAGMan graph executing a 50-job parallel ddsim + FCCAnalyses campaign reading/writing via XRootD ( root://eospublic.cern.ch/... ) with software sourced from /cvmfs/sw.hsf.org/key4hep , plus a DIRAC job-description ( JDL ) template for grid submission.
deliverables.problemSet: Compute storage footprints and network bandwidth for 10 FCC-ee Z-pole events across GEN , SIM , RECO , and MiniEDM4hep tiers under 9 2× replication vs. (10, 2) erasure coding; debug an HTCondor hold-reason log ( MemoryExceeded , TransferInput failure) and implement automatic max_retries + dynamic memory requests; trace a CVMFS cold-cache vs. warm-cache lookup path; exit criterion: 50-job DAG completes with ≥ 98% efficiency and zero corrupted output ROOT files.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: HTCondor Manual, CernVM-FS 2.12 docs, Peters et al. EOS papers (2020, 2025), Tsaregorodtsev et al. DIRAC (2003, 2019), Ganis et al. FCC-ee offline computing (2021); Advanced: XRootD docs, Barisits et al. Rucio (2019), IRIS-HEP 200 Gbps Analysis Facility challenge (2025).

lectures.abstract: Scientific credibility in decade-long collider programs requires that every figure, cutflow, and statistical limit be bitwise or statistically reproducible long after the original analyst moves on. This lecture formalizes computational reproducibility through four integrated layers: declarative DAG workflow managers ( Snakemake , b2luigi / FLARE ), Linux containerization ( Apptainer /OCI images), continuous integration and deployment ( GitHub Actions , GitLab CI with automated physics-regression tests), and institutional analysis preservation ( REANA , CERN Analysis Preservation , HEPData , CERN Open Data ). Students package a full multi-stage FCC-ee analysis into a self-contained, CI-verified workflow executable identically on a laptop, HTCondor cluster, and REANA Kubernetes backend.

deliverables.lectureNote: Taxonomy of reproducibility (bitwise vs. statistical), Snakemake rule/wildcard/profile/caching semantics, Apptainer SIF immutability and CVMFS bind-mounting, GitHub Actions / GitLab CI matrix testing with container runners, REANA reana.yaml specification, and FAIR data- preservation standards ( HEPData YAML, CAP , CERN Open Data ).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Write a minimal Python content-addressed build cache (SHA-256 hashing of script + parameters + inputs) illustrating deter- ministic memoization. Stage 2: Encapsulate the Lecture 10.6/10.7 e + e − → ZH pipeline into a modular Snakemake Snakefile with pinned Apptainer /Conda environments, add a .github/workflows/ci.yml pipeline running pytest + mini-sample physics-regression checks, and author a reana.yaml manifest submitting the workflow to REANA and exporting a HEPData -compliant YAML table.
deliverables.problemSet: Refactor a brittle Bash-script analysis chain into an idempotent Snakemake DAG with automatic wildcard expansion over sig- nal/background processes and systematic shifts; configure a CI job that flags > 3σ shifts in validation histograms via automated artifact diffs; prepare a CERN Analysis Preservation metadata record and HEPData submission package; exit criterion: clean-room execution of snakemake use-apptainer and reana-client run reproduces all final figures with zero manual intervention.

Snakemake (2021), Snakemake docs, REANA docs ( docs.reana.io ), Apptainer User Guide, HSF CI/CD GitHub/GitLab modules; Advanced: Šimko et al. scalable ATLAS REANA workflows (2024), FLARE FCC-ee workflow orchestrator (2026), HEPData (2017), CERN Analysis Preservation .

lectures.abstract: Modern collider experiments rely on open-source community software stewarded by distributed teams of physicists and research software engineers across Key4hep , Scikit-HEP , ROOT , and HSF . This capstone lecture transitions students from software users to effective contributors and maintainers. We cover collaborative Git workflows (atomic commits, interactive rebase, bisecting regressions), writing reviewable pull requests, conducting constructive technical code reviews, adhering to the C++ Core Guidelines ( clang-format , clang-tidy ) and modern Python packaging ( pyproject.toml , pre-commit , pytest ), semantic versioning, open-source licensing (Apache-2.0, BSD-3, GPLv3), and software citation/credit mechanisms promoted by HSF and IRIS-HEP .

deliverables.lectureNote: Practical handbook of HEP open-source engineering: Git history hygiene, PR anatomy and review checklists, static analysis ( clang-tidy , ruff , mypy ), pyproject.toml wheel distribution, ABI/API semantic versioning, license compatibility (e.g., Apache-2.0 vs. GPLv3 in Key4hep / DD4hep ), and software citation ( CITATION.cff , Zenodo DOIs).
deliverables.lab: Stage 1: Practice a simulated two-person maintainer/contributor workflow on a seeded buggy repository: locate a regression via git bisect , write a minimal failing unit test, implement the fix with clean atomic commits, configure pre-commit hooks, and exchange formal line-by-line PR reviews. Stage 2: Triage a real good_first_issue or documentation/test gap in a community repository ( key4hep-doc , FCCAnalyses , EDM4hep , or Scikit-HEP ), build/test locally against CI standards, and prepare a submission-ready pull request with tests and CITATION.cff /changelog entries.
deliverables.problemSet: Perform a structured code review on a 250-line C++/Python PR containing deliberate memory-safety, numerical-precision, and API-breaking bugs; package a standalone physics utility with pyproject.toml , pytest , and automated GitHub Actions release publishing; evaluate license compatibility when linking a GPLv3 library into an Apache-2.0 package; exit criterion: peer-reviewed PR passes all automated linters, unit tests, and reviewer sign-off with zero unresolved review threads.

parts.abstract: Part 11 synthesizes the theoretical, experimental, and computational pillars of the curriculum into complete, publication-grade physics analyses anchored √ to the FCC-ee programme across all four baseline centre-of-mass energies ( s = 91.2, 161, 240, 365 GeV). Students progress from blinding protocols and control-region architecture to flagship electroweak, Higgs, flavour, top-threshold, and beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) measurements. Every analysis confronts the defining challenge of the FCC-ee era: controlling theoretical, instrumental, and beam-energy systematic uncertainties to the 10 −5 –10 −4 level where statistical errors vanish. The part culminates in global SMEFT interpretations, production statistical workspaces ( pyhf , RooFit, Combine), and FAIR analysis preservation for long-term scientific reuse.

deliverables.lectureNote: Unified 10-chapter graduate monograph (~250 pages) establishing consistent natural-unit conventions (ℏ = c = 1, energies in GeV/MeV, cross sections in pb/fb, luminosities in ab −1 ), master uncertainty-budget templates, analytical derivations of recoil mass, Z/W/top lineshapes, SMEFT operator mappings, and worked end-to-end statistical model specifications.

deliverables.problemSet: Ten progressive problem sets blending analytical derivations (lineshape convolutions, kinematic-fit Lagrange multipliers, SMEFT matching) with quantitative computational benchmarks; exit criterion requires reproducing projected FCC-ee statistical and leading systematic precision targets within 15% across at least four benchmark channels.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine anchored on the FCC Feasibility Study Report Vol. 1, the FCC-ee EPJ+ essays, and the LEP Electroweak Working Group reports; advanced progression branches into multi-loop theory uncertainties, global SMEFT toolboxes, and statistical-model publication standards.

lectures.abstract: This lecture formalizes the methodological architecture of a modern collider physics analysis before touching real collision data. We examine cognitive experimenter bias and establish rigorous blinding protocols—hidden signal boxes, salted offsets, and prescaled unblinding criteria—alongside quantitative selection optimization via asymptotic discovery significance and the Punzi figure of merit. Students learn to design orthogonal signal regions (SR), background-enriched control regions (CR), and independent validation regions (VR), construct data-driven transfer-factor and ABCD estimators, and audit every selection stage with reproducible cut-flows and N-1 distributions. Emphasis is placed on decoupling background normalization from signal contamination and controlling the look-elsewhere effect in multi-region scans.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivations of the Asimov discovery significance Z A = 2[(s + b) ln(1 + s/b) − s] and its background-uncertainty generalization, the √ Punzi figure of merit ϵ S /(a/2 + B), ABCD correlation-factor corrections, and a canonical blinding-review checklist.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a Python cut-flow engine and 2D ABCD/transfer-factor prototype on synthetic signal+background tuples with injected correlation bias; Stage 2 implements a multi-region FCCAnalyses RDataFrame pipeline producing cut-flow tables, N-1 plots, and SR/CR/VR histograms in EDM4hep .
deliverables.problemSet: Three analytical problems (deriving Asimov Z A with Gaussian background uncertainty σ b , proving ABCD bias under linear feature correlation, and evaluating trial factors via Gross–Vitells upcrossings) plus a computational optimization of a 4-cut selection; exit criterion: validated CR-to-VR closure within 1σ prior to unblinding.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Klein & Roodman (2005), Cowan et al. (2011), Punzi (2003); advanced progression: Cranmer (2015), Gross & Vitells (2010), and multichannel Punzi optimization.

learningOutcomes: Distinguish among box-blinding, offset-blinding, and fraction-blinding
strategies and select the appropriate protocol for precision measurements versus searches.
Formulate and optimize selection criteria using Asimov significance and the Punzi figure of merit for unknown signal cross sections.
Construct weighted and unweighted cut-flow tables with exact binomial/Poisson statistical uncertainties and N-1 diagnostic plots. Partition phase space into orthogonal SR, CR, and VR domains with
minimal signal leakage (S/B < 1% in CRs) and verified extrapolation closure.
Derive and implement data-driven background estimation via transfer factors and the ABCD matrix method, quantifying non-closure from variable correlations.
Evaluate global significance and trial factors using the Gross–Vitells upcrossing formalism for multi-bin or multi-mass scans.

lectures.abstract: √ s = 240 GeV, FCC-ee enables a uniquely model-independent measurement of the Higgsstrahlung cross section σ(e + e − → ZH) and the Higgs boson At mass m H via the recoil-mass technique. Because the initial-state four-momentum is known up to beam-energy spread and initial-state radiation (ISR), √ reconstructing only the leptonic decay Z → ℓ + ℓ − (ℓ = e, µ) yields m 2 recoil = s + m 2 ℓℓ − 2 s(E ℓ + + E ℓ − ) independently of how the Higgs decays. We derive the recoil-mass resolution budget—tracking resolution, beam-energy spread (σ √ s ∼ 0.17%), ISR, and final-state radiation (FSR)—and implement photon-recovery algorithms and unbinned/binned signal-plus-background template fits targeting δσ(ZH)/σ(ZH) ∼ 0.5% and δm H ∼ 4 MeV.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact derivation of m recoil and its partial derivatives with respect to s, p ℓ ± , and θ ℓℓ ; analytical modeling of the double-sided Crystal Ball + ISR tail lineshape; worked error propagation comparing IDEA drift-chamber and CLD silicon-tracker momentum resolutions. + −

deliverables.problemSet: Analytical derivation of the optimal s balancing σ(ZH) against instantaneous luminosity; calculation of the recoil-mass bias −4 from a 10 momentum-scale shift; computational study quantifying δm H improvement from FSR recovery; exit criterion: δm H < 6 MeV and δσ(ZH)/σ(ZH) < 0.7% on benchmark 10.8 ab −1 Asimov dataset.

lectures.abstract: FCC-ee delivers two complementary, sub-MeV determinations of the W boson mass m W and total width Γ W . First, a dedicated threshold cross-section √ √ scan of e + e − → W + W − across s ∈ [157, 163] GeV exploits the sharp turn-on sensitivity of σ W W ( s; m W , Γ W ) with resonant-depolarization energy calibration, avoiding final-state hadronic modeling systematics. Second, direct reconstruction of semileptonic (q q̄ℓν) and fully hadronic (q q̄q q̄) final states at 161, 240, and 365 GeV uses constrained kinematic fits enforcing energy-momentum conservation and equal W masses, calibrated in situ with Zγ and ZZ control samples while confronting colour reconnection (CR) and Bose–Einstein correlations (BEC).

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivation of the threshold σ W W ( s) lineshape including Coulomb singularity, finite-width effects, and unstable-particle EFT corrections; optimal luminosity allocation across 2–4 scan points via Fisher information; full Lagrangian-multiplier formulation of 4C and 5C kinematic fits with covariance propagation.

lectures.abstract: Producing ∼ 10 12 Z → bb̄ and ∼ 1.7 × 10 11 Z → τ + τ − pairs in a hermetic, low-background environment with large Lorentz boosts (γβ ∼ 6–25), FCC-ee functions as a premier heavy-flavour and τ factory complementary to LHCb and Belle II. We examine the reconstruction of exclusive b-hadron decays with missing neutrinos (B c + → τ + ν τ , B 0 → K ∗0 τ + τ − ) using vertex-constrained kinematics and hemisphere missing-energy tagging, precision τ lifetime, mass, and branching-fraction tests of lepton-flavour universality (LFU), and ultra-sensitive searches for charged-lepton-flavour violation (cLFV) in Z → eµ, eτ, µτ and τ → 3µ, µγ. Detector requirements on vertex resolution (σ d 0 ∼ 3 µm), K/π separation, and π 0 reconstruction are linked directly to physics reach.

deliverables.lectureNote: Analytical treatment of b-hadron flight-distance resolution, kinematic reconstruction of multi-neutrino τ decays using primary-to- secondary-to-tertiary vertex vectors, LFU ratio observables R τ /µ and R τ /e , and cLFV effective-operator bounds.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a Python vertex-kinematics solver for B 0 → K ∗0 τ + τ − (τ → 3πν) reconstructing the B 0 mass from flight directions and τ decay vertices; Stage 2 runs an FCCAnalyses study of B c + → τ + ν τ or Z → τ µ on Tera-Z EDM4hep samples, evaluating hemisphere missing-energy discrimination and cLFV upper limits in pyhf .
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical derivation of the 3-prong τ momentum reconstruction equations given B and τ decay vertices; sensitivity scaling of LFU ratios with τ lifetime and mass precision; computational study of K/π PID efficiency impact on B s → D s K vs. B d → Dπ; exit criterion: achieving < 2% statistical precision projection on B c + → τ + ν τ yield extraction and 95% CL cLFV branching-ratio upper limit below 10 −9 .

lectures.abstract: √ A threshold scan of e + e − → tt̄ across s ≈ 340–345 GeV provides the cleanest determination of the top-quark mass m t in a theoretically well-defined short-distance scheme (such as the potential-subtracted m PS t or 1S mass), free from the O(Λ QCD ) renormalon ambiguity that limits Monte Carlo mass interpretations at hadron colliders. Because the top width Γ t ≈ 1.4 GeV ≫ Λ QCD acts as an infrared cutoff, the toponium 1S quasi-bound-state enhancement is calculable in non-relativistic QCD (NRQCD) to NNNLO QCD plus NNLO electroweak and non-resonant corrections. We analyze the strong correlation between (m t , Γ t , α s , y t ), the smearing effect of the FCC-ee luminosity spectrum, and multi-parameter lineshape fits targeting δm t ≲ 20–40 MeV including theory uncertainties.

deliverables.lectureNote: Derivation of the Green’s function threshold cross section in pNRQCD, conversion relations between pole, MS, PS, and MSR top-mass schemes, convolution with ISR and Gaussian beam-energy spread, and breakdown of experimental vs. NNNLO scale uncertainties.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a Python threshold-scan simulator using tabulated NNNLO QQbar_threshold cross sections convolved with FCC-ee luminosity spectra to perform 2D (m PS PS + − → tt̄ → bb̄q q̄ℓν and bb̄q q̄q q̄ events in t , α s ) and (m t , Γ t ) profile-likelihood fits; Stage 2 analyzes simulated e e FCCAnalyses to measure signal efficiency and W W/ZZ/HZ background contamination near threshold.
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical calculation of the Bohr radius and binding energy of the tt̄ 1S state; quantitative demonstration of the pole-mass renormalon divergence versus PS-mass perturbative convergence; computational optimization of a 10-point vs. 8-point scan schedule over 200 fb −1 ; exit criterion: reproducing δm stat < 10 MeV and quantifying the α s –m t correlation coefficient ρ. t

lectures.abstract: Individual cross-section and branching-ratio measurements achieve their full discovery power only when synthesized in global combinations. This lecture contrasts the leading-order κ-framework—showing how FCC-ee’s model-independent σ(ZH) removes the LHC Γ H flat direction—with the gauge-invariant, renormalizable Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) in the Warsaw basis. We derive the linear and quadratic dependence of Higgs, diboson (W + W − ), electroweak pole, and top observables on dimension-six Wilson coefficients c i /Λ 2 , examine flat directions and how combining Tera-Z, W W , ZH, tt̄, and HL-LHC datasets lifts degeneracies, and explore indirect sensitivity to the Higgs trilinear self-coupling κ λ via NLO electroweak loops in single-Higgs production.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact mapping from (σ(ZH), σ × B i ) to κ i and Γ H ; derivation of Warsaw-basis dimension-six operators affecting HV V , Hf f ¯ , and Zf f ¯ vertices; Fisher-information and covariance-matrix algebra for global χ 2 fits; discussion of linear (O(Λ −2 )) versus quadratic (O(Λ −4 )) truncation systematics.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 constructs a Python Gaussian global-fit engine combining synthetic HL-LHC + FCC-ee observables in the κ-framework and a 12-operator Warsaw-basis SMEFT subset, diagnosing flat directions via singular value decomposition (SVD); Stage 2 runs a full multi-sector SMEFT fit using the open-source SMEFiT workflow, comparing FCC-ee-only versus HL-LHC+FCC-ee marginalized and individual bounds.
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical proof that κ-scaling cannot capture momentum-dependent HZZ tensor structures (c HW , c HB ); explicit computation of how W + W − angular distributions break the Z-pole–Higgs degeneracy; computational comparison of linear vs. quadratic SMEFT bounds and NLO κ λ extraction; exit criterion: reproducing the FCC-ee δκ Z ≈ 0.17% and marginalized SMEFT scale reach within 10% of benchmark tables.

(2010) Warsaw basis; advanced progression: Brivio & Trott (2019) SMEFT review, Celada et al. (2024) SMEFiT 3.0 , and 2025 Higgs-SMEFT impact updates.

lectures.abstract: Beyond indirect precision probes, FCC-ee offers world-leading direct discovery reach for feebly interacting particles (FIPs) and long-lived particles (LLPs) with masses below m Z or m H /2, where hadron colliders face severe trigger and pileup bottlenecks. Focusing on three flagship signatures—Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs) from Z → νN , Axion-Like Particles (ALPs) from Z → γa or Z → ℓ + ℓ − a, and exotic Higgs decays H → LLP LLP—we derive proper decay-length distributions cτ , geometric acceptance as a function of tracker volume (vertex detector, drift chamber, timing layers), and displaced-vertex (DV), kinked-track, and delayed-photon reconstruction strategies. Special attention is given to non-standard backgrounds: K S 0 /Λ, nuclear material interactions, photon conversions, and cosmic rays.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact derivation of HNL mixing-angle vs. lifetime scaling (cτ ∝ |U | −2 m N ), ALP effective-Lagrangian decay widths (a → γγ, ℓ + ℓ − ), radial geometric acceptance integral P dec (r min , r max ; βγcτ ), and zero-background Feldman–Cousins / CL s limit formulas. 2
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 writes a Python geometric-acceptance and lifetime-reweighting calculator mapping (m N , |U µN | ) to expected HNL yields in an IDEA-like cylindrical tracker; Stage 2 executes a displaced-vertex HNL (N → µq q̄ ′ or µµν) selection in FCCAnalyses , applying material-map vetoes and K S 0 mass rejection, and computes 95% CL exclusion contours in pyhf . 2 2
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical derivation of the lower and upper |U | sensitivity boundaries in the (m N , |U | ) plane; calculation of the time-of-flight delay ∆t for a heavy LLP reaching an outer timing layer; computational lifetime reweighting of a single MC sample across three decades of cτ ; exit criterion: reproducing FCC-ee HNL sensitivity down to |U | 2 ∼ 10 −11 for m N ∈ [10, 80] GeV in the displaced regime.

lectures.abstract: Translating histograms and unbinned spectra into publication-grade confidence intervals requires industrial-strength likelihood tooling and ruthless diagnostic discipline. This lecture dissects the HistFactory probability model—multiplicative normalization systematics, vertical template morphing, and Barlow–Beeston lite Monte Carlo statistical uncertainties—and compares its modern implementations: pyhf (pure-Python with NumPy/JAX/PyTorch autodiff backends and declarative JSON serialization), RooFit / RooStats (unbinned and binned C++ modeling), and CMS Combine (datacard-driven multi-channel combinations). Students master the full suite of pre- and post-fit diagnostics: nuisance-parameter pulls and constraints, parameter-of- interest (POI) impact rankings, goodness-of-fit (saturated model) tests, likelihood profile scans, and signal-injection linearity checks.

deliverables.lectureNote: Exact mathematical specification of the HistFactory likelihood L(µ, θ), piecewise-exponential/polynomial interpolation formulas ( code 04 ), Barlow–Beeston lite analytic profiling, and formal definitions of nuisance pulls ( θ̂ − θ 0 )/∆θ, constraints σ θ̂ /∆θ, and impacts ∆µ̂ ± .
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a minimal HistFactory -style binned Poisson likelihood in JAX with autodiff Hesse/MINOS uncertainties; Stage 2 constructs an identical multi-channel Higgs-recoil workspace in both pyhf (JSON spec) and CMS Combine (datacard), executes Asimov and pseudo-experiment CL s scans, and generates automated pull/impact plots and saturated goodness-of-fit p-values.
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical derivation of the Barlow–Beeston lite per-bin scaling equation; diagnostic case study identifying an over-constrained nuisance parameter (σ θ̂ /∆θ = 0.25) caused by a two-point template-smoothing artifact; computational cross-validation verifying agreement between pyhf (JAX) and Combine to < 10 −4 in −2∆ ln L; exit criterion: passing all 5 standard fit diagnostics (pulls, impacts, GoF, profile scan, signal injection) on a 3-region, 15-nuisance workspace.

(2021) pyhf JOSS paper, CMS Collaboration (2024) COMBINE paper, and Verkerke & Kirkby (2003) RooFit ; advanced progression: Cranmer et al. (2012) HistFactory specification, Feickert et al. (2022) pyhf autodiff/tensors, and Cranmer et al. (2022) publishing statistical models.

learningOutcomes: Write down the complete HistFactory likelihood function
incorporating Poisson counts, normalization systematics, shape morphing, and Barlow–Beeston lite MC statistical nuisances.
Construct, patch, and serialize multi-channel binned statistical models in pyhf JSON and CMS Combine datacard formats.
Build unbinned parametric and composite PDFs (Crystal Ball, RooKeysPdf, simultaneous fits) in RooFit .
Compute asymptotic and toy-based profile-likelihood intervals, discovery p-values, and CL s upper limits, recognizing when asymptotic approximations break down.
Diagnose pathological fits using nuisance-parameter pull/constraint plots, POI impact rankings, correlation matrices, and saturated goodness-of-fit tests.
Validate unbiasedness and coverage of a statistical model via Asimov validation, signal-injection linearity tests, and pruning/symmetrization audits.

lectures.abstract: A physics measurement is scientifically complete only when it survives peer scrutiny and remains reusable decades after the collaboration winds down. This lecture covers the sociology, rigor, and infrastructure of experimental HEP publication: drafting internal analysis notes (ANA/INT notes), navigating editorial-board and collaboration-wide review, presenting complete covariance matrices and fiducial definitions, and adhering to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles. Students learn to deposit numerical tables and full pyhf /HS3 likelihoods in HEPData, encode particle-level unfolded analyses in Rivet for generator tuning and BSM reinterpretation, and containerize end-to-end computational pipelines in REANA so any researcher can re-execute the exact analysis from input tuples to final plots.

deliverables.lectureNote: Structural blueprint of a collaboration internal note and journal paper; taxonomy of HEPData YAML submission schemas and correlation-matrix conventions; architecture of declarative workflow engines (CWL, Yadage, Snakemake) on REANA; checklist for fiducial-region definition and truth-level Rivet preservation.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 validates a mock HEPData submission bundle (YAML tables + pyhf JSON likelihood) using hepdata_validator and writes a particle-level Rivet routine comparing two MC generator tunes; Stage 2 packages an end-to-end FCCAnalyses + pyhf pipeline into a containerized reana.yaml workflow and executes a full clean-room reproduction.
deliverables.problemSet: Editorial-board peer-review exercise auditing a flawed mock internal note (identifying missing correlation matrices, unblinding violations, and ambiguous fiducial cuts); designing a FAIR metadata and DOI archival plan; computational verification that a containerized REANA pipeline reproduces paper numbers to machine precision; exit criterion: validated HEPData YAML + passing Rivet routine + green REANA dry-run.

object definitions, systematic studies, and fit diagnostics for collaboration review.
Define detector-independent fiducial phase spaces to minimize theory-extrapolation uncertainties and maximize long-term reinterpretation value.

Prepare schema-validated HEPData submissions containing cross-section tables, full statistical/systematic covariance matrices, and serialized pyhf /HS3 likelihoods. Implement and validate particle-level Rivet analysis routines linked
directly to HEPData reference records.
Containerize software environments and encode multi-step analysis DAGs in reana.yaml for reproducible cloud execution on REANA.
Apply FAIR data-stewardship principles (persistent DOIs, open licensing, provenance metadata) across code, datasets, and statistical artifacts.

parts.abstract: Part 12 bridges statistical learning theory, modern deep learning, and the domain-specific symmetries and constraints of experimental particle physics. Rather than treating machine learning as a black-box classifier, students approach every architecture through physics-informed inductive biases: likelihood-ratio optimality, permutation and Lorentz equivariance for unordered particle clouds, tractable-density generative surrogates for high- granularity calorimeters, simulation-based inference (SBI) for intractable detector likelihoods, and weakly supervised anomaly detection. The part closes the full lifecycle from PyTorch research prototypes to deterministic, quantized, sub-microsecond hardware deployment via ONNX Runtime and hls4ml on FPGAs, preparing students to build trustworthy ML components for HL-LHC and FCC-ee experiments.

deliverables.lectureNote: Six-chapter graduate monograph (~180 pages) unifying Neyman–Pearson optimality, gradient boosting, deep-learning optimiza- tion, geometric/transformer architectures ( GravNet , ParticleNet , ParT ), generative flows and diffusion ( CaloFlow , CaloScore , CaloClouds ), SBI/CWoLa/CATHODE theory, and fixed-point FPGA quantization mathematics.
deliverables.lab: Progressive two-stage labs: Stage 1 implements core algorithms from scratch in NumPy/PyTorch on compact physics benchmarks (HIGGS, JetClass subsets, CaloChallenge Dataset 1, LHC Olympics); Stage 2 deploys production pipelines using XGBoost , PyTorch + ONNX Runtime , FCCAnalyses inference hooks, and hls4ml HLS synthesis.
deliverables.problemSet: Six analytical + computational problem sets spanning likelihood-ratio calibration proofs, GNN/Transformer complexity analysis, flow Jacobian derivations, SBI score-matching derivations, and fixed-point bit-width budgeting; exit criterion: training, calibrating, exporting to ONNX, and benchmarking an end-to-end HEP ML model meeting strict physics-metric and latency budgets.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Guest, Cranmer & Whiteson (2018), Feickert & Nachman Living Review, Carleo et al. (2019), and Plehn et al. (2022) Modern ML for LHC Physicists; advanced progression: primary research papers for each specialized paradigm (ParT, CaloChallenge, Cranmer–Brehmer–Louppe SBI, hls4ml).

learningOutcomes: Connect binary cross-entropy minimization to the Neyman–Pearson
likelihood ratio and calibrate classifier outputs for downstream statistical inference.
Engineer, train, and systematically debug deep neural networks in PyTorch using modern normalization, scheduling, mixed precision, and reproducibility controls.

Design permutation-invariant and physics-informed architectures (Deep Sets, GravNet, ParticleNet, Particle Transformer) for irregular detector hits and jet flavour tagging. Train and rigorously evaluate generative calorimeter surrogates (GANs,
normalizing flows, diffusion, and flow matching) using classifier-based fidelity tests.
Apply neural ratio estimation (NRE/SBI) and weakly supervised anomaly detection (CWoLa, CATHODE) to high-dimensional EFT measurements and model-agnostic searches.
Export, quantize (PTQ/QAT), and compile neural networks into ONNX Runtime and hls4ml FPGA firmware satisfying strict microsecond latency and DSP/LUT budgets.

lectures.abstract: This lecture grounds supervised machine learning in statistical decision theory tailored for particle physics. Starting from empirical risk minimization, we prove that minimizing binary cross-entropy or mean-squared-error loss recovers a monotonic transformation of the Neyman–Pearson optimal likelihood ratio p(x|S)/p(x|B). We analyze bias–variance trade-offs, k-fold cross-validation without data leakage, and second-order gradient-boosted decision trees ( XGBoost ), which remain formidable baselines for tabular collider observables. Crucially, we confront two HEP-specific failure modes: miscalibrated posterior probabilities—addressed via reliability diagrams, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Platt/temperature scaling, and isotonic regression—and sculpting of resonant mass spectra, mitigated via adversarial pivoting ( Learning to Pivot ) and mass decorrelation.

deliverables.lectureNote: Variational proof of Bayes-optimal classifiers under BCE and MSE losses; derivation of XGBoost second-order Taylor split-gain objective; mathematical definitions of ECE, Brier score, and temperature scaling; formulation of the minimax adversarial-pivot objective for nuisance invariance.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 implements a from-scratch gradient-boosted stump classifier and reliability-diagram calibrator in NumPy on a tabular ZH → µ + µ − bb̄ vs. ZZ dataset; Stage 2 trains XGBoost with stratified 5-fold cross-validation, evaluates SHAP feature importances, applies Platt/isotonic calibration, and quantifies background-mass sculpting. ∗ ∗
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical proof that s (x)/(1 − s (x)) = p(x|S)/p(x|B) for balanced BCE training; derivation of how negative MC event weights destabilize standard BCE loss and how to handle them; computational benchmark comparing uncalibrated vs. temperature-scaled classifier scores in a downstream pyhf fit; exit criterion: ECE < 0.015 and < 2% mass-sculpting distortion across background sidebands.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Chen & Guestrin (2016) XGBoost , Guo et al. (2017) Calibration, and Cranmer, Pavez & Louppe (2015) Calibrated Likelihood Ratios; advanced progression: Baldi, Sadowski & Whiteson (2014) HIGGS benchmark, Louppe, Kagan & Cranmer (2017) Learning to Pivot, and Punzi-loss training.

learningOutcomes: Prove the equivalence between optimal binary classification under
proper scoring rules and the Neyman–Pearson likelihood ratio.
Derive the regularized second-order tree-splitting criterion in XGBoost and tune tree depth, learning rate, and subsampling to prevent overfitting.
Implement leak-free nested/stratified k-fold cross-validation pipelines that respect event weights and physical groupings.
Diagnose probability miscalibration using reliability diagrams, Brier scores, and Expected Calibration Error, and apply temperature scaling or isotonic regression.
Explain how classifier cuts sculpt kinematic spectra (e.g., m recoil or m jj ) and apply adversarial pivoting to enforce decorrelation from nuisance variables.
Evaluate classifier performance using physics-meaningful metrics (ROC/AUC, background rejection 1/ϵ B at fixed ϵ S , and downstream Asimov significance).

lectures.abstract: This lecture establishes production-grade deep-learning engineering in PyTorch for scientific computing. We dissect reverse-mode automatic differentiation ( autograd ), dynamic computation graphs, residual skip connections ( ResNet ), normalization layers ( BatchNorm vs. LayerNorm ), and adaptive stochastic optimization ( Adam and decoupled weight decay AdamW with cosine-annealing schedules). Emphasis is placed on scientific training discipline: deterministic seeding, input-feature standardization for multi-scale collider kinematics (p T , η, ϕ, d 0 , z 0 ), handling variable-length padded batches, mixed-precision ( bf16 / fp16 ) training, and systematic debugging protocols—gradient-norm telemetry, overfit-one-batch sanity checks, and ablation studies—to eliminate silent numerical bugs before scaling to GPU clusters.

deliverables.lectureNote: Mathematical derivation of reverse-mode autodiff (vector-Jacobian products), variance propagation in Kaiming/Xavier initialization, Adam vs. AdamW update equations, and a structured 10-point deep-learning debugging playbook tailored to physics datasets.
deliverables.lab: Stage 1 builds a minimal scalar/tensor reverse-mode autograd engine in NumPy to verify gradients against PyTorch; Stage 2 implements a modular PyTorch residual MLP with AdamW , cosine warmup, torch.amp mixed precision, and TensorBoard/MLflow gradient-norm logging on the HIGGS or FCC-ee tabular dataset.
deliverables.problemSet: Analytical derivation of why BatchNorm statistics drift under small batches or domain shift compared to LayerNorm ; diagnosing three intentionally broken PyTorch training scripts (detached graph, missing zero_grad , unscaled log(p_T) features causing NaN gradients); computational ablation study of learning-rate schedules and weight decay; exit criterion: clean convergence reproducing baseline HIGGS AUC > 0.88 with deterministic reproducibility across runs.
deliverables.readingListStructure: Core spine: Paszke et al. (2019) PyTorch paper, Kingma & Ba (2015) Adam, and Loshchilov & Hutter (2019) AdamW; advanced progression: Ioffe & Szegedy (2015) BatchNorm, Vaswani et al. (2017) attention/normalization foundations, and PyTorch official AdamW /mixed-precision documentation.

learningOutcomes: Explain PyTorch’s imperative execution model, tensor memory layouts,
and reverse-mode automatic differentiation ( autograd ).
Design stable deep architectures combining residual connections, appropriate activations (GELU/SiLU), and BatchNorm or LayerNorm layers.
Configure AdamW with decoupled weight decay, gradient clipping, and warmup + cosine-annealing learning-rate schedules.
Preprocess heavy-tailed, periodic, and variable-length HEP observables (log p T , sin ϕ, cos ϕ, impact-parameter sign-log transforms) without train/validation leakage.
Apply systematic debugging workflows (single-batch overfit tests, activation/gradient histogram checks, NaN anomaly detection, and seed determinism).
Accelerate training and evaluate throughput bottlenecks using custom Dataset / DataLoader workers and automatic mixed precision ( torch.amp ).
